+/*
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+lookup3.c, by Bob Jenkins, May 2006, Public Domain.
+
+These are functions for producing 32-bit hashes for hash table lookup.
+hashword(), hashlittle(), hashlittle2(), hashbig(), mix(), and final() 
+are externally useful functions.  Routines to test the hash are included 
+if SELF_TEST is defined.  You can use this free for any purpose.  It's in
+the public domain.  It has no warranty.
+
+You probably want to use hashlittle().  hashlittle() and hashbig()
+hash byte arrays.  hashlittle() is is faster than hashbig() on
+little-endian machines.  Intel and AMD are little-endian machines.
+On second thought, you probably want hashlittle2(), which is identical to
+hashlittle() except it returns two 32-bit hashes for the price of one.  
+You could implement hashbig2() if you wanted but I haven't bothered here.
+
+If you want to find a hash of, say, exactly 7 integers, do
+  a = i1;  b = i2;  c = i3;
+  mix(a,b,c);
+  a += i4; b += i5; c += i6;
+  mix(a,b,c);
+  a += i7;
+  final(a,b,c);
+then use c as the hash value.  If you have a variable length array of
+4-byte integers to hash, use hashword().  If you have a byte array (like
+a character string), use hashlittle().  If you have several byte arrays, or
+a mix of things, see the comments above hashlittle().  
+
+Why is this so big?  I read 12 bytes at a time into 3 4-byte integers, 
+then mix those integers.  This is fast (you can do a lot more thorough
+mixing with 12*3 instructions on 3 integers than you can with 3 instructions
+on 1 byte), but shoehorning those bytes into integers efficiently is messy.
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+*/
+
+#include <stdlib.h>
+
+#ifdef HAVE_CONFIG_H
+#include <config.h>
+#endif
+
+#ifdef HAVE_STDINT_H
+#include <stdint.h>     /* defines uint32_t etc */
+#endif
+
+#ifdef HAVE_SYS_PARAM_H
+#include <sys/param.h>  /* attempt to define endianness */
+#endif
+
+#ifdef HAVE_ENDIAN_H
+# include <endian.h>    /* attempt to define endianness */
+#endif
+
+/*
+ * My best guess at if you are big-endian or little-endian.  This may
+ * need adjustment.
+ */
+#if (defined(__BYTE_ORDER) && defined(__LITTLE_ENDIAN) && \
+     __BYTE_ORDER == __LITTLE_ENDIAN) || \
+    (defined(i386) || defined(__i386__) || defined(__i486__) || \
+     defined(__i586__) || defined(__i686__) || defined(vax) || defined(MIPSEL))
+# define HASH_LITTLE_ENDIAN 1
+# define HASH_BIG_ENDIAN 0
+#elif (defined(__BYTE_ORDER) && defined(__BIG_ENDIAN) && \
+       __BYTE_ORDER == __BIG_ENDIAN) || \
+      (defined(sparc) || defined(POWERPC) || defined(mc68000) || defined(sel))
+# define HASH_LITTLE_ENDIAN 0
+# define HASH_BIG_ENDIAN 1
+#else
+# define HASH_LITTLE_ENDIAN 0
+# define HASH_BIG_ENDIAN 0
+#endif
+
+#define hashsize(n) ((uint32_t)1<<(n))
+#define hashmask(n) (hashsize(n)-1)
+#define rot(x,k) (((x)<<(k)) | ((x)>>(32-(k))))
+
+/*
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+mix -- mix 3 32-bit values reversibly.
+
+This is reversible, so any information in (a,b,c) before mix() is
+still in (a,b,c) after mix().
+
+If four pairs of (a,b,c) inputs are run through mix(), or through
+mix() in reverse, there are at least 32 bits of the output that
+are sometimes the same for one pair and different for another pair.
+This was tested for:
+* pairs that differed by one bit, by two bits, in any combination
+  of top bits of (a,b,c), or in any combination of bottom bits of
+  (a,b,c).
+* "differ" is defined as +, -, ^, or ~^.  For + and -, I transformed
+  the output delta to a Gray code (a^(a>>1)) so a string of 1's (as
+  is commonly produced by subtraction) look like a single 1-bit
+  difference.
+* the base values were pseudorandom, all zero but one bit set, or 
+  all zero plus a counter that starts at zero.
+
+Some k values for my "a-=c; a^=rot(c,k); c+=b;" arrangement that
+satisfy this are
+    4  6  8 16 19  4
+    9 15  3 18 27 15
+   14  9  3  7 17  3
+Well, "9 15 3 18 27 15" didn't quite get 32 bits diffing
+for "differ" defined as + with a one-bit base and a two-bit delta.  I
+used http://burtleburtle.net/bob/hash/avalanche.html to choose 
+the operations, constants, and arrangements of the variables.
+
+This does not achieve avalanche.  There are input bits of (a,b,c)
+that fail to affect some output bits of (a,b,c), especially of a.  The
+most thoroughly mixed value is c, but it doesn't really even achieve
+avalanche in c.
+
+This allows some parallelism.  Read-after-writes are good at doubling
+the number of bits affected, so the goal of mixing pulls in the opposite
+direction as the goal of parallelism.  I did what I could.  Rotates
+seem to cost as much as shifts on every machine I could lay my hands
+on, and rotates are much kinder to the top and bottom bits, so I used
+rotates.
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+*/
+#define mix(a,b,c) \
+{ \
+  a -= c;  a ^= rot(c, 4);  c += b; \
+  b -= a;  b ^= rot(a, 6);  a += c; \
+  c -= b;  c ^= rot(b, 8);  b += a; \
+  a -= c;  a ^= rot(c,16);  c += b; \
+  b -= a;  b ^= rot(a,19);  a += c; \
+  c -= b;  c ^= rot(b, 4);  b += a; \
+}
+
+/*
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+final -- final mixing of 3 32-bit values (a,b,c) into c
+
+Pairs of (a,b,c) values differing in only a few bits will usually
+produce values of c that look totally different.  This was tested for
+* pairs that differed by one bit, by two bits, in any combination
+  of top bits of (a,b,c), or in any combination of bottom bits of
+  (a,b,c).
+* "differ" is defined as +, -, ^, or ~^.  For + and -, I transformed
+  the output delta to a Gray code (a^(a>>1)) so a string of 1's (as
+  is commonly produced by subtraction) look like a single 1-bit
+  difference.
+* the base values were pseudorandom, all zero but one bit set, or 
+  all zero plus a counter that starts at zero.
+
+These constants passed:
+ 14 11 25 16 4 14 24
+ 12 14 25 16 4 14 24
+and these came close:
+  4  8 15 26 3 22 24
+ 10  8 15 26 3 22 24
+ 11  8 15 26 3 22 24
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+*/
+#define final(a,b,c) \
+{ \
+  c ^= b; c -= rot(b,14); \
+  a ^= c; a -= rot(c,11); \
+  b ^= a; b -= rot(a,25); \
+  c ^= b; c -= rot(b,16); \
+  a ^= c; a -= rot(c,4);  \
+  b ^= a; b -= rot(a,14); \
+  c ^= b; c -= rot(b,24); \
+}
+
+/*
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+hashlittle() -- hash a variable-length key into a 32-bit value
+  k       : the key (the unaligned variable-length array of bytes)
+  length  : the length of the key, counting by bytes
+  initval : can be any 4-byte value
+Returns a 32-bit value.  Every bit of the key affects every bit of
+the return value.  Two keys differing by one or two bits will have
+totally different hash values.
+
+The best hash table sizes are powers of 2.  There is no need to do
+mod a prime (mod is sooo slow!).  If you need less than 32 bits,
+use a bitmask.  For example, if you need only 10 bits, do
+  h = (h & hashmask(10));
+In which case, the hash table should have hashsize(10) elements.
+
+If you are hashing n strings (uint8_t **)k, do it like this:
+  for (i=0, h=0; i<n; ++i) h = hashlittle( k[i], len[i], h);
+
+By Bob Jenkins, 2006.  bob_jenkins@burtleburtle.net.  You may use this
+code any way you wish, private, educational, or commercial.  It's free.
+
+Use for hash table lookup, or anything where one collision in 2^^32 is
+acceptable.  Do NOT use for cryptographic purposes.
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+*/
+
+static uint32_t hashlittle(const void *key, size_t length, uint32_t initval)
+{
+  uint32_t a,b,c;                                          /* internal state */
+  union { const void *ptr; size_t i; } u;     /* needed for Mac Powerbook G4 */
+
+  /* Set up the internal state */
+  a = b = c = 0xdeadbeef + ((uint32_t)length) + initval;
+
+  u.ptr = key;
+  if (HASH_LITTLE_ENDIAN && ((u.i & 0x3) == 0)) {
+    const uint32_t *k = (const uint32_t *)key;         /* read 32-bit chunks */
+
+#ifdef VALGRIND
+    const uint8_t  *k8;
+#endif
+
+    /*------ all but last block: aligned reads and affect 32 bits of (a,b,c) */
+    while (length > 12)
+    {
+      a += k[0];
+      b += k[1];
+      c += k[2];
+      mix(a,b,c);
+      length -= 12;
+      k += 3;
+    }
+
+    /*----------------------------- handle the last (probably partial) block */
+    /* 
+     * "k[2]&0xffffff" actually reads beyond the end of the string, but
+     * then masks off the part it's not allowed to read.  Because the
+     * string is aligned, the masked-off tail is in the same word as the
+     * rest of the string.  Every machine with memory protection I've seen
+     * does it on word boundaries, so is OK with this.  But VALGRIND will
+     * still catch it and complain.  The masking trick does make the hash
+     * noticably faster for short strings (like English words).
+     */
+#ifndef VALGRIND
+
+    switch(length)
+    {
+    case 12: c+=k[2]; b+=k[1]; a+=k[0]; break;
+    case 11: c+=k[2]&0xffffff; b+=k[1]; a+=k[0]; break;
+    case 10: c+=k[2]&0xffff; b+=k[1]; a+=k[0]; break;
+    case 9 : c+=k[2]&0xff; b+=k[1]; a+=k[0]; break;
+    case 8 : b+=k[1]; a+=k[0]; break;
+    case 7 : b+=k[1]&0xffffff; a+=k[0]; break;
+    case 6 : b+=k[1]&0xffff; a+=k[0]; break;
+    case 5 : b+=k[1]&0xff; a+=k[0]; break;
+    case 4 : a+=k[0]; break;
+    case 3 : a+=k[0]&0xffffff; break;

If two CPUs invoked megasas_complete_abort on the same cmd concurrently, they could race on reading and clearing sync_cmd or updating cmd_status_drv. Proper serialization (e.g. a lock held by the caller) is required to avoid lost wakeups or inconsistent status.  
   - Lack of memory barriers: Clearing the flag and then waking up the wait queue assumes the caller or the surrounding environment provides the necessary memory ordering. On weakly ordered architectures, a missing barrier could let a waiting thread see the wakeup before the field update. Usually wake_up invokes the required smp_mb().

- The function rndis_set_response handles an RNDIS “set” message from the host.  
- It first allocates a response buffer of the exact size of rndis_set_cmplt_type by calling rndis_queue_response.  
- It reads the two 32-bit little‐endian fields from the incoming message:  
  • InformationBufferOffset (offset from the start of the message header to the data to be set)  
  • InformationBufferLength (length of that data)  
- It adds 8 to the offset (per the RNDIS spec the offset field is measured from the start of the header, which itself is 8 bytes long) and stores these in bufoffs and buflen.  
- It verifies that bufoffs + buflen does not exceed the total USB transfer length. If it would exceed, it returns USB_RET_STALL to reject the request.  
- Assuming the bounds check passes, it calls ndis_set(s, OID, pointer_to_data, buflen) to apply the requested configuration.  
- It then fills in the response message fields (MessageType, RequestID, MessageLength) and sets Status to either SUCCESS or NOT_SUPPORTED depending on the return value of ndis_set.

- All subsequent accesses to the data region are bounded by the original packet length, so there is no out-of-bounds read or write on arbitrary memory.  
- The code does not perform any heap or stack writes using untrusted length fields, and the only data passed into ndis_set is from the USB packet itself.

original_information.commit_message:
crypto: aesni - fix memory usage in GCM decryption

The kernel crypto API logic requires the caller to provide the
length of (ciphertext || authentication tag) as cryptlen for the
AEAD decryption operation. Thus, the cipher implementation must
calculate the size of the plaintext output itself and cannot simply use
cryptlen.

The RFC4106 GCM decryption operation tries to overwrite cryptlen memory
in req->dst. As the destination buffer for decryption only needs to hold
the plaintext memory but cryptlen references the input buffer holding
(ciphertext || authentication tag), the assumption of the destination
buffer length in RFC4106 GCM operation leads to a too large size. This
patch simply uses the already calculated plaintext size.

In addition, this patch fixes the offset calculation of the AAD buffer
pointer: as mentioned before, cryptlen already includes the size of the
tag. Thus, the tag does not need to be added. With the addition, the AAD
will be written beyond the already allocated buffer.

Note, this fixes a kernel crash that can be triggered from user space
via AF_ALG(aead) -- simply use the libkcapi test application
from [1] and update it to use rfc4106-gcm-aes.

Using [1], the changes were tested using CAVS vectors to demonstrate
that the crypto operation still delivers the right results.

[1] http://www.chronox.de/libkcapi.html

original_information.commit_message:
ipc,shm: fix shm_file deletion races

When IPC_RMID races with other shm operations there's potential for
use-after-free of the shm object's associated file (shm_file).

Here's the race before this patch:

  TASK 1                     TASK 2
  ------                     ------
  shm_rmid()
    ipc_lock_object()
                             shmctl()
                             shp = shm_obtain_object_check()

    shm_destroy()
      shum_unlock()
      fput(shp->shm_file)
                             ipc_lock_object()
                             shmem_lock(shp->shm_file)
                             <OOPS>

The oops is caused because shm_destroy() calls fput() after dropping the
ipc_lock.  fput() clears the file's f_inode, f_path.dentry, and
f_path.mnt, which causes various NULL pointer references in task 2.  I
reliably see the oops in task 2 if with shmlock, shmu

This patch fixes the races by:
1) set shm_file=NULL in shm_destroy() while holding ipc_object_lock().
2) modify at risk operations to check shm_file while holding
   ipc_object_lock().

Example workloads, which each trigger oops...

Workload 1:
  while true; do
    id=$(shmget 1 4096)
    shm_rmid $id &
    shmlock $id &
    wait
  done

  The oops stack shows accessing NULL f_inode due to racing fput:
    _raw_spin_lock
    shmem_lock
    SyS_shmctl

Workload 2:
  while true; do
    id=$(shmget 1 4096)
    shmat $id 4096 &
    shm_rmid $id &
    wait
  done

  The oops stack is similar to workload 1 due to NULL f_inode:
    touch_atime
    shmem_mmap
    shm_mmap
    mmap_region
    do_mmap_pgoff
    do_shmat
    SyS_shmat

Workload 3:
  while true; do
    id=$(shmget 1 4096)
    shmlock $id
    shm_rmid $id &
    shmunlock $id &
    wait
  done

  The oops stack shows second fput tripping on an NULL f_inode.  The
  first fput() completed via from shm_destroy(), but a racing thread did
  a get_file() and queued this fput():
    locks_remove_flock
    __fput
    ____fput
    task_work_run
    do_notify_resume
    int_signal

ioctl(TIOCGETD) retrieves the line discipline id directly from the
ldisc because the line discipline id (c_line) in termios is untrustworthy;

- The function `setJSTestObjLongLongAttr` is a native C++ binding invoked from JavaScript.  
- Parameters:
  - `ExecState* exec`: the current JavaScript execution context.  
  - `JSObject* thisObject`: the JavaScript “this” object on which the method was called.  
  - `JSValue value`: the JavaScript argument to be converted to a C++ integer.  
- Inside the function:  
  a. `jsCast<JSTestObj*>(thisObject)` converts the generic `JSObject*` into the engine’s internal `JSTestObj*`.  
  b. `castedThis->impl()` returns a pointer (`void*` or base class) to the actual C++ implementation object, then `static_cast<TestObj*>` reinterprets it as `TestObj*`.  
  c. `value.toInteger(exec)` performs the JavaScript ToInteger conversion:  
     - If `value` is NaN → 0  
     - If it’s a finite number → truncates toward zero (floor of absolute value, re-applies sign)  
     - If it’s ±Infinity → remains ±∞  
     - Non-number types are coerced (e.g. strings → parsed number or NaN → 0).  
  d. `static_cast<long long>(...)` then casts the resulting `double` to a C++ `long long`.  
  e. The method `impl->setLongLongAttr(...)` stores or uses that `long long` in the C++ object’s internal state.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Memory Safety:  
  • All casts from `JSObject*` to `JSTestObj*` and then to `TestObj*` assume the JS engine’s internal type tags are correct. In normal engine operation, these casts are validated, so there is no raw pointer arithmetic or buffer manipulation here.  
  • There is no direct allocation, indexing, or copying of user-supplied data into fixed-size buffers.

- Integer Conversion / Overflow:  
  • The ToInteger step is well-defined for all finite doubles and NaN, producing a value within the 64-bit range of safe IEEE-754 integers (±2^53).  
  • However, if JavaScript produces ±Infinity (for example, via `1/0` or overflow in a prior calculation), `toInteger` will still return ±Infinity.  
  • Casting ±Infinity (a `double`) to `long long` with `static_cast<long long>` is UB if the `double` value lies outside the representable range of `long long`. In practice, many compilers convert out-of-range doubles to `LLONG_MAX` or `LLONG_MIN`, but the C++ standard does not guarantee that.

- Exception or Edge‐Case Handling:  
  • No explicit checks are performed to detect or clamp infinite or otherwise out-of-range values before the cast.  
  • If the engine or platform handles out-of-range double-to-integer casts benignly (clamping under the hood), the risk is low. If it triggers undefined behavior, that could lead to crashes or other unpredictable behavior.

3. Decision

No, the code does not introduce typical memory or code-injection vulnerabilities. The only potential issue is an undefined‐behavior risk when casting a JavaScript ±Infinity to `long long` without explicit clamping.

fragmentation is not used very frequently and would normally have

original_information.Summary: An issue was discovered in Open vSwitch (OvS) 2.7.x through 2.7.6, affecting parse_group_prop_ntr_selection_method in lib/ofp-util.c. When decoding a group mod, it validates the group type and command after the whole group mod has been decoded. inet: add RCU protection to inet->opt

We lack proper synchronization to manipulate inet->opt ip_options

Problem is ip_make_skb() calls ip_setup_cork() and

Add a check for disallowing remote frame navigations to local resources.

Previously, RemoteFrame navigations did not perform any renderer-side
checks and relied solely on the browser-side logic to block disallowed

original_information.Summary: An issue was discovered in Open vSwitch (OvS) 2.7.x through 2.7.6, affecting ofproto_rule_insert__ in ofproto/ofproto.c. During bundle commit, flows that are added in a bundle are applied to ofproto in order. If a flow cannot be added (e.g., the flow action is a go-to for a group id that does not exist), OvS tries to revert back all previous flows that were successfully applied from the same bundle. This is possible since OvS maintains list of old flows that were replaced by flows from the bundle. While reinserting old flows, OvS has an assertion failure due to a check on rule state != RULE_INITIALIZED. This would work for new flows, but for an old flow the rule state is RULE_REMOVED. The assertion failure causes an OvS crash.
original_information.commit_message:
ofproto: Fix OVS crash when reverting old flows in bundle commit

During bundle commit flows which are added in bundle are applied
to ofproto in-order. In case if a flow cannot be added (e.g. flow
action is go-to group id which does not exist), OVS tries to
revert back all previous flows which were successfully applied
from the same bundle. This is possible since OVS maintains list
of old flows which were replaced by flows from the bundle.

While reinserting old flows ovs asserts due to check on rule
state != RULE_INITIALIZED.  This will work only for new flows, but
for old flow the rule state will be RULE_REMOVED. This is causing
an assert and OVS crash.

The ovs assert check should be modified to != RULE_INSERTED to prevent
any existing rule being re-inserted and allow new rules and old rules
(in case of revert) to get inserted.

Here is an example to trigger the assert:

$ ovs-vsctl add-br br-test -- set Bridge br-test datapath_type=netdev

$ cat flows.txt
flow add table=1,priority=0,in_port=2,actions=NORMAL
flow add table=1,priority=0,in_port=3,actions=NORMAL

$ ovs-ofctl dump-flows -OOpenflow13 br-test
 cookie=0x0, duration=2.465s, table=1, n_packets=0, n_bytes=0, priority=0,in_port=2 actions=NORMAL
 cookie=0x0, duration=2.465s, table=1, n_packets=0, n_bytes=0, priority=0,in_port=3 actions=NORMAL

$ cat flow-modify.txt
flow modify table=1,priority=0,in_port=2,actions=drop
flow modify table=1,priority=0,in_port=3,actions=group:10

$ ovs-ofctl bundle br-test flow-modify.txt -OOpenflow13

First flow rule will be modified since it is a valid rule. However second
rule is invalid since no group with id 10 exists. Bundle commit tries to
revert (insert) the first rule to old flow which results in ovs_assert at
ofproto_rule_insert__() since old rule->state = RULE_REMOVED.

Make MediaStreamDispatcherHost per-request instead of per-frame.

Instead of having RenderFrameHost own a single MSDH to handle all
requests from a frame, MSDH objects will be owned by a strong binding.

A consequence of this is that an additional requester ID is added to
requests to MediaStreamManager, so that an MSDH is able to cancel only
requests generated by it.

In practice, MSDH will continue to be per frame in most cases since
each frame normally makes a single request for an MSDH object.

This fixes a lifetime issue caused by the IO thread executing tasks
after the RenderFrameHost dies.

original_information.commit_message:
af_netlink: force credentials passing [CVE-2012-3520]

Pablo Neira Ayuso discovered that avahi and
potentially NetworkManager accept spoofed Netlink messages because of a
kernel bug.  The kernel passes all-zero SCM_CREDENTIALS ancillary data
to the receiver if the sender did not provide such data, instead of not
including any such data at all or including the correct data from the
peer (as it is the case with AF_UNIX).

This bug was introduced in commit 16e572626961
(af_unix: dont send SCM_CREDENTIALS by default)

This patch forces passing credentials for netlink, as
before the regression.

Another fix would be to not add SCM_CREDENTIALS in
netlink messages if not provided by the sender, but it
might break some programs.

With help from Florian Weimer & Petr Matousek

This issue is designated as CVE-2012-3520

original_information.Summary: The prepare_vmcs02 function in arch/x86/kvm/vmx.c in the Linux kernel through 4.13.3 does not ensure that the *CR8-load exiting* and *CR8-store exiting* L0 vmcs02 controls exist in cases where L1 omits the *use TPR shadow* vmcs12 control, which allows KVM L2 guest OS users to obtain read and write access to the hardware CR8 register.
original_information.commit_message:
kvm: nVMX: Don't allow L2 to access the hardware CR8

If L1 does not specify the "use TPR shadow" VM-execution control in
vmcs12, then L0 must specify the "CR8-load exiting" and "CR8-store
exiting" VM-execution controls in vmcs02. Failure to do so will give
the L2 VM unrestricted read/write access to the hardware CR8.

This fixes CVE-2017-12154.

original_information.commit_message:
perf/core: Fix concurrent sys_perf_event_open() vs. 'move_group' race

Di Shen reported a race between two concurrent sys_perf_event_open()
calls where both try and move the same pre-existing software group
into a hardware context.

The problem is exactly that described in commit:

  f63a8daa5812 ("perf: Fix event->ctx locking")

... where, while we wait for a ctx->mutex acquisition, the event->ctx
relation can have changed under us.

That very same commit failed to recognise sys_perf_event_context() as an
external access vector to the events and thereby didn't apply the
established locking rules correctly.

So while one sys_perf_event_open() call is stuck waiting on
mutex_lock_double(), the other (which owns said locks) moves the group
about. So by the time the former sys_perf_event_open() acquires the
locks, the context we've acquired is stale (and possibly dead).

Apply the established locking rules as per perf_event_ctx_lock_nested()
to the mutex_lock_double() for the 'move_group' case. This obviously means
we need to validate state after we acquire the locks.

original_information.commit_message:
Btrfs: make xattr replace operations atomic

Replacing a xattr consists of doing a lookup for its existing value, delete
the current value from the respective leaf, release the search path and then
finally insert the new value. This leaves a time window where readers (getxattr,
listxattrs) won't see any value for the xattr. Xattrs are used to store ACLs,
so this has security implications.

This change also fixes 2 other existing issues which were:

*) Deleting the old xattr value without verifying first if the new xattr will
   fit in the existing leaf item (in case multiple xattrs are packed in the
   same item due to name hash collision);

*) Returning -EEXIST when the flag XATTR_CREATE is given and the xattr doesn't
   exist but we have have an existing item that packs muliple xattrs with
   the same name hash as the input xattr. In this case we should return ENOSPC.

A test case for xfstests follows soon.

Thanks to Alexandre Oliva for reporting the non-atomicity of the xattr replace
implementation.

1. Functional Analysis

   The function `smb1cli_conn_server_time_zone` takes a single argument:
   - `struct smbXcli_conn *conn` — a pointer to an SMB1 client connection context.

   Inside the function, it reads the nested field `time_zone` from:
   - `conn->smb1` — the SMB1-specific substructure of the connection
   - `.server`     — the server-related substructure
   - `.time_zone`  — an `int` holding the server’s time zone

   It then returns that integer value.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

   - Null‑pointer dereference:  
     If `conn` is ever passed in as NULL, the call to `conn->smb1.server.time_zone` will dereference NULL and cause undefined behavior. The function itself does not check for a NULL pointer.

   - Data exposure:  
     The function simply exposes an internal integer field. There is no sanitization or validation of that value, but time zone is not sensitive or user‑provided in a way that typically leads to a vulnerability.

   - Buffer overflows / memory corruption:  
     The function does no pointer arithmetic or indexing; it only reads a single field. There is no risk of buffer overflow or out‑of‑bounds access beyond the potential NULL pointer issue noted above.

   - Integer overflow / type confusion:  
     The function returns an `int`. There is no arithmetic performed, so no risk of overflow or type mismatch arises here.

3. Decision

No, the code itself contains no buffer‑overflow, format‑string, or authentication bypass vulnerabilities. The only possible flaw is a missing NULL check on its single pointer argument.

1. Functional Analysis  
- The function `jswrap_graphics_clear` is called with a pointer to a JavaScript variable (`JsVar *parent`).  
- It declares a local `JsGraphics gfx` structure.  
- It calls `graphicsGetFromVar(&gfx, parent)`: if that fails (returns false), the function returns immediately without doing anything.  
- If the graphics object was successfully extracted, it calls `graphicsClear(&gfx)`, which clears or resets the graphic’s drawing surface.  
- Finally, it calls `graphicsSetVar(&gfx)`, writing the modified `gfx` data back into the original `parent` `JsVar` to reflect the cleared state.

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
- Memory safety: There is no dynamic allocation here; `gfx` lives on the stack. All operations on it occur only after `graphicsGetFromVar` succeeds, so `gfx` is properly initialized before use.  
- Null-pointer checks: The code relies on `graphicsGetFromVar` to validate `parent` and to initialize `gfx`; there is no unchecked dereference of `parent`.  
- Boundary overflows/underflows: There is no raw buffer manipulation in this snippet.  
- Injection risks: No string or code is constructed from user input.  
- Error handling: Failures in retrieving the graphics object simply cause an early return, preventing any further operations on invalid data.

3. Decision  
No, the code does not contain vulnerabilities. It correctly guards against invalid inputs and performs its intended operations safely.

1. Functional Analysis

- The method `setTitleElement` takes two parameters: 
  - `title`: a `StringWithDirection` representing the new document title.
  - `titleElement`: a pointer to an `Element` that represents an HTML (or XML) `<title>` element in the DOM.

- On entry, it checks whether the incoming `titleElement` pointer differs from the current stored `m_titleElement`.

- If they differ:
  a. It tests whether a title element has already been set (`m_titleElement != nullptr`) or whether the title was explicitly set via some other API flag (`m_titleSetExplicitly`).  
  b. If either of those is true, it bails out immediately (`return`), leaving the existing title element in place.
  c. Otherwise, it updates the member `m_titleElement` to point to the new `titleElement`.

- After potentially updating `m_titleElement`, it calls `updateTitle(title)`, which actually applies the new string to the document’s title (e.g., updating the DOM, notifying observers, etc.).

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Memory Safety / Null Pointers  
  The code does not dereference `titleElement` before storing or comparing it. It allows a null pointer, but never uses it directly (calling `updateTitle` only on `title`, not on the element). There is no direct risk of a null-dereference in the shown snippet.

- Buffer Overflows  
  The snippet deals only with a string wrapper (`StringWithDirection`) and pointer assignments. No raw buffer manipulation or unbounded copies occur here, so there is no buffer overflow risk in this code.

- Injection / Encoding Issues  
  The code merely forwards the `title` to `updateTitle`. Any concerns around HTML injection, scripting, or directionality exploits would have to be handled inside `updateTitle`, not here. This wrapper imposes no additional vulnerabilities.

- Race Conditions / Reentrancy  
  There is no locking or thread-safety logic shown. If `Document::setTitleElement` were called concurrently on different threads, there could be a data race on `m_titleElement` or `m_titleSetExplicitly`. But in typical DOM implementations, such calls are serialized on the main thread, so this is not inherently unsafe in that usage model.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any obvious vulnerabilities. It safely checks and assigns a pointer, prevents unintentional overwrites, and delegates string handling to `updateTitle`.

original_information.commit_message:
kvm: fix kvm_ioctl_create_device() reference counting (CVE-2019-6974)

kvm_ioctl_create_device() does the following:

1. creates a device that holds a reference to the VM object (with a borrowed
   reference, the VM's refcount has not been bumped yet)
2. initializes the device
3. transfers the reference to the device to the caller's file descriptor table
4. calls kvm_get_kvm() to turn the borrowed reference to the VM into a real
   reference

The ownership transfer in step 3 must not happen before the reference to the VM
becomes a proper, non-borrowed reference, which only happens in step 4.
After step 3, an attacker can close the file descriptor and drop the borrowed
reference, which can cause the refcount of the kvm object to drop to zero.

This means that we need to grab a reference for the device before
anon_inode_getfd(), otherwise the VM can disappear from under us.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function takes three parameters:  
  • addr: the current program break address  
  • request: the requested new size for the heap  
  • flags: VM flags to apply to the new region  
- It computes len = PAGE_ALIGN(request), i.e. rounds request up to a whole number of pages.  
- If rounding overflowed (len < request), it immediately returns –ENOMEM.  
- If the rounded length is zero, it returns success (0) without doing anything.  
- It acquires the mm_struct’s write‐lock (mmap_sem) in a killable fashion; if interrupted, returns –EINTR.  
- It calls do_brk_flags(addr, len, flags, &uf) to adjust the break, collecting any userfaultfd unmap notifications into uf.  
- It records whether VM_LOCKED is set in mm->def_flags (populate).  
- It releases the write‐lock, then completes any pending userfaultfd unmap operations.  
- If VM_LOCKED was set and do_brk_flags succeeded, it calls mm_populate(addr, len) to fault in all the pages.  
- Returns the result of do_brk_flags.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Integer overflow is guarded by checking if PAGE_ALIGN overflowed (len < request).  
- Zero‐length requests are short‐circuited, avoiding needless work.  
- The mmap_sem write lock serializes concurrent brk/mmap operations, preventing race conditions in the address space layout.  
- The lock is acquired killably, so the task can be interrupted cleanly, and the code always releases the lock before returning.  
- do_brk_flags is responsible for validating addr, merging or splitting VMA as needed, and enforcing address‐space layout constraints. This wrapper does not bypass those checks.  
- userfaultfd bookkeeping is done after the lock is dropped, but that follows the kernel’s established pattern and does not expose a use‐after‐free or double‐free.  
- Page population is only done if the VM_LOCKED bit was set and if the break operation succeeded, so it cannot accidentally touch unmapped or freed memory.  

No unchecked user data dereferences, no missing locks around critical updates, no neglected error‐paths that would leak resources or corrupt VMA state.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any obvious vulnerabilities. It performs the necessary overflow checks, uses the mmap_sem correctly to serialize access, and defers to do_brk_flags for address validation.

original_information.commit_message:
coredump: fix race condition between mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm() and core dumping

The core dumping code has always run without holding the mmap_sem for
writing, despite that is the only way to ensure that the entire vma
layout will not change from under it.  Only using some signal
serialization on the processes belonging to the mm is not nearly enough.
This was pointed out earlier.  For example in Hugh's post from Jul 2017:

  https://lkml.kernel.org/r/alpine.LSU.2.11.1707191716030.2055@eggly.anvils

  "Not strictly relevant here, but a related note: I was very surprised
   to discover, only quite recently, how handle_mm_fault() may be called
   without down_read(mmap_sem) - when core dumping. That seems a
   misguided optimization to me, which would also be nice to correct"

In particular because the growsdown and growsup can move the
vm_start/vm_end the various loops the core dump does around the vma will
not be consistent if page faults can happen concurrently.

Pretty much all users calling mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm() and then
taking the mmap_sem had the potential to introduce unexpected side
effects in the core dumping code.

Adding mmap_sem for writing around the ->core_dump invocation is a
viable long term fix, but it requires removing all copy user and page
faults and to replace them with get_dump_page() for all binary formats
which is not suitable as a short term fix.

For the time being this solution manually covers the places that can
confuse the core dump either by altering the vma layout or the vma flags
while it runs.  Once ->core_dump runs under mmap_sem for writing the
function mmget_still_valid() can be dropped.

Allowing mmap_sem protected sections to run in parallel with the
coredump provides some minor parallelism advantage to the swapoff code
(which seems to be safe enough by never mangling any vma field and can
keep doing swapins in parallel to the core dumping) and to some other
corner case.

In order to facilitate the backporting I added "Fixes: 86039bd3b4e6"
however the side effect of this same race condition in /proc/pid/mem
should be reproducible since before 2.6.12-rc2 so I couldn't add any
other "Fixes:" because there's no hash beyond the git genesis commit.

Because find_extend_vma() is the only location outside of the process
context that could modify the "mm" structures under mmap_sem for
reading, by adding the mmget_still_valid() check to it, all other cases
that take the mmap_sem for reading don't need the new check after
mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm().  The expand_stack() in page fault
context also doesn't need the new check, because all tasks under core
dumping are frozen.

When opening files for write, ensure they aren't symbolic links

Issue #1048 identified that if, for example, a non privileged user
created a symbolic link from /etc/keepalvied.data to /etc/passwd,
writing to /etc/keepalived.data (which could be invoked via DBus)
would cause /etc/passwd to be overwritten.

component is a symbolic link, by setting O_NOFOLLOW whenever opening
a file for writing.

instead create a symbolic link from /home/fred/keepalived.data to
/tmp/keepalived.data, so that the file is still accessible via

since even checking if the pathname is a symbolic link prior to opening
for writing would create a race condition.

mime-actions: use file metadata for trusting desktop files

set, and don't replace the displayed icon or the displayed name until
it's trusted, which prevents for running random programs by a malicious
desktop file.

comes from a compressed file.

user acknowledges the file as trusted. This adds metadata to the file,
which cannot be added unless it has access to the computer.

original_information.Summary: The Linux kernel 4.x (starting from 4.1) and 5.x before 5.0.8 allows Information Exposure (partial kernel address disclosure), leading to a KASLR bypass. Specifically, it is possible to extract the KASLR kernel image offset using the IP ID values the kernel produces for connection-less protocols (e.g., UDP and ICMP). When such traffic is sent to multiple destination IP addresses, it is possible to obtain hash collisions (of indices to the counter array) and thereby obtain the hashing key (via enumeration). This key contains enough bits from a kernel address (of a static variable) so when the key is extracted (via enumeration), the offset of the kernel image is exposed. This attack can be carried out remotely, by the attacker forcing the target device to send UDP or ICMP (or certain other) traffic to attacker-controlled IP addresses. Forcing a server to send UDP traffic is trivial if the server is a DNS server. ICMP traffic is trivial if the server answers ICMP Echo requests (ping). For client targets, if the target visits the attacker's web page, then WebRTC or gQUIC can be used to force UDP traffic to attacker-controlled IP addresses. NOTE: this attack against KASLR became viable in 4.1 because IP ID generation was changed to have a dependency on an address associated with a network namespace.

original_information.commit_message:
When opening files for write, ensure they aren't symbolic links

Issue #1048 identified that if, for example, a non privileged user
created a symbolic link from /etc/keepalvied.data to /etc/passwd,
writing to /etc/keepalived.data (which could be invoked via DBus)
would cause /etc/passwd to be overwritten.

This commit stops keepalived writing to pathnames where the ultimate
component is a symbolic link, by setting O_NOFOLLOW whenever opening
a file for writing.

This might break some setups, where, for example, /etc/keepalived.data
was a symbolic link to /home/fred/keepalived.data. If this was the case,
instead create a symbolic link from /home/fred/keepalived.data to
/tmp/keepalived.data, so that the file is still accessible via
/home/fred/keepalived.data.

There doesn't appear to be a way around this backward incompatibility,
since even checking if the pathname is a symbolic link prior to opening
for writing would create a race condition.

This function, mov_read_close(), is the cleanup routine for the MOV/MP4 demuxer in FFmpeg. On entry it has an AVFormatContext pointer (s) whose priv_data is the MOVContext. The code proceeds through several phases:

 A. Per‐stream teardown  
   - Loop over all streams (s->streams[i]).  
   - For each MOVStreamContext (sc) in st->priv_data:  
     • Free any composition‐to‐decode timestamp (ctts) data.  
     • For each data reference entry (drefs), free the path and dir strings, then free the drefs array and reset count.  
     • If the private I/O context (sc->pb) was opened here (pb_is_copied == false), close it with ff_format_io_close().  
     • Null out sc->pb.  
     • Free all arrays holding offsets, chunk maps, sample sizes, keyframe lists, timing tables (stts, stps, elst), RAP groups, display matrix, index ranges.  
     • If extradata arrays exist, free each extradata buffer and then the array of pointers and sizes.  
     • Free any CENC (Common Encryption) auxiliary info and AES‐CTR context.  
     • Free any 3D stereo, spherical video, mastering display metadata, and collection atom data.

 B. DV demux subcontext  
   - If a DV demux context was created, free its AVFormatContext and null the pointer.

 C. Global MOV‐level metadata  
   - If meta_keys (array of strings) exists, free entries 1..meta_keys_count−1, then free the meta_keys pointer itself.  
   - Free trex_data and bitrates arrays.

 D. Fragment index cleanup  
   - For each MOVFragmentIndex pointer in fragment_index_data, free its items array and then the index struct.  
   - Free the fragment_index_data array.

 E. Other misc. arrays  
   - Free any AES decrypt context pointers and chapter_tracks array.

 Finally, return 0.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

• Memory leaks:  
  - The code calls av_freep(&mov->meta_keys) after freeing entries 1..meta_keys_count−1, but it never frees meta_keys[0] itself. That single string pointer is lost, causing a one‐string leak on close.  
  - Otherwise, every dynamically allocated array or buffer is freed via av_freep (which sets the pointer to NULL) or the appropriate free function, so there are no widespread leaks.

• Double‐free / use‐after‐free:  
  - av_freep() zeros out pointers after freeing, so repeated calls on the same pointer are safe.  
  - ff_format_io_close() is only called when sc->pb_is_copied is false, and sc->pb is nulled right afterward. There is no path that frees sc->pb twice.

• Buffer overflows or invalid indexing:  
  - All loops use their counts (nb_streams, drefs_count, stsd_count, fragment_index_count, etc.) correctly, with no out‐of‐bounds accesses.

• Other issues:  
  - All frees happen at teardown; there is no use of freed memory afterward.  
  - No security‐critical operations (parsing or copying untrusted data) take place in this function.

No, the code does not contain any security vulnerabilities. It correctly releases nearly all allocated resources (with a single minor leak of meta_keys[0]) and prevents double‐free or use‐after‐free.

original_information.Summary: GNOME Nautilus before 3.23.90 allows attackers to spoof a file type by using the .desktop file extension, as demonstrated by an attack in which a .desktop file's Name field ends in .pdf but this file's Exec field launches a malicious *sh -c* command. mime-actions: use file metadata for trusting desktop files

Currently we only trust desktop files that have the executable bit
set, and don't replace the displayed icon or the displayed name until
it's trusted, which prevents for running random programs by a malicious
desktop file.

However, the executable permission is preserved if the desktop file
comes from a compressed file.

To prevent this, add a metadata::trusted metadata to the file once the
user acknowledges the file as trusted. This adds metadata to the file,
which cannot be added unless it has access to the computer.

Also remove the SHEBANG "trusted" content we were putting inside the
desktop file, since that doesn't add more security since it can come
with the file itself.

original_information.commit_message:
cifs: ensure that uncached writes handle unmapped areas correctly

It's possible for userland to pass down an iovec via writev() that has a
bogus user pointer in it. If that happens and we're doing an uncached
write, then we can end up getting less bytes than we expect from the
call to iov_iter_copy_from_user. This is CVE-2014-0069

cifs_iovec_write isn't set up to handle that situation however. It'll
blindly keep chugging through the page array and not filling those pages
with anything useful. Worse yet, we'll later end up with a negative
number in wdata->tailsz, which will confuse the sending routines and
cause an oops at the very least.

Fix this by having the copy phase of cifs_iovec_write stop copying data
in this situation and send the last write as a short one. At the same
time, we want to avoid sending a zero-length write to the server, so
break out of the loop and set rc to -EFAULT if that happens. This also
allows us to handle the case where no address in the iovec is valid.

[Note: Marking this for stable on v3.4+ kernels, but kernels as old as
       v2.6.38 may have a similar problem and may need similar fix]

original_information.commit_message:
tcp: fix zero cwnd in tcp_cwnd_reduction

Patch 3759824da87b ("tcp: PRR uses CRB mode by default and SS mode
conditionally") introduced a bug that cwnd may become 0 when both
inflight and sndcnt are 0 (cwnd = inflight + sndcnt). This may lead
to a div-by-zero if the connection starts another cwnd reduction
phase by setting tp->prior_cwnd to the current cwnd (0) in
tcp_init_cwnd_reduction().

To prevent this we skip PRR operation when nothing is acked or
sacked. Then cwnd must be positive in all cases as long as ssthresh
is positive:

1) The proportional reduction mode
   inflight > ssthresh > 0

2) The reduction bound mode
  a) inflight == ssthresh > 0

  b) inflight < ssthresh
     sndcnt > 0 since newly_acked_sacked > 0 and inflight < ssthresh

Therefore in all cases inflight and sndcnt can not both be 0.
We check invalid tp->prior_cwnd to avoid potential div0 bugs.

In reality this bug is triggered only with a sequence of less common
events.  For example, the connection is terminating an ECN-triggered
cwnd reduction with an inflight 0, then it receives reordered/old
ACKs or DSACKs from prior transmission (which acks nothing). Or the
connection is in fast recovery stage that marks everything lost,
but fails to retransmit due to local issues, then receives data
packets from other end which acks nothing.

Fixes: 3759824da87b ("tcp: PRR uses CRB mode by default and SS mode conditionally")

  It zeroes out an array `headers[3]` (to hold NT, USN, LOCATION), sets default SSDP values (`method = –1`, default lifetime 180 s, etc.), then reads the initial token of the packet into `methodlen`. Based on that token it classifies the message as M-SEARCH, NOTIFY, or an HTTP/1.1 response (treated as a NOTIFY with NTS=ssdp:alive).

- Line‐based header parsing  
  It loops over each line, finding the end at `\r` or `\n`. For each line it:  
  • Splits at the first `:` to separate name and value.  
  • Trims leading/trailing whitespace and optional quotes.  
  • Compares the header name case‐insensitively against “NT”, “USN”, “NTS”, “LOCATION”, “CACHE-CONTROL”, and “ST”.  
  • On CACHE-CONTROL it extracts a `max-age=` field to override the default lifetime.  
  • Stores recognized header values (pointer + length) into the `headers[]` array or into `st/st_len` for search targets.

- Dispatch and action  
  It logs a debug line summarizing method, NTS, NT/ST. Then in a switch on `method`:  
  • For METHOD_NOTIFY with NTS=alive or update, if NT, USN, and LOCATION are present (and match `searched_device` if given), it calls `updateDevice(headers, now + lifetime)`.  
  • For METHOD_NOTIFY with NTS=byebye, if NT and USN are present it calls `removeDevice(headers)`.  
  • For METHOD_MSEARCH it calls `processMSEARCH(s, st, st_len, addr)`.  
  • Otherwise it logs an unknown‐method warning.  
  Finally it returns `r` (the result of update/remove).

- Bounds checking in header parsing  
  All pointer arithmetic stays within `p` … `p+n`. Lines end detection and trimming honor the `n` limit. No copying into fixed‐size stacks beyond the small `headers[3]` array.

- Format‐string and String‐print safety  
  All syslog/printf calls use `%.*s` or fixed‐length formats, so no risk of unterminated strings overrunning buffers.

- Integer handling  
  Parsing of `max-age` uses `strtoul` into an unsigned `lifetime`; no signed overflow or format string vulnerability here. An attacker could request a huge max-age but that merely extends an entry’s timeout, not memory safety.

- Header count limits  
  The code only tracks three headers (NT, USN, LOCATION) plus ST; it will ignore extras. There is no unbounded array or realloc in the parser itself.

- Out‐of‐bounds read in the SSDP‐filter memcmp  
  In the “filter if needed” step it does

  If `searched_device` is a shorter buffer than the NT header length, this could read past the end of the `searched_device` string. In practice `searched_device` is usually a constant or fully‐specified device type, so its lifetime and size are known. A prudent fix would be to compare up to `strlen(searched_device)` or ensure `searched_device` is at least as long as any advertised NT.

- Denial‐of‐service considerations  
  A malicious peer could send a very large SSDP packet or no line terminators, causing the parser to spin, but it cannot overflow the stack or heap. The worst outcome is high CPU or extended device cache lifetimes.

No, the code contains no critical buffer‐overflow or injection vulnerabilities. The only minor issue is the unchecked length passed to memcmp when filtering against `searched_device`, which can be hardened by bounding the comparison to the shorter of the two lengths.

original_information.Summary: An issue was discovered in Open vSwitch (OvS) 2.7.x through 2.7.6, affecting ofproto_rule_insert__ in ofproto/ofproto.c. During bundle commit, flows that are added in a bundle are applied to ofproto in order. If a flow cannot be added (e.g., the flow action is a go-to for a group id that does not exist), OvS tries to revert back all previous flows that were successfully applied from the same bundle. This is possible since OvS maintains list of old flows that were replaced by flows from the bundle. While reinserting old flows, OvS has an assertion failure due to a check on rule state != RULE_INITIALIZED. This would work for new flows, but for an old flow the rule state is RULE_REMOVED. The assertion failure causes an OvS crash.
original_information.commit_message:
ofproto: Fix OVS crash when reverting old flows in bundle commit

During bundle commit flows which are added in bundle are applied
to ofproto in-order. In case if a flow cannot be added (e.g. flow
action is go-to group id which does not exist), OVS tries to
revert back all previous flows which were successfully applied
from the same bundle. This is possible since OVS maintains list
of old flows which were replaced by flows from the bundle.

While reinserting old flows ovs asserts due to check on rule
state != RULE_INITIALIZED.  This will work only for new flows, but
for old flow the rule state will be RULE_REMOVED. This is causing
an assert and OVS crash.

The ovs assert check should be modified to != RULE_INSERTED to prevent
any existing rule being re-inserted and allow new rules and old rules
(in case of revert) to get inserted.

Here is an example to trigger the assert:

$ ovs-vsctl add-br br-test -- set Bridge br-test datapath_type=netdev

$ cat flows.txt
flow add table=1,priority=0,in_port=2,actions=NORMAL
flow add table=1,priority=0,in_port=3,actions=NORMAL

$ ovs-ofctl dump-flows -OOpenflow13 br-test
 cookie=0x0, duration=2.465s, table=1, n_packets=0, n_bytes=0, priority=0,in_port=2 actions=NORMAL
 cookie=0x0, duration=2.465s, table=1, n_packets=0, n_bytes=0, priority=0,in_port=3 actions=NORMAL

$ cat flow-modify.txt
flow modify table=1,priority=0,in_port=2,actions=drop
flow modify table=1,priority=0,in_port=3,actions=group:10

$ ovs-ofctl bundle br-test flow-modify.txt -OOpenflow13

First flow rule will be modified since it is a valid rule. However second
rule is invalid since no group with id 10 exists. Bundle commit tries to
revert (insert) the first rule to old flow which results in ovs_assert at
ofproto_rule_insert__() since old rule->state = RULE_REMOVED.

original_information.Summary: The WRMSR processing functionality in the KVM subsystem in the Linux kernel through 3.17.2 does not properly handle the writing of a non-canonical address to a model-specific register, which allows guest OS users to cause a denial of service (host OS crash) by leveraging guest OS privileges, related to the wrmsr_interception function in arch/x86/kvm/svm.c and the handle_wrmsr function in arch/x86/kvm/vmx.c.
original_information.commit_message:
KVM: x86: Check non-canonical addresses upon WRMSR

Upon WRMSR, the CPU should inject #GP if a non-canonical value (address) is
written to certain MSRs. The behavior is "almost" identical for AMD and Intel
(ignoring MSRs that are not implemented in either architecture since they would
anyhow #GP). However, IA32_SYSENTER_ESP and IA32_SYSENTER_EIP cause #GP if
non-canonical address is written on Intel but not on AMD (which ignores the top
32-bits).

Accordingly, this patch injects a #GP on the MSRs which behave identically on
Intel and AMD.  To eliminate the differences between the architecutres, the
value which is written to IA32_SYSENTER_ESP and IA32_SYSENTER_EIP is turned to
canonical value before writing instead of injecting a #GP.

Some references from Intel and AMD manuals:

According to Intel SDM description of WRMSR instruction #GP is expected on
WRMSR "If the source register contains a non-canonical address and ECX
specifies one of the following MSRs: IA32_DS_AREA, IA32_FS_BASE, IA32_GS_BASE,
IA32_KERNEL_GS_BASE, IA32_LSTAR, IA32_SYSENTER_EIP, IA32_SYSENTER_ESP."

According to AMD manual instruction manual:
LSTAR/CSTAR (SYSCALL): "The WRMSR instruction loads the target RIP into the
LSTAR and CSTAR registers.  If an RIP written by WRMSR is not in canonical
form, a general-protection exception (#GP) occurs."
IA32_GS_BASE and IA32_FS_BASE (WRFSBASE/WRGSBASE): "The address written to the
base field must be in canonical form or a #GP fault will occur."
IA32_KERNEL_GS_BASE (SWAPGS): "The address stored in the KernelGSbase MSR must
be in canonical form."

This patch fixes CVE-2014-3610.

1. Functional Analysis  
   - If Chromium is running in single-process mode (`run_renderer_in_process()`), it asserts that the host’s BrowserContext matches the requested one and always returns true, since all pages share one process.  
   - It rejects any host whose `BrowserContext` differs from the requested `browser_context`.  
   - It rejects hosts marked “for guests only.”  
   - It obtains the storage partition for the target `site_url` and rejects hosts not in that partition.  
   - It checks whether the process’s WebUI bindings status matches what the URL actually requires; if a mismatch occurs, it rejects the host.  
   - It queries the child‐process security policy for an origin lock on that host.  
     • If there is a lock, it only accepts the host if the lock is exactly for the same origin.  
     • If there is no lock but the host is already used and the embedder policy dictates that we should lock processes by origin, it rejects the host.  
   - Finally, after all built-in checks pass, it defers to `GetContentClient()->browser()->IsSuitableHost(host, site_url)` for any embedder-specific logic.

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Cross-site data leaks: By enforcing BrowserContext equality, storage‐partition matching, and (when configured) origin locking, the code prevents a single renderer process from being reused across contexts or partitions that shouldn’t share data.  
   - WebUI privilege escalation: By comparing whether the process already has WebUI bindings against what the URL needs, it prevents unprivileged pages ending up in a privileged WebUI process or vice versa.  
   - Origin‐lock bypass: Processes with an origin lock only host same‐origin URLs; unused processes don’t get co-opted if the policy says to lock them.  
   - Guest isolation: “Guests only” processes can’t be used for non-guest pages.  
   - Overall, each check is in place to close off a different avenue for process reuse that might leak data or privileges. No obvious gaps in these chained tests appear.

3. Decision  
   No, the code does not contain a vulnerability. It implements multiple consistent checks to ensure a renderer process is only reused when it is safe to do so.

respond_before:
1. Functional Analysis  
   - The function `get_xps_queue()` is meant to pick a transmit queue for an outgoing packet (`skb`) on a given network device `dev` when XPS (Transmit Packet Steering) is enabled.  
   - It acquires an RCU read lock to safely dereference the per-device XPS maps (`dev->xps_maps`).  
   - It looks up the map for the current CPU (`cpu_map[raw_smp_processor_id()]`).  
   - If that per-CPU map has exactly one queue, it returns that queue index.  
   - If there are multiple queues, it computes a 32-bit hash:  
     • Prefers the socket’s `sk_hash` if present; otherwise XORs the packet’s `protocol` and `rxhash`.  
     • Feeds this value into `jhash_1word()` with a random seed `hashrnd`.  
     • Uses a multiply-shift (`((u64)hash * map->len) >> 32`) to uniformly pick one of `map->len` queues.  
   - It bounds-checks the resulting queue index against `dev->real_num_tx_queues`. If out of range, it falls back to `-1`.  
   - Finally, it releases the RCU lock and returns the chosen queue index (or `-1` if none).

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - RCU synchronization protects against concurrent updates to `dev->xps_maps` and the per-CPU map, preventing use-after-free or invalid-pointer races.  
   - The hash-based queue selection uses a 64-bit multiply-and-shift technique to avoid modulo bias; overflow in the `u64` multiply is intentional and well-defined.  
   - The cast of `skb->protocol` to `u16` (via `__force u16`) then to `u32` simply truncates to the lower 16 bits—this cannot overflow unsafely.  
   - The final check ensures `queue_index` never exceeds the device’s actual number of transmit queues.  
   - No unbounded loops, no unchecked array indices beyond the final guard, and no arbitrary-pointer dereferences occur outside RCU protection.

3. Decision  
   No – the code correctly uses RCU for safe pointer access, bounds-checks its queue index, and employs a sound hash-to-index conversion. There is no evident vulnerability.

original_information.Summary: The dev_load function in net/core/dev.c in the Linux kernel before 2.6.38 allows local users to bypass an intended CAP_SYS_MODULE capability requirement and load arbitrary modules by leveraging the CAP_NET_ADMIN capability.
original_information.commit_message:
net: don't allow CAP_NET_ADMIN to load non-netdev kernel modules

Since a8f80e8ff94ecba629542d9b4b5f5a8ee3eb565c any process with
CAP_NET_ADMIN may load any module from /lib/modules/.  This doesn't mean
that CAP_NET_ADMIN is a superset of CAP_SYS_MODULE as modules are
limited to /lib/modules/**.  However, CAP_NET_ADMIN capability shouldn't
allow anybody load any module not related to networking.

This patch restricts an ability of autoloading modules to netdev modules
with explicit aliases.  This fixes CVE-2011-1019.

Arnd Bergmann suggested to leave untouched the old pre-v2.6.32 behavior
of loading netdev modules by name (without any prefix) for processes
with CAP_SYS_MODULE to maintain the compatibility with network scripts
that use autoloading netdev modules by aliases like "eth0", "wlan0".

Currently there are only three users of the feature in the upstream
kernel: ipip, ip_gre and sit.

    root@albatros:~# capsh --drop=$(seq -s, 0 11),$(seq -s, 13 34) --
    root@albatros:~# grep Cap /proc/$$/status
    CapInh:	0000000000000000
    CapPrm:	fffffff800001000
    CapEff:	fffffff800001000
    CapBnd:	fffffff800001000
    root@albatros:~# modprobe xfs
    FATAL: Error inserting xfs
    (/lib/modules/2.6.38-rc6-00001-g2bf4ca3/kernel/fs/xfs/xfs.ko): Operation not permitted
    root@albatros:~# lsmod | grep xfs
    root@albatros:~# ifconfig xfs
    xfs: error fetching interface information: Device not found
    root@albatros:~# lsmod | grep xfs
    root@albatros:~# lsmod | grep sit
    root@albatros:~# ifconfig sit
    sit: error fetching interface information: Device not found
    root@albatros:~# lsmod | grep sit
    root@albatros:~# ifconfig sit0
    sit0      Link encap:IPv6-in-IPv4
	      NOARP  MTU:1480  Metric:1

    root@albatros:~# lsmod | grep sit
    sit                    10457  0
    tunnel4                 2957  1 sit

For CAP_SYS_MODULE module loading is still relaxed:

    root@albatros:~# grep Cap /proc/$$/status
    CapInh:	0000000000000000
    CapPrm:	ffffffffffffffff
    CapEff:	ffffffffffffffff
    CapBnd:	ffffffffffffffff
    root@albatros:~# ifconfig xfs
    xfs: error fetching interface information: Device not found
    root@albatros:~# lsmod | grep xfs
    xfs                   745319  0

1. Functional Analysis

- The function `rt_cache_seq_open` is defined as a `static int` and takes two parameters: a pointer to an `inode` and a pointer to a `file`.
- Inside the function, it calls the kernel helper `seq_open`, passing it the `file` pointer and the address of a `seq_operations` structure named `rt_cache_seq_ops`.
- The return value of `seq_open` (0 on success, negative error code on failure) is returned directly by `rt_cache_seq_open`.
- In effect, this function serves as the `.open` callback for a seq‑file–based procfs or debugfs entry. It initializes and associates the `seq_file` state with the file descriptor so that subsequent reads iterate via the `rt_cache_seq_ops` callbacks.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Memory Safety  
  - The code itself merely calls the well‑tested kernel helper `seq_open`. It does not perform any manual pointer arithmetic or unbounded buffer operations.
  - Any allocations or initializations are handled internally by `seq_open`. There is no direct heap or stack overflow risk in this wrapper.
- Input Validation / Access Control  
  - This function does not inspect or validate user input; it simply establishes a seq_file context. Any permission checks (mode bits, uid/gid) would have occurred before invoking the `.open` callback.
- Race Conditions  
  - No global or shared state is modified here. `seq_open` will set up per‑file instance state; concurrency control is managed by the seq‑file infrastructure.
- Resource Leaks  
  - On failure, `seq_open` will return a negative code, and no resources are left hanging by this wrapper. On success, the kernel’s seq_file cleanup code will release resources when the file is closed.
- Other Kernel‑Specific Concerns  
  - There is no use of `copy_from_user`, `copy_to_user`, string operations, or arithmetic on user‑supplied values.  
  - The function follows the conventional pattern for seq‑file open handlers and aligns with common kernel examples.

3. Decision

No, this code does not contain any obvious vulnerabilities. It is a thin, standard wrapper around the safe, built‑in `seq_open` mechanism.

original_information.Summary: The IPv4 implementation in the Linux kernel before 3.18.8 does not properly consider the length of the Read-Copy Update (RCU) grace period for redirecting lookups in the absence of caching, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption or system crash) via a flood of packets.
original_information.commit_message:
ipv4: try to cache dst_entries which would cause a redirect

Not caching dst_entries which cause redirects could be exploited by hosts
on the same subnet, causing a severe DoS attack. This effect aggravated
since commit f88649721268999 ("ipv4: fix dst race in sk_dst_get()").

Lookups causing redirects will be allocated with DST_NOCACHE set which
will force dst_release to free them via RCU.  Unfortunately waiting for
RCU grace period just takes too long, we can end up with >1M dst_entries
waiting to be released and the system will run OOM. rcuos threads cannot
catch up under high softirq load.

Attaching the flag to emit a redirect later on to the specific skb allows
us to cache those dst_entries thus reducing the pressure on allocation
and deallocation.

This issue was discovered by Marcelo Leitner.

Cc: Julian Anastasov <ja@ssi.bg>
Signed-off-by: Marcelo Leitner <mleitner@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Hannes Frederic Sowa <hannes@stressinduktion.org>
Signed-off-by: Julian Anastasov <ja@ssi.bg>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>

1. Functional Analysis  
   - The function em_sysexit handles the emulation of a SYSENTER/SYSEXIT sequence in an x86 context.  
   - It begins by checking if the CPU is in real mode or VM86 mode; if so, it injects a #GP exception and bails out.  
   - It then fetches the default code (CS) and stack (SS) segment descriptors via setup_syscalls_segments.  
   - Based on the REX.W prefix bit, it determines whether the return should use 32‑bit protected mode (PROT32) or 64‑bit protected mode (PROT64).  
   - It reads the user’s RCX (new user stack pointer) and RDX (new user instruction pointer) registers.  
   - It forces the DPL of both CS and SS descriptors to 3 (user privilege).  
   - It retrieves the SYSENTER_CS MSR (model‑specific register) to compute the user CS and SS selectors:  
     • In PROT32, it offsets the MSR value by +16 for CS and +24 for SS, truncates RCX/RDX to 32‑bit, and validates the MSR base.  
     • In PROT64, it offsets by +32 for CS, sets SS = CS+8, marks CS as a 64‑bit code segment, and checks that RCX/RDX are canonical addresses.  
   - It ORs in the RPL mask (to ensure CPL=3), installs the new CS/SS descriptors via ops->set_segment,  
     writes RDX into the instruction pointer (EIP/RIP), and writes RCX into RSP.  
   - Finally, it returns X86EMUL_CONTINUE to indicate successful emulation.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Argument validation: the code explicitly rejects real/VM86 modes by raising #GP.  
   - MSR checks:  
     • In PROT32 it ensures (msr_data & 0xfffc) ≠ 0 before proceeding.  
     • In PROT64 it requires msr_data ≠ 0.  
   - Address checks: in 64‑bit mode, it disallows non‑canonical user addresses for RCX/RDX.  
   - Selector computation: offsets are small constants added to an MSR‑fetched base. These cannot overflow into an attacker‑controlled region—SYSENTER_CS is privileged state.  
   - Segment DPL and RPL masking ensure the target CPL is user (3).

original_information.commit_message:
Fix up non-directory creation in SGID directories

sgid directories have special semantics, making newly created files in
the directory belong to the group of the directory, and newly created
subdirectories will also become sgid.  This is historically used for
group-shared directories.

But group directories writable by non-group members should not imply
that such non-group members can magically join the group, so make sure
to clear the sgid bit on non-directories for non-members (but remember
that sgid without group execute means "mandatory locking", just to
confuse things even more).

ALSA: pcm : Call kill_fasync() in stream lock

Currently kill_fasync() is called outside the stream lock in
snd_pcm_period_elapsed().  This is potentially racy, since the stream
may get released even during the irq handler is running.  Although
snd_pcm_release_substream() calls snd_pcm_drop(), this doesn't
guarantee that the irq handler finishes, thus the kill_fasync() call
outside the stream spin lock may be invoked after the substream is
detached, as recently reported by KASAN.

lock.  The fasync is rarely used interface, so this shouldn't have a
big impact from the performance POV.

Ideally, we should implement some sync mechanism for the proper finish
of stream and irq handler.  But this oneliner should suffice for most
cases, so far.

convert the extent to initialized after io completes.

initialized after it has been written with new data so
we can safely drop the i_mutex lock in ext4 DIO read without
exposing stale data. This helps to improve multi-thread DIO
read performance on high-speed disks.

1. Functional Analysis  
   - The function read_object_list_from_stdin reads lines one by one from standard input into a fixed-size buffer `line`.  
   - On EOF it breaks out; on an interrupted syscall (errno == EINTR) it clears the error and retries; other errors are fatal.  
   - For each line:  
     - If it begins with ‘-’, it parses the next 40 characters as a SHA-1 hex string via `get_sha1_hex`, then calls `add_preferred_base(sha1)` and continues to the next line.  
     - Otherwise it treats the first 40 characters of the line as a SHA-1 hex string, calls `get_sha1_hex` on them, and on success:  
       • Calls `add_preferred_base_object(line+41)`  
       • Calls `add_object_entry(sha1, 0, line+41, 0)`  
   - If any `get_sha1_hex` invocation fails (invalid hex or wrong length), or any unexpected I/O error occurs, the code calls `die()` (aborting the program with an error message).

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Buffer overflow: The code uses `fgets(line, sizeof(line), stdin)`, so it will read at most `sizeof(line)-1` characters plus null terminator. There is no unbounded strcpy/strcat or index beyond the buffer size.  
   - SHA-1 parsing: `get_sha1_hex` is passed exactly 40 chars (or fewer if the line is malformed), and on failure it aborts. The code never proceeds with malformed hashes.  
   - Path handling: The code passes the substring `line+41` directly to object-registration functions without stripping a trailing newline. That can lead to object names or paths containing embedded newline characters, but does not by itself create a memory safety issue.  
   - Error handling: EOF, normal errors, and EINTR are handled explicitly; no infinite loop or use-after-error occurs.  
   - Stack usage: `line` is allocated statically on the stack; for typical PATH_MAX values this is a few kilobytes but not uncontrolled.  
   - There is no evidence of injection (the code never invokes a shell), no format‐string calls on user input, and no arithmetic on the parsed data that could overflow.  

3. Decision  
   No—the code does not contain any obvious memory-safety or I/O-handling vulnerabilities under normal constraints.

original_information.commit_message:
list-objects: pass full pathname to callbacks

When we find a blob at "a/b/c", we currently pass this to
our show_object_fn callbacks as two components: "a/b/" and
"c". Callbacks which want the full value then call
path_name(), which concatenates the two. But this is an
inefficient interface; the path is a strbuf, and we could
simply append "c" to it temporarily, then roll back the
length, without creating a new copy.

So we could improve this by teaching the callsites of
path_name() this trick (and there are only 3). But we can
also notice that no callback actually cares about the
broken-down representation, and simply pass each callback
the full path "a/b/c" as a string. The callback code becomes
even simpler, then, as we do not have to worry about freeing
an allocated buffer, nor rolling back our modification to
the strbuf.

This is theoretically less efficient, as some callbacks
would not bother to format the final path component. But in
practice this is not measurable. Since we use the same
strbuf over and over, our work to grow it is amortized, and
we really only pay to memcpy a few bytes.

Signed-off-by: Jeff King <peff@peff.net>
Signed-off-by: Junio C Hamano <gitster@pobox.com>

1. Functional Analysis

   The function MountDevice performs the following steps:

   a. Drive‐Letter Validation  
      – Checks that the requested DOS drive number (0–25 for A:–Z:) is within range.  
      – Calls IsDriveLetterAvailable in both the default and global device namespaces to ensure the letter is not already in use.  
      – On failure, sets mount->nReturnCode to ERR_DRIVE_NOT_FOUND and returns that error.

   b. Self‐Test Enforcement  
      – Verifies that built‐in self‐tests have passed (SelfTestsPassed).  
      – If they have not, returns ERR_SELF_TESTS_FAILED.

   c. Device Object Creation  
      – Calls TCCreateDeviceObject to create a new device object and associated extension.  
      – On failure, logs the NTSTATUS and returns it.

   d. Security Token Capture  
      – Captures the caller’s security subject context and locks it.  
      – Chooses the impersonation token if present with at least SecurityImpersonation level, otherwise the primary token.  
      – Calls SeQueryInformationToken(TokenUser) to obtain the SID of the user and allocates NewExtension->UserSid to store a copy via RtlCopySid.  
      – Frees the temporary token information and releases the subject context.

   e. Volume‐Thread Startup  
      – Calls TCStartVolumeThread to begin background I/O for the volume.  
      – On failure, deletes the device object and returns the error.

   f. Post‐Thread Initialization (on success)  
      – Checks mount->nReturnCode (from the thread) for any volume‐specific errors.  
      – If still zero:  
         • Propagates the read‐only flag into the device characteristics.  
         • Marks the device no longer initializing.  
         • Assigns a UniqueVolumeId.  
         • Re‐validates the drive‐letter availability and aborts on a race if already taken.  
         • Optionally registers with the Mount Manager.  
         • Creates the DOS‐drive symbolic link.  
         • Opens the file‐system volume and issues FSCTL_IS_VOLUME_DIRTY to detect a dirty file system, and FSCTL_GET_NTFS_VOLUME_DATA to detect NTFS.  
         • Records dirty bit and NTFS flag in both the extension and mount struct.  
         • If a volume label was requested, truncates it to 32 WCHAR for NTFS or 11 for FAT, zero‐pads the in‐memory buffer, copies it back to mount->wszLabel, and calls ZwSetVolumeInformationFile to apply it.  
         • Closes the volume handle and returns STATUS_SUCCESS.  
      – On nonzero mount->nReturnCode, deletes the device object and returns STATUS_SUCCESS anyway (mount‐specific error communicated via mount->nReturnCode).

2. Vulnerability Analysis

   – TOCTOU on Drive‐Letter Checks  
     The code checks availability twice (once before creating the device, once after the volume thread starts) to reduce a race—but it is still subject to a small window in which another mount could claim the letter.  
     Mitigation: the second check aborts if the letter is gone, but there remains a brief period after the second check during which the letter could be stolen before CreateDriveLink is called.  
     Severity: Low risk in typical driver scenarios; would require a malicious driver racing at high IRQL.

   – Memory‐Allocation & Cleanup  
     • UserSid allocation: if TCStartVolumeThread succeeds but a later step fails, there is no explicit free of NewExtension->UserSid before deleting the device. This can leak memory until device detach.  
     • TokenUser buffer is freed correctly.  
     • LabelInfo is freed.  
     Severity: Low (device‐lifetime leaks only).

   – Buffer Size Assumptions for Labels  
     The code zeroes and memcpy’s up to 33 WCHAR (66 bytes) into NewExtension->wszLabel and mount->wszLabel. If either buffer is allocated or declared smaller than 33 WCHAR + terminator, this could overflow.  
     Mitigation: Presumably both arrays are dimensioned at 33 WCHAR (0–32 plus NUL). If not, this is a potential buffer overflow.  
     Severity: Medium if the external declaration is smaller; otherwise none.

   – Exception Handlers around FSCTL Calls  
     The __try/__except guards protect against filesystem‐side faults. No vulnerability here.

   – Security Context Handling  
     The code properly captures the impersonation or primary token and does not enable needless privileges. No elevation‐of‐privilege issues are evident.

   – General Resource Management  
     The code checks all major NTSTATUS returns and performs cleanup on failure (device deletion). Aside from the noted SID‐buffer leak, resource handling is disciplined.

3. Decision

   No, the code does not contain any critical vulnerabilities. It exhibits only a minor TOCTOU race on drive‐letter assignment and a potential memory‐leak of the UserSid allocation, both of which are low‐risk in this driver context.

- The function `set_one_prio(struct task_struct *p, int niceval, int error)` attempts to change the “nice” value (scheduling priority) of task `p`.  
- It first calls `set_one_prio_perm(p)`, which checks whether the caller has basic permission to adjust any priority at all.

- Next, if the new nice value represents a “higher priority” (a lower numeric nice) than the task’s current nice, it calls `can_nice(p, niceval)` to see if the caller may raise the task’s priority. On failure it sets `error = -EACCES` and returns.

   The function `decode_modrm` interprets the ModR/M and (optionally) SIB bytes of an x86 instruction to determine whether an operand refers to a register or memory, and if memory, to compute the effective address (EA).  The major steps are:

   a. Handle REX prefix (64‑bit extended registers)  
      - If `ctxt->rex_prefix` is set, extract REX.R (for the ModR/M.reg field), REX.X (for SIB index), and REX.B (for ModR/M.rm or SIB base).  
      - Initialize `index_reg` and `base_reg` with the high bits from the REX prefix.

   b. Fetch and split the ModR/M byte  
      - Read one byte (`insn_fetch(u8, ctxt)`).  
      - Extract `mod` (top two bits), `reg` (middle three bits), and `rm` (low three bits).  
      - Combine with any high bits from REX to form full register indices.  
      - Default the segment for memory operands to DS.

   c. Register operand case (`mod == 3`)  
      - Set `op->type = OP_REG` (or `OP_XMM` if an SSE register).  
      - Determine byte-width (`1` or full operand size) and read the register value into the operand.

   d. Memory operand case (`mod != 3`)  
      - Set `op->type = OP_MEM`.  
      - Distinguish 16‑bit addressing mode (`ctxt->ad_bytes == 2`) versus 32/64‑bit.  

      • 16‑bit mode:  
         – Possibly fetch a displacement of size 0, 1, or 2 bytes depending on `mod`.  
         – Select one of the eight address formulas using registers BX, BP, SI, DI.  
         – Sign‑extend or zero‑extend the final 16‑bit EA.  
         – Switch to SS segment if BP is used as a base.

All arithmetic on `modrm_ea` is either on unsigned types or explicit sign‑extensions on small displacements.
