- The function PSDPackbitsEncodeImage takes an image descriptor, a pixel count length, an input byte stream pixels, and an output buffer compact_pixels. It encodes the input according to the PackBits run‐length scheme and returns the number of bytes written.
- It begins by asserting its inputs, logging if requested, and allocating a small temporary buffer packbits (128 bytes) for building literal runs.
- A write‐pointer q is set to the start of the output buffer. A loop runs until all length bytes are consumed, dispatching on the remaining byte‐count i:
  - For i=1,2,3 it handles these short tails explicitly (either as literal sequences or a short replicate run).
  - For i≥4 it tests whether the next three bytes are identical.  
    – If so, it does a “packed run”: it extends as far as the same byte repeats (up to 127 bytes), writes a single-length marker byte `(256-count+1)` and the repeated value.  
    – Otherwise it builds a “literal run”: it copies up to 128 non-repeating bytes into the packbits buffer, then writes a length marker `(count-1)` followed by those bytes.
- After all input is consumed, it writes an end‐of‐data marker (128) to q, frees the temporary buffer, and returns the number of bytes written (q - compact_pixels).

  – Allocated to 128 bytes.  
  – The literal‐run loop writes packbits[count+1] only while count<127, so the highest index written is packbits[127].  
  – Later it sets packbits[0] and reads indices 0..count inclusive (≤127). No out-of-bounds on that temporary buffer.
- Input‐pointer arithmetic:  
  – The code reads up to pixels+count+2 inside the loop. Because the switch handles length<4 separately, when i≥4 it is guaranteed that reading +2 stays within the original `length` bounds.
- Output‐buffer growth:  
  – The code does not itself check that `compact_pixels` has enough capacity. In normal use the caller allocates an appropriate worst-case size (roughly length+length/127+1). If the caller provides too small a buffer, a write overflow could occur—but that is a precondition violation, not an internal bug.
- Integer conversion:  
  – `length` is size_t and is cast to `ssize_t i`. If `length` exceeds `SSIZE_MAX`, `i` could become negative or wrap; in practice MagickCore ensures image row sizes fit in signed types, so no realistic overflow.

No, the function correctly bounds its temporary buffer and logically advances through the input. Under its intended preconditions (caller‐allocated output buffer large enough and length ≤ SSIZE_MAX) it contains no exploitable vulnerabilities.

1. Functional Analysis

- Signature & setup  
  The function yurex_write handles writes from user space to a USB device. It takes a file pointer, a user buffer, a byte count, and a file position pointer. It declares a small stack buffer (16 bytes), a device pointer, some integer flags and counters, and a kernel wait structure.

- Truncate input length  
  It clamps the requested write size (`count`) to at most 16 bytes (the size of the stack buffer) to prevent over‐reading beyond `buffer`.

- Early exits  
  If `count` is zero, it jumps to the error path and returns. It then grabs the device context from `file->private_data`.

- Mutex & disconnect check  
  It locks `dev->io_mutex` to serialize I/O. If the underlying USB interface is gone (`dev->interface == NULL`), it unlocks, sets `retval = -ENODEV`, and bails out.

- Copy from user  
  It copies up to `count` bytes from user space into the stack buffer. On error, it unlocks and returns `-EFAULT`.

- Prepare control message  
  It first fills the device’s control buffer (`dev->cntl_buffer`) entirely with a padding byte. It then inspects `buffer[0]` to decide which command to send:  
    • CMD_ANIMATE and CMD_LED take a 1‑byte argument in `buffer[1]`.  
    • CMD_READ and CMD_VERSION take no argument (zero).  
    • CMD_SET or a digit prefix triggers parsing of an unsigned 64‑bit value via `simple_strtoull`, which is broken into five bytes and placed into slots 1–5 of the control buffer.  

- Submit URB and wait  
  It enqueues a kernel wait entry, submits the control URB to the USB core, and sleeps with a timeout (`YUREX_WRITE_TIMEOUT`). After waking, it cleans up the wait entry and unlocks the mutex.

- Finalize  
  If the USB submission failed, it logs and returns an error. If it was a “set” command and the sleep did not time out, it updates `dev->bbu` with the parsed value. Finally, it returns the number of bytes written (`count`) if the operation completed in time, or `-EIO` on timeout.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Buffer bounds  
  The code clamps `count` to `sizeof(buffer)` (16) before `copy_from_user`, preventing stack overflow on `buffer`.

- Uninitialized-byte use  
  In the cases CMD_ANIMATE and CMD_LED, the code blindly reads `buffer[1]` even if `count` was only 1. If the user passes a single‐byte write, `buffer[1]` remains uninitialized stack data, which then gets sent to the device. This is not a host memory corruption, but it can lead to unpredictable commands being issued to the device.

- Missing EOF for SET path  
  In the CMD_SET path, the code sets `buffer[6] = CMD_EOF` rather than `dev->cntl_buffer[6]`. As a result, the EOF marker may never be written into the control buffer. The device sees whatever padding was placed there. This is a logic bug but not a host‐side buffer overflow.

- Race and locking  
  The I/O mutex protects submissions and the disconnect check from races. The wait queue usage is paired correctly (`prepare_to_wait` / `finish_wait`), so there’s no sleep‐in‐atomic or deadlock scenario in normal use.

- Integer parsing  
  `simple_strtoull` returns zero on invalid input. An attacker can only cause the code to send zero or a truncated integer. There is no signed‐integer overflow risk on the kernel side.

3. Decision

No, the code contains no outright buffer‐overflow or use‐after‐free vulnerabilities. It does have a minor logic bug (uninitialized byte read for 1‐byte commands) and a misplaced EOF assignment, but no exploitable memory‐corruption issues.

original_information.Summary: An issue was discovered in yurex_read in drivers/usb/misc/yurex.c in the Linux kernel before 4.17.7. Local attackers could use user access read/writes with incorrect bounds checking in the yurex USB driver to crash the kernel or potentially escalate privileges.
original_information.commit_message:
USB: yurex: fix out-of-bounds uaccess in read handler

In general, accessing userspace memory beyond the length of the supplied
buffer in VFS read/write handlers can lead to both kernel memory corruption
(via kernel_read()/kernel_write(), which can e.g. be triggered via
sys_splice()) and privilege escalation inside userspace.

Fix it by using simple_read_from_buffer() instead of custom logic.

Fixes: 6bc235a2e24a ("USB: add driver for Meywa-Denki & Kayac YUREX")

  - The function’s goal is to reduce (“shrink”) the number of free pages cached in blkif->free_pages down to at most num.  
  - It maintains a small stack-allocated array page[NUM_BATCH_FREE_PAGES] to collect pages in batches.  
  - It acquires blkif->free_pages_lock (with irq‐save) and then loops as long as free_pages_num > num:  
    • Assert that the list is not empty.  
    • Pull the first page off the list, decrement free_pages_num, and stash the page pointer in the array.  
    • Whenever the batch array fills (num_pages == NUM_BATCH_FREE_PAGES), it drops the lock, calls free_xenballooned_pages() on that batch, re-acquires the lock, and resets the batch count.

  - Concurrency: The list and counter are always protected by the spinlock; the lock is dropped only around the external free_xenballooned_pages() call, which is intended.

- Use-after-free

original_information.commit_message:
fix autofs/afs/etc. magic mountpoint breakage

We end up trying to kfree() nd.last.name on open("/mnt/tmp", O_CREAT)
if /mnt/tmp is an autofs direct mount.  The reason is that nd.last_type
is bogus here; we want LAST_BIND for everything of that kind and we
get LAST_NORM left over from finding parent directory.

So make sure that it *is* set properly; set to LAST_BIND before
doing ->follow_link() - for normal symlinks it will be changed
by __vfs_follow_link() and everything else needs it set that way.

Signed-off-by: Al Viro <viro@zeniv.linux.org.uk>

original_information.commit_message:
Sched: fix skip_clock_update optimization

idle_balance() drops/retakes rq->lock, leaving the previous task
vulnerable to set_tsk_need_resched().  Clear it after we return
from balancing instead, and in setup_thread_stack() as well, so
no successfully descheduled or never scheduled task has it set.

Need resched confused the skip_clock_update logic, which assumes
that the next call to update_rq_clock() will come nearly immediately
after being set.  Make the optimization robust against the waking
a sleeper before it sucessfully deschedules case by checking that
the current task has not been dequeued before setting the flag,
since it is that useless clock update we're trying to save, and
clear unconditionally in schedule() proper instead of conditionally
in put_prev_task().

- The function `oidc_check_userid_openidc` enforces OpenID Connect authentication for an incoming Apache request.
- It first verifies that a Redirect URI is configured; if not, it logs an error and returns an internal server error.
- It then distinguishes between “initial” requests and sub-requests.
  - Initial requests:
    - A session is loaded (or created empty if none exists).
    - If the request URL matches the configured Redirect URI, the code delegates to `oidc_handle_redirect_uri_request`, which typically processes the OIDC authorization response (or a logout callback).
    - Otherwise, if `session->remote_user` is already set, the code invokes `oidc_handle_existing_session` to apply the existing authentication to the request.
    - If neither condition holds, the code lets the request fall through to the unauthenticated handler.
    - In all initial‐request branches it frees the `session` structure before returning.
  - Sub-requests:
    - The handler tries to recycle the `r->user` value from the main or previous request.
    - If a user is found, it verifies whether ID token or claims are present in the request state. If not, it reloads them from session storage and copies them into the request state.
    - It then returns `OK`, inheriting all authentication headers and cookies stripping logic already applied by the parent request.
    - If no user context exists, it defers to the unauthenticated handler.

- Authentication Enforcement: The code ensures that only requests with a valid OIDC session or valid redirect‐URI response are treated as authenticated. All other requests are explicitly routed to the unauthenticated handler.
- Open Redirects: The only redirect‐URI comparison is against a statically configured value returned by `oidc_get_redirect_uri`. As long as that configuration value is set correctly, there is no arbitrary redirect target derived from user input.
- Session Fixation / Hijacking: The snippet loads and frees sessions in a controlled manner but does not itself manage session identifiers. We assume that the underlying session store and `oidc_handle_redirect_uri_request` properly regenerate or validate session IDs on login.
- CSRF / State Parameter: The code delegates all redirect‐URI processing to `oidc_handle_redirect_uri_request`, which in a correct OIDC flow will validate the `state` parameter. There is no direct CSRF vector exposed here.
- Injection / XSS: There is no concatenation of request data into SQL, HTML, or shell commands. Error messages and debug logs use statically defined strings or pre‐validated configuration.

- The code does rely on helper functions (e.g., `oidc_util_request_matches_url`, session loaders, handlers) being implemented securely, but within this snippet there is no apparent insecure trust of user input or bypass of authentication checks.

No,[The code cleanly enforces OpenID Connect authentication, delegates security‐critical checks (state validation, token management, session handling) to well‐defined helper routines, and does not itself introduce redirects or injections from user‐supplied data.]

1. Functional Analysis

- The code begins by extracting the IPv6 Differentiated Services field (DS field) from the incoming IPv6 header (`ipv6h`) via `ipv6_get_dsfield(ipv6h)` and then masks out the ECN bits (`& ~INET_ECN_MASK`), leaving only the DSCP portion in the local variable `dsfield`.  
- If the tunnel parameters (`t->parms.flags`) include the flag `IP6_TNL_F_RCV_DSCP_COPY`, it calls `ipv4_change_dsfield()` on the decapsulated IPv4 header (`ip_hdr(skb)`).  In that call:  
  • The first argument, `INET_ECN_MASK`, specifies which bits of the original IPv4 TOS (the two ECN bits) to preserve.  
  • The second argument, `dsfield` (masked DSCP from IPv6) is OR‑ed into the IPv4 TOS field’s upper 6 bits, thus copying the IPv6 DSCP into IPv4 while preserving any pre‑existing IPv4 ECN bits.  
- Finally, it checks whether the reconstructed `dsfield` indicates an ECN Congestion Experienced (CE) codepoint via `INET_ECN_is_ce(dsfield)`.  If so, it explicitly marks the IPv4 header as CE by calling `IP_ECN_set_ce(ip_hdr(skb))`.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Memory safety: All operations use well‑defined kernel helpers on valid pointers (`ipv6h`, `skb`, `ip_hdr(skb)`).  There is no unbounded copy, no pointer arithmetic on user data, nor any indexing that could overflow or underflow.  
- Integer arithmetic: The bitwise masks operate on a one‑byte field (`__u8`); there is no overflow or signedness issue.  
- Logical correctness:  
  - DSCP extraction and injection are done via standard masks and kernel helpers, preserving ECN bits correctly when `RCV_DSCP_COPY` is set.  
  - The separate ECN‑flag check uses the same masked `dsfield`, but because the code zeroes out ECN bits before testing, the CE test will never succeed.  This is a logic bug (it never propagates CE from the IPv6 header), but it does not introduce a memory corruption or privilege escalation vulnerability.  
- Race conditions: There is no shared mutable state in this snippet outside the skb/TNL context, and standard locking conventions of the networking stack apply. No new race is introduced here.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain a memory‑safety or control‑flow vulnerability. It does have a logic issue in that the ECN‑CE test is performed on a value whose ECN bits were explicitly cleared, but this is a correctness bug, not a security vulnerability.

original_information.Summary: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 4.17.2. 1. Functional Analysis

The function jpc_dec_tileinit initializes decoding structures for a single JPEG-2000 tile. In broad strokes it does the following:

• Determine “real” (integer) vs. “irreversible” (floating) transform mode  
• Loop over each component in the tile:  
  – Read component parameters (number of resolution levels, quantization, precinct size exponents, code-block size exponents, etc.)  
  – Allocate and initialize the component’s resolution‐level array  
  – Create a 2D sample‐buffer for the tile component, sized to the tile’s image‐space bounds divided by the component sampling factors  
  – Fetch the transform‐filter‐bank object (tsfb) and derive subband information (x/y starts and ends, orientations, step‐sizes)  
  – For each resolution level:  
    · Compute the RL’s image‐space bounds by subsampling up or down  
    · Compute precinct grid parameters: exponent, tile‐aligned starts/ends, number of precincts horizontally/vertically  
    · If this RL actually covers any area, compute code‐block grid parameters at either the same or half‐sample resolution (depending on RL)  
    · Allocate and initialize the array of subbands (1 for LL at RL 0, 3 for HL/LH/HH otherwise)  
    · For each subband:  
      – Record orientation, quantization step size, analysis gain, derived bit‐shift parameters, ROI shift  
      – Create a 2D view into the component’s sample buffer for just that subband’s spatial region  
      – Allocate an array of precincts (prcs)  
      – For each precinct:  
        * Compute the precinct’s actual x/y bounds clipped to the subband’s extents  
        * If non‐empty, compute code‐block grid parameters within that precinct  
        * Allocate tag trees for inclusion bits and MSB-start bits  
        * Allocate an array of code-block structures  
        * For each code-block tile:  
         – Compute block‐limited bounds (clipped to precinct & subband)  
         – Allocate a tiny 2D image buffer for the block, and bind it to the subband’s buffer  
• After all components are set up, create a packet‐iterator (pi) for tile‐packet construction, apply progression‐changes (pchg) and initialize it  

Throughout, most allocations are followed by a null‐check, returning an error on failure. Many loops use explicit counters and shifts but always clip to valid ranges via max/min or div/ceil macros.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis

After careful inspection, there is no obvious memory‐safety or bounds‐checking flaw:  
 • All dynamic allocations (arrays of resolution‐levels, bands, precincts, code‐blocks, tag‐trees, 2D buffers) are null‐checked.  
 • All subband and precinct extents are clipped with JAS_MAX/JAS_MIN against their parent buffers, preventing out‐of‐bounds binding.  
 • Loop counters for precincts and code‐blocks are derived from clipped, non‐negative dimensions—asserted nonzero where required.  
 • There are no divisions by run‐time parameters that could be zero, nor unchecked array indexing.  
 • Shifts (1 << exponent) use exponents drawn from the codestream header; these are bounded by JPEG-2000 limits and used only to size grids, then immediately clipped.  
 • No raw pointer arithmetic appears to escape its allocated bounds.  
 • Error paths return immediately but do not free earlier allocations—this is a resource leak, not a memory‐corruption or code‐execution vulnerability.  

Given these checks, the code does not exhibit buffer overflows, integer underflows, divides by zero, or use‐after‐free. Standard JPEG-2000–sized images will not cause integer wrap or negative sizes in this logic.  

3. Decision

No, the code does not appear to contain exploitable vulnerabilities. It includes thorough bounds clipping and checks every allocation.

   c. It then builds an SCTP_ASSOC_CHANGE event with cause SCTP_COMM_LOST and the supplied error code; if the triggering chunk was an ABORT, it attaches that chunk to the event.

   e. If the association’s overall retransmit count has already reached or exceeded max_retrans, it generates a protocol-violation abort chunk and queues it for transmission.

   g. It records the error code into asoc->outqueue.error for later SEND_FAILED notification.  
   h. Finally, it schedules the TCB (Transmission Control Block) for deletion (SCTP_CMD_DELETE_TCB).

   - Information leakage: No sensitive data is included in the assoc_change other than the SCTP error cause.  
   - Race conditions: The entire function runs under the SCTP stack’s lock or in atomic context (GFP_ATOMIC), so no unlocked shared data is touched.

original_information.commit_message:
x86,kvm,vmx: Preserve CR4 across VM entry

CR4 isn't constant; at least the TSD and PCE bits can vary.

TBH, treating CR0 and CR3 as constant scares me a bit, too, but it looks
like it's correct.

This adds a branch and a read from cr4 to each vm entry.  Because it is
extremely likely that consecutive entries into the same vcpu will have
the same host cr4 value, this fixes up the vmcs instead of restoring cr4
after the fact.  A subsequent patch will add a kernel-wide cr4 shadow,
reducing the overhead in the common case to just two memory reads and a
branch.

1. Functional Analysis  
   - The function apply_to_pte_range() walks through a single page-table page (a PTE page) covering addresses from addr up to end, invoking a callback fn on each PTE.  
   - It first allocates or maps the PTE page:  
     • If mm == &init_mm (the kernel’s own address space), it calls pte_alloc_kernel() which returns a direct pointer to the PTE page (no locking).  
     • Otherwise it calls pte_alloc_map_lock(), which allocates or ensures the page-table page is present, acquires the page-table lock, and returns a mapped pointer (and lock) in ptl.  
   - It checks that the PMD is not in “huge” form (BUG_ON).  
   - It enters “lazy MMU” mode (arch_enter_lazy_mmu_mode()), useful on some architectures to batch TLB or PTE writes.  
   - It retrieves the token (the pgtable base) with pmd_pgtable(*pmd) and then loops:  
       – For each page (incrementing addr by PAGE_SIZE), it calls fn(pte, token, addr, data).  
       – If fn returns a non-zero error, it breaks out.  
   - After finishing the range or on error it leaves lazy‐MMU mode, unmaps/unlocks the PTE page if needed, and returns fn’s error code (or 0 if none).

   - Out-of-bounds / infinite loop: The code assumes that addr < end and that (end – addr) is a positive multiple of PAGE_SIZE. These preconditions normally hold in kernel callers, so the loop will terminate cleanly.

   No, the code does not contain any obvious vulnerabilities. It correctly allocates or maps the PTE page, holds/releases locks, batches TLB/MMU updates in lazy mode, loops safely over a well-defined range, and propagates errors cleanly.

mm: thp: fix pmd_bad() triggering in code paths holding mmap_sem read mode

commit 1a5a9906d4e8d1976b701f889d8f35d54b928f25 upstream.

In some cases it may happen that pmd_none_or_clear_bad() is called with
the mmap_sem hold in read mode.  In those cases the huge page faults can
allocate hugepmds under pmd_none_or_clear_bad() and that can trigger a
false positive from pmd_bad() that will not like to see a pmd
materializing as trans huge.

It's not khugepaged causing the problem, khugepaged holds the mmap_sem
in write mode (and all those sites must hold the mmap_sem in read mode
to prevent pagetables to go away from under them, during code review it
seems vm86 mode on 32bit kernels requires that too unless it's
restricted to 1 thread per process or UP builds).  The race is only with
the huge pagefaults that can convert a pmd_none() into a
pmd_trans_huge().

Effectively all these pmd_none_or_clear_bad() sites running with
mmap_sem in read mode are somewhat speculative with the page faults, and
the result is always undefined when they run simultaneously.  This is
probably why it wasn't common to run into this.  For example if the
madvise(MADV_DONTNEED) runs zap_page_range() shortly before the page
fault, the hugepage will not be zapped, if the page fault runs first it
will be zapped.

Altering pmd_bad() not to error out if it finds hugepmds won't be enough
to fix this, because zap_pmd_range would then proceed to call
zap_pte_range (which would be incorrect if the pmd become a
pmd_trans_huge()).

The simplest way to fix this is to read the pmd in the local stack
(regardless of what we read, no need of actual CPU barriers, only
compiler barrier needed), and be sure it is not changing under the code
that computes its value.  Even if the real pmd is changing under the
value we hold on the stack, we don't care.  If we actually end up in
zap_pte_range it means the pmd was not none already and it was not huge,
and it can't become huge from under us (khugepaged locking explained
above).

All we need is to enforce that there is no way anymore that in a code
path like below, pmd_trans_huge can be false, but pmd_none_or_clear_bad
can run into a hugepmd.  The overhead of a barrier() is just a compiler
tweak and should not be measurable (I only added it for THP builds).  I
don't exclude different compiler versions may have prevented the race
too by caching the value of *pmd on the stack (that hasn't been
verified, but it wouldn't be impossible considering
pmd_none_or_clear_bad, pmd_bad, pmd_trans_huge, pmd_none are all inlines
and there's no external function called in between pmd_trans_huge and
pmd_none_or_clear_bad).

1. Functional Analysis  
   
   - The function `inet_proto_csum_replace4` performs an incremental update of a 16-bit internet checksum when a 32-bit field (for example, an IPv4 address) is changed from `from` to `to`.  
   - It first constructs a two-element array `diff` where:  
     • `diff[0] = ~from` (the one's-complement of the old 32-bit value)  
     • `diff[1] = to` (the new 32-bit value)  
   - It branches on `skb->ip_summed`:  
     a. If not `CHECKSUM_PARTIAL` (i.e. checksum fully computed in software):  
        • Recomputes `*sum` by folding the partial sum of `diff` into the inverse-unfolded original `*sum`.  
        • If the skb was previously fully checksummed (`CHECKSUM_COMPLETE`) and `pseudohdr` is set, it also updates the packet’s hardware checksum field `skb->csum`.  
     b. Else if `CHECKSUM_PARTIAL` and `pseudohdr` is set:  
        • Performs a similar update on `*sum`, but adjusts the invert/fold logic to match the offload conventions.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   
   - Memory Safety: The code uses only a fixed-size local array of two 32-bit words and standard pointer dereferences (`*sum`, `skb->csum`), with no unbounded loops or user-controlled indexing. There is no risk of buffer overflow or out-of-bounds access.  
   - Arithmetic Safety: All arithmetic is done in one's-complement style for checksums; there are no unguarded signed integer overflows or divisions by zero.  
   - Control Flow: The branches are on well-defined enum values (`ip_summed`), not on attacker-controlled data in a way that could lead to misprediction of safety.  
   - Offload and Pseudohdr Handling: The code correctly distinguishes between software full checksumming vs. partial offload and applies the proper inversion/folding sequence.  
   
   This is the standard Linux kernel routine for incremental IPv4 checksum adjustment. There are no apparent vulnerabilities (no memory corruption, no integer overflows, no conditional bypasses of checksum updates).

3. Decision  
   
   No, the code does not contain vulnerabilities. It correctly implements an incremental checksum update without unsafe memory or arithmetic operations.

original_information.Summary: The net_get_random_once implementation in net/core/utils.c in the Linux kernel 3.13.x and 3.14.x before 3.14.5 on certain Intel processors does not perform the intended slow-path operation to initialize random seeds, which makes it easier for remote attackers to spoof or disrupt IP communication by leveraging the predictability of TCP sequence numbers, TCP and UDP port numbers, and IP ID values.
original_information.commit_message:
net: avoid dependency of net_get_random_once on nop patching

net_get_random_once depends on the static keys infrastructure to patch up
the branch to the slow path during boot. This was realized by abusing the
static keys api and defining a new initializer to not enable the call
site while still indicating that the branch point should get patched
up. This was needed to have the fast path considered likely by gcc.

The static key initialization during boot up normally walks through all
the registered keys and either patches in ideal nops or enables the jump
site but omitted that step on x86 if ideal nops where already placed at
static_key branch points. Thus net_get_random_once branches not always
became active.

This patch switches net_get_random_once to the ordinary static_key
api and thus places the kernel fast path in the - by gcc considered -
unlikely path.  Microbenchmarks on Intel and AMD x86-64 showed that
the unlikely path actually beats the likely path in terms of cycle cost
and that different nop patterns did not make much difference, thus this
switch should not be noticeable.

Fixes: a48e42920ff38b ("net: introduce new macro net_get_random_once")
Reported-by: Tuomas Räsänen <tuomasjjrasanen@tjjr.fi>

1. Functional Analysis  
   - The function `process_mic` takes as inputs an optional incoming MIC token (`mic_in`), a SPNEGO context `sc`, and outputs an MIC token (`*mic_out`) when required. It also updates negotiation state (`*negState`) and a flag indicating whether to send a token (`*tokflag`).  
   - If `mic_in` is non‐NULL, it calls `gss_verify_mic` to validate that token. On success, it marks in the context that a MIC was received and that a reply MIC is now required. On failure, it sets the negotiation state to REJECT, requests an error‐token send, and returns immediately.  
   - If the context requires a MIC and one has not yet been sent, it calls `gss_get_mic` to generate one over the same DER‐encoded mechTypes data. It then allocates a `gss_buffer_desc` on the heap, copies the returned MIC token descriptor into it, sets the “sent” flag in the context, and returns success. All errors along this path release any partial buffers, set the token‐send flag appropriately, and return the GSS error code.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - buffer overflows: None. The code neither writes past fixed buffers nor does it manipulate raw pointers or unbounded memory.  
   - integer overflows: None. Length fields come from the GSS library, and no arithmetic is performed on them.  
   - use‑after‑free / invalid free: None. Buffers returned by GSS are either released on error or transferred unmodified to the caller, who is responsible for cleanup.  
   - NULL‐pointer dereferences: The code checks `malloc` return against `NULL` (via `GSS_C_NO_BUFFER`) and bails out on failure. It assumes valid non‐NULL `sc` and other required arguments, which is typical in GSS‐API wrappers.  
   - resource leaks: There is no leak on the error paths—the temporary `tmpmic` buffer is always released on failure. On the success path the temporary buffer is intentionally transferred to the caller by copying its descriptor into the freshly allocated `gss_buffer_desc`.  
   - minor‐status handling: The code routes cleanup through a local `tmpmin` so as not to overwrite the caller’s `minor_status` on cleanup calls; this is safe because `gss_release_buffer` writes only to its out‐parameter.  

   In short, there are no indications of common vulnerabilities (buffer overflows, double‐free, use‑after‑free, integer overflows, or unchecked pointer arithmetic). The memory‐management discipline is correct for a GSS‐API style function: errors clean up, successes transfer ownership.  

3. Decision  
   No, the code does not contain any security vulnerabilities.

original_information.Summary: The acc_ctx_cont function in the SPNEGO acceptor in lib/gssapi/spnego/spnego_mech.c in MIT Kerberos 5 (aka krb5) 1.5.x through 1.12.x before 1.12.2 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and application crash) via an empty continuation token at a certain point during a SPNEGO negotiation.
original_information.commit_message:
Fix null deref in SPNEGO acceptor [CVE-2014-4344]

When processing a continuation token, acc_ctx_cont was dereferencing
the initial byte of the token without checking the length.  This could
result in a null dereference.

CVE-2014-4344:

In MIT krb5 1.5 and newer, an unauthenticated or partially
authenticated remote attacker can cause a NULL dereference and
application crash during a SPNEGO negotiation by sending an empty
token as the second or later context token from initiator to acceptor.
The attacker must provide at least one valid context token in the
security context negotiation before sending the empty token.  This can
be done by an unauthenticated attacker by forcing SPNEGO to
renegotiate the underlying mechanism, or by using IAKERB to wrap an
unauthenticated AS-REQ as the first token.

    CVSSv2 Vector: AV:N/AC:L/Au:N/C:N/I:N/A:C/E:POC/RL:OF/RC:C

   - The function `status_unused` outputs a line of text to a `seq_file` (commonly used in the Linux kernel’s procfs/debugfs interfaces).  
   - It starts by printing the literal "unused devices: ".  
   - Then it walks the linked list `pending_raid_disks`, treating each node as an `md_rdev` pointer `rdev`.  
   - For each `rdev`, it allocates a local buffer `b` of size `BDEVNAME_SIZE`, increments a counter `i`, calls `bdevname(rdev->bdev, b)` to fill `b` with the block‑device name, and prints that name followed by a space.  
   - If no entries were encountered (`i == 0`), it prints the literal "<none>".  
   - Finally it prints a newline.

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Buffer overflow: `b` is allocated with the size `BDEVNAME_SIZE`, which is the intended maximum length for `bdevname` output; there is no overrun of `b`.  
   - Format‑string safety: `seq_printf` is given constant format strings and well‑defined arguments, so there is no format‑string vulnerability.  
   - Null pointer safety: the code assumes that every `rdev` in `pending_raid_disks` has a valid `bdev` member; in typical kernel use this list is managed under locks so only initialized entries are present.  
   - Concurrency: iteration over `pending_raid_disks` is assumed to be done under the appropriate lock in the caller; no unsafe concurrent list manipulation occurs inside this function.  
   - Resource exhaustion / DoS: the function only allocates a fixed‑size stack buffer and performs bounded I/O; it cannot crash or hang by oversized input.

3. Decision  
   No, the code as shown does not contain any obvious vulnerabilities.

original_information.Summary: The get_bitmap_file function in drivers/md/md.c in the Linux kernel before 4.1.6 does not initialize a certain bitmap data structure, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information from kernel memory via a GET_BITMAP_FILE ioctl call.
original_information.commit_message:
md: use kzalloc() when bitmap is disabled

In drivers/md/md.c get_bitmap_file() uses kmalloc() for creating a
mdu_bitmap_file_t called "file".

5769         file = kmalloc(sizeof(*file), GFP_NOIO);
5770         if (!file)
5771                 return -ENOMEM;

This structure is copied to user space at the end of the function.

5786         if (err == 0 &&
5787             copy_to_user(arg, file, sizeof(*file)))
5788                 err = -EFAULT

But if bitmap is disabled only the first byte of "file" is initialized
with zero, so it's possible to read some bytes (up to 4095) of kernel
space memory from user space. This is an information leak.

5775         /* bitmap disabled, zero the first byte and copy out */
5776         if (!mddev->bitmap_info.file)
5777                 file->pathname[0] = '\0';

1. Functional Analysis  
   - The function kvm_arch_vcpu_ioctl_set_fpu takes two arguments: a pointer to a KVM virtual CPU structure (vcpu) and a pointer to a kvm_fpu structure (fpu) containing user-supplied FPU register state.  
   - It retrieves the guest’s stored FXSAVE-area (an i387_fxsave_struct) from vcpu->arch.guest_fpu.state.  
   - It copies the 128 bytes of x87/MMX register data from fpu->fpr into fxsave->st_space.  
   - It assigns the floating-point control word (fcw), status word (fsw), tag word (ftwx), last executed opcode, last instruction pointer, and last data pointer from the user-supplied fpu structure into the corresponding fields in the fxsave area.  
   - Finally it copies the SSE/XMM register state from fpu->xmm into fxsave->xmm_space.  
   - Returns 0 on completion.

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Buffer overflows: All memcpy calls use fixed-size destinations whose sizes exactly match (or exceed) the size of the source arrays (128 bytes for st_space, sizeof fxsave->xmm_space for xmm). No out-of-bounds copy is evident.  
   - Null-pointer dereferences: The code assumes vcpu->arch.guest_fpu.state is non-NULL. In typical KVM usage this is guaranteed by higher-level initialization. No additional null checks are present here but are not strictly necessary if the caller’s contract ensures a valid state pointer.  
   - Integer overflows: No arithmetic is performed.  
   - Control/state poisoning: The code directly writes user-supplied control and status words (fcw, fsw, twd) and last-ip/last-dp values without sanitization. However, on x86 the hardware will mask reserved bits on FXRSTOR, so invalid bit patterns in these registers are automatically filtered by the CPU.  
   - Timing or side-channel: Not applicable to this straightforward copy/assignment code.  

   Overall, there is no evidence of classic memory-safety or control-flow vulnerabilities in this snippet.  
   
3. Decision  
   No, the code does not contain vulnerabilities. It safely copies fixed-size arrays and relies on the CPU to mask reserved control bits.

original_information.Summary: The KVM implementation in the Linux kernel before 3.3.6 allows host OS users to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and host OS crash) by making a KVM_CREATE_IRQCHIP ioctl call after a virtual CPU already exists.
original_information.commit_message:
KVM: Ensure all vcpus are consistent with in-kernel irqchip settings

(cherry picked from commit 3e515705a1f46beb1c942bb8043c16f8ac7b1e9e)

If some vcpus are created before KVM_CREATE_IRQCHIP, then
irqchip_in_kernel() and vcpu->arch.apic will be inconsistent, leading
to potential NULL pointer dereferences.

Fix by:
- ensuring that no vcpus are installed when KVM_CREATE_IRQCHIP is called
- ensuring that a vcpu has an apic if it is installed after KVM_CREATE_IRQCHIP

This is somewhat long winded because vcpu->arch.apic is created without
kvm->lock held.

Based on earlier patch by Michael Ellerman.

1. Functional Analysis

1.1 Parameter handling  
- The function `_kdc_add_KRB5SignedPath` takes context, KDC configuration, the TGT principal entry, an enctype, a client principal, an optional server principal, a list of delegated principals, and the ticket’s EncTicketPart structure.  
- If both `server` and `principals` are provided, the server principal is appended to the principals list.

1.2 ASN.1 encoding of the SignedPathData  
- A local `KRB5SignedPathData` structure (`spd`) is populated with the client, authentication time, delegated principals, and no method-data.  
- `ASN1_MALLOC_ENCODE` is used to DER‐encode `spd` into a temporary `krb5_data` buffer; a size check ensures the encoder’s output length equals the reported size.

1.3 Key retrieval and crypto initialization  
- The TGT’s entry is queried for a key matching the requested enctype via `hdb_enctype2key`.  
- If successful, a `krb5_crypto` context is initialized over that key.

1.4 Checksum (signature) creation  
- A `KRB5SignedPath` structure (`sp`) is populated with the enctype, delegated principals, and no method-data.  
- `krb5_create_checksum` is called with the earlier‐encoded `SignedPathData` as input, producing a checksum (the “signature”).  
- The `krb5_crypto` context and the temporary encoding buffer are freed once the checksum is obtained.

1.5 ASN.1 encoding of the full SignedPath  
- The filled `KRB5SignedPath` structure (including the checksum) is DER‐encoded into a fresh `krb5_data` buffer.  
- The checksum substructure is freed, and an internal check enforces that the DER encoder’s output length matches the expected size.

1.6 Adding authorization-data  
- The fully encoded `KRB5SignedPath` blob is added to the ticket’s authorization data as an IF-RELEVANT entry of type `KRB5_AUTHDATA_SIGNTICKET`.  
- The temporary DER buffer is freed, and the function returns the result code.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

2.1 Memory safety and buffer sizes  
- All ASN.1 encodings use `ASN1_MALLOC_ENCODE`, which allocates exactly the needed buffer and returns actual length. The code checks for a mismatch (`data.length != size`) and aborts if it occurs.  
- Temporary buffers are freed on all error paths.

2.2 Error handling and crashes  
- On an unexpected encoder length mismatch, the code calls `krb5_abortx`, forcibly terminating the process. While this protects against a corrupted ASN.1 library producing bad encodings, it introduces a potential denial‐of‐service: a maliciously crafted internal data structure (or a library bug) could trigger the abort. This is an intentional “fail‐stop” design rather than silent corruption.

2.3 Key and crypto context management  
- The key structure returned by `hdb_enctype2key` is not explicitly freed in this function; it may be managed elsewhere in the KDC. The `krb5_crypto` context is properly destroyed.

2.4 Cryptographic correctness  
- A keyed checksum (signature) is used with a proper key usage value (`KRB5_KU_KRB5SIGNEDPATH`). No direct use of unauthenticated data.  

2.5 Injection or overflow risks  
- No string operations or manual buffer copies are present. ASN.1 encoder functions handle length calculations internally.  
- No apparent integer overflows occur (sizes are size_t and checked after encoding).

Conclusion: Aside from the deliberate abort‐on‐mismatch (which trades availability for integrity), there is no evidence of buffer overflows, unchecked pointer dereferences, or cryptographic misuse.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain a traditional exploitable vulnerability; it enforces strict ASN.1 length checks (at the cost of aborting on mismatch) and correctly manages memory and crypto contexts.

original_information.Summary: The transit path validation code in Heimdal before 7.3 might allow attackers to bypass the capath policy protection mechanism by leveraging failure to add the previous hop realm to the transit path of issued tickets.
original_information.commit_message:
Fix transit path validation CVE-2017-6594

Commit f469fc6 (2010-10-02) inadvertently caused the previous hop realm
to not be added to the transit path of issued tickets.  This may, in
some cases, enable bypass of capath policy in Heimdal versions 1.5
through 7.2.

Note, this may break sites that rely on the bug.  With the bug some
incomplete [capaths] worked, that should not have.  These may now break
authentication in some cross-realm configurations.

   - It obtains the local and remote IPv6 addresses (`loc_addr` and `rmt_addr`) and their TCP ports, converting ports from network to host byte order.  
   - It then calls `seq_printf` with a fixed format string, printing:  
     • Entry index (`i`)  
     • Source and destination IPv6 addresses in eight‐hex‐digit groups plus port  
     • TCP state (hardcoded to `TCP_SYN_RECV`)  
     • Placeholder fields for options size, active timers, time left on the expire timer, retransmit count, UID, nonstandard timer, inode placeholder  
     • Finally the pointer value of the `request_sock` structure (`req`)  
   - All fields are derived from kernel‐side data structures.

   - Buffer safety: `seq_printf` writes into a kernel‐managed `seq_file` buffer using a constant format string and a bounded internal buffer; there is no risk of overflow from user‐controlled input.

   - Information leakage: The only pointer printed is `req` via `%p`. Modern Linux kernels render `%p` with a randomized or hashed representation rather than the raw address, preventing practical KASLR breaks.

3. Decision

code:
static void get_openreq6(struct seq_file *seq,
			 struct sock *sk, struct request_sock *req, int i, int uid)
{
	int ttd = req->expires - jiffies;
	const struct in6_addr *src = &inet6_rsk(req)->loc_addr;
	const struct in6_addr *dest = &inet6_rsk(req)->rmt_addr;

	if (ttd < 0)
		ttd = 0;

	seq_printf(seq,
		   "%4d: %08X%08X%08X%08X:%04X %08X%08X%08X%08X:%04X "
		   "%02X %08X:%08X %02X:%08lX %08X %5d %8d %d %d %p\n",
		   i,
		   src->s6_addr32[0], src->s6_addr32[1],
		   src->s6_addr32[2], src->s6_addr32[3],
		   ntohs(inet_rsk(req)->loc_port),
		   dest->s6_addr32[0], dest->s6_addr32[1],
		   dest->s6_addr32[2], dest->s6_addr32[3],
		   ntohs(inet_rsk(req)->rmt_port),
		   TCP_SYN_RECV,
		   0,0, /* could print option size, but that is af dependent. */
		   1,   /* timers active (only the expire timer) */
		   jiffies_to_clock_t(ttd),
		   req->retrans,
		   uid,
		   0,  /* non standard timer */
		   0, /* open_requests have no inode */
		   0, req);
}

Problem is ip_make_skb() calls ip_setup_cork() and

1. Functional Analysis

   • The function `_zip_write4` takes two parameters:  
     – `i`: a 32-bit unsigned integer.  
     – `fp`: a pointer to an open `FILE` stream.  
   • It extracts each of the four bytes of `i` in little‐endian order:  
     – Byte 0: `i & 0xff`  
     – Byte 1: `(i >> 8) & 0xff`  
     – Byte 2: `(i >> 16) & 0xff`  
     – Byte 3: `(i >> 24) & 0xff`  
   • For each byte, it calls `putc()` to write that single byte to the stream `fp`.  
   • The function returns `void`, signaling completion without a status code.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

   • Buffer overflows:  
     – The code writes directly to a `FILE *` using `putc()`. There is no manual buffer indexing or pointer arithmetic against an in‐memory buffer, so no classic stack or heap overflow arises here.  
   • Integer issues:  
     – The input is an unsigned 32‐bit value. Shifts and masks on this value cannot overflow or cause undefined behavior in C when applied to an unsigned type.  
   • NULL or invalid `FILE *`:  
     – If `fp` is NULL or otherwise invalid, calls to `putc()` will fail (and potentially set `errno`), but this is a misuse of the API rather than an exploitable vulnerability in the function itself.  
   • Error handling:  
     – The return values of `putc()` are not checked, so I/O errors (e.g., disk full, closed stream) go unnoticed. Still, this omission is at most a robustness issue, not a security flaw.  
   • Endianness and portability:  
     – The function explicitly writes in little‐endian order, which is intentional design, not a vulnerability. Consumers must match that expectation when reading back.

3. Decision

   No, the code does not contain any security vulnerabilities. It safely writes four bytes of an unsigned integer to a file stream in little‐endian order without buffer overflows or undefined behavior.

original_information.commit_message:
powerpc/tm: Check for already reclaimed tasks

Currently we can hit a scenario where we'll tm_reclaim() twice.  This
results in a TM bad thing exception because the second reclaim occurs
when not in suspend mode.

The scenario in which this can happen is the following.  We attempt to
deliver a signal to userspace.  To do this we need obtain the stack
pointer to write the signal context.  To get this stack pointer we
must tm_reclaim() in case we need to use the checkpointed stack
pointer (see get_tm_stackpointer()).  Normally we'd then return
directly to userspace to deliver the signal without going through
__switch_to().

Unfortunatley, if at this point we get an error (such as a bad
userspace stack pointer), we need to exit the process.  The exit will
result in a __switch_to().  __switch_to() will attempt to save the
process state which results in another tm_reclaim().  This
tm_reclaim() now causes a TM Bad Thing exception as this state has
already been saved and the processor is no longer in TM suspend mode.
Whee!

This patch checks the state of the MSR to ensure we are TM suspended
before we attempt the tm_reclaim().  If we've already saved the state
away, we should no longer be in TM suspend mode.  This has the
additional advantage of checking for a potential TM Bad Thing
exception.

Found using syscall fuzzer.

Fixes: fb09692e71f1 ("powerpc: Add reclaim and recheckpoint functions for context switching transactional memory processes")

Signed-off-by: Michael Neuling <mikey@neuling.org>

     • If none is found (es.es_len == 0) or the first found extent begins strictly after newes->es_lblk, it concludes that the range is a hole, possibly shortens newes->es_len, and returns 0 to indicate “no delayed extent here.”  
     • Otherwise it adjusts newes->es_len to span exactly from newes->es_lblk up through the end of that delayed extent.  
   - It then computes the first block immediately after the (adjusted) range and again calls ext4_es_find_delayed_extent_range from that block up to EXT_MAX_BLOCKS.  
   - If a delayed extent is found there, it returns its starting logical block; if none is found, it returns EXT_MAX_BLOCKS.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - There is no unbounded memory access or use-after-free. The only arithmetic operations are additions/subtractions on logical‐block indices (ext4_lblk_t), which are always constrained by caller‐provided limits (newes->es_lblk, newes->es_len) and by EXT_MAX_BLOCKS.

original_information.commit_message:
ext4: allocate entire range in zero range

Currently there is a bug in zero range code which causes zero range
calls to only allocate block aligned portion of the range, while
ignoring the rest in some cases.

In some cases, namely if the end of the range is past i_size, we do
attempt to preallocate the last nonaligned block. However this might
cause kernel to BUG() in some carefully designed zero range requests
on setups where page size > block size.

Fix this problem by first preallocating the entire range, including
the nonaligned edges and converting the written extents to unwritten
in the next step. This approach will also give us the advantage of
having the range to be as linearly contiguous as possible.

original_information.commit_message:
block: fail SCSI passthrough ioctls on partition devices

Linux allows executing the SG_IO ioctl on a partition or LVM volume, and
will pass the command to the underlying block device.  This is
well-known, but it is also a large security problem when (via Unix
permissions, ACLs, SELinux or a combination thereof) a program or user
needs to be granted access only to part of the disk.

This patch lets partitions forward a small set of harmless ioctls;
others are logged with printk so that we can see which ioctls are
actually sent.  In my tests only CDROM_GET_CAPABILITY actually occurred.
Of course it was being sent to a (partition on a) hard disk, so it would
have failed with ENOTTY and the patch isn't changing anything in
practice.  Still, I'm treating it specially to avoid spamming the logs.

In principle, this restriction should include programs running with
CAP_SYS_RAWIO.  If for example I let a program access /dev/sda2 and
/dev/sdb, it still should not be able to read/write outside the
boundaries of /dev/sda2 independent of the capabilities.  However, for
now programs with CAP_SYS_RAWIO will still be allowed to send the
ioctls.  Their actions will still be logged.

This patch does not affect the non-libata IDE driver.  That driver
however already tests for bd != bd->bd_contains before issuing some
ioctl; it could be restricted further to forbid these ioctls even for
programs running with CAP_SYS_ADMIN/CAP_SYS_RAWIO.

original_information.commit_message:
SELinux:  Fix kernel BUG on empty security contexts.

Setting an empty security context (length=0) on a file will
lead to incorrectly dereferencing the type and other fields
of the security context structure, yielding a kernel BUG.
As a zero-length security context is never valid, just reject
all such security contexts whether coming from userspace
via setxattr or coming from the filesystem upon a getxattr
request by SELinux.

Setting a security context value (empty or otherwise) unknown to
SELinux in the first place is only possible for a root process
(CAP_MAC_ADMIN), and, if running SELinux in enforcing mode, only
if the corresponding SELinux mac_admin permission is also granted
to the domain by policy.  In Fedora policies, this is only allowed for
specific domains such as livecd for setting down security contexts
that are not defined in the build host policy.

Reproducer:
su
setenforce 0
touch foo
setfattr -n security.selinux foo

Caveat:
Relabeling or removing foo after doing the above may not be possible
without booting with SELinux disabled.  Any subsequent access to foo
after doing the above will also trigger the BUG.

  • `totalLogicalWidth`: cumulative width already occupied by boxes (passed by reference, and updated as expansions are applied)  
  • `availableLogicalWidth`: the target width for the line after justification

  • For each text run, reads the number of slots from `expansionOpportunities[i++]`.  
  • Asserts that this run’s slots do not exceed the remaining total slots.  
  • If the run’s style collapses whitespace, it computes an integer `expansion` proportional to its slot share:  
    expansion = (availableLogicalWidth – totalLogicalWidth) × slots / remainingSlots

  • Subtracts this run’s slots from `expansionOpportunityCount`. Breaks out once all slots are used.

Simplify "WouldTaintOrigin" concept in media/blink

Currently WebMediaPlayer has three predicates:
 - DidGetOpaqueResponseFromServiceWorker
 - HasSingleSecurityOrigin
 - DidPassCORSAccessCheck
. These are used to determine whether the response body is available
for scripts. They are known to be confusing, and actually
MediaElementAudioSourceHandler::WouldTaintOrigin misuses them.

the confusion. Now the "response type" concept is available and we
don't need a custom CORS check, so this CL removes

URLData::has_opaque_data_ and its (direct and indirect) data accessors

Separate repaint and layout requirements of StyleDifference (Step 1)

Previously StyleDifference was an enum that proximately bigger values
imply smaller values (e.g. StyleDifferenceLayout implies
StyleDifferenceRepaint). This causes unnecessary repaints in some cases
on layout change.

Convert StyleDifference to a structure containing relatively independent
flags.

This change doesn't directly improve the result, but can make further
repaint optimizations possible.

Step 1 doesn't change any functionality. RenderStyle still generate the
legacy StyleDifference enum when comparing styles and convert the result
to the new StyleDifference. Implicit requirements are not handled during
the conversion.

Converted call sites to use the new StyleDifference according to the
following conversion rules:
- diff == StyleDifferenceEqual (&& !context) => diff.hasNoChange()
- diff == StyleDifferenceRepaint => diff.needsRepaintObjectOnly()
- diff == StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsRepaintLayer()
- diff == StyleDifferenceRepaint || diff == StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsRepaintLayer()
- diff >= StyleDifferenceRepaint => diff.needsRepaint() || diff.needsLayout()
- diff >= StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsRepaintLayer() || diff.needsLayout()
- diff > StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsLayout()
- diff == StyleDifferencePositionedMovementLayoutOnly => diff.needsPositionedMovementLayoutOnly()
- diff == StyleDifferenceLayout => diff.needsFullLayout()

      • CLA = 0x80 (secure messaging bit OR‑ed in)  
      • INS = 0x14 (SIGN instruction)  
      • P1 = 0x01 (sign operation parameter)  
      • P2 = 0x00  

  - It then sets the APDU’s data length (`lc`/`datalen`) and points `apdu.data` at the input buffer, and allocates a response buffer `rbuf` of size `SC_MAX_APDU_BUFFER_SIZE`, with an expected response length `le` of 256.

  - It transmits the APDU via `sc_transmit_apdu`. On communication error it returns immediately; if the card returns a status word other than 0x90/0x00 it translates that status into an error code and returns it.

  - If the APDU succeeded, it checks that the actual response length `apdu.resplen` will fit into the caller’s output buffer length `outlen`; if not, it returns `SC_ERROR_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL`.

  - Finally it copies the response (the raw signature) into `out` and returns the number of bytes written.

  - Buffer Overflow in Response Copy  
    • The code ensures `apdu.resplen <= outlen` before calling `memcpy`, so there is no out‑of‑bounds write into `out`.  

  - Integer Overflow / Truncation  
    • Input `datalen` is a `size_t`, but `apdu.lc` may be a narrower type (u8 or u16). If `datalen` exceeds what the APDU format allows, the construction of the APDU could be malformed or truncated. In practice the library’s `sc_format_apdu` should either reject too‑large lengths or select extended APDU format properly. Without seeing its implementation, one cannot say it’s a bug here—normally smart‑card libraries enforce a maximum data field length.  

  - APDU Parameter Limits  
    • There is no explicit ceiling check on `datalen` against `SC_MAX_APDU_BUFFER_SIZE` or a protocol limit. If a caller passes an extremely large `datalen`, this function will attempt to send an oversized APDU (though the underlying transmit function or the card itself will reject it).  

  - Return‑Value Casting  
    • The function returns an `int` but on success returns the unsigned `apdu.resplen`. In theory if `resplen` were larger than `INT_MAX` that would overflow the return value, but real signature lengths are bounded well below that.

     • Compute a weighted CPU-side fault contribution based on this task’s runtime share, subtract half the old smoothed CPU faults, reset the CPU-fault buffer, then add the delta to the smoothed CPU faults.  
     • Update per-task aggregates: total faults on that node, total NUMA faults of the task.

sched/fair: Fix infinite loop in update_blocked_averages() by reverting a9e7f6544b9c

Zhipeng Xie, Xie XiuQi and Sargun Dhillon reported lockups in the
scheduler under high loads, starting at around the v4.18 time frame,
and Zhipeng Xie tracked it down to bugs in the rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list
manipulation.

Do a (manual) revert of:

  a9e7f6544b9c ("sched/fair: Fix O(nr_cgroups) in load balance path")

It turns out that the list_del_leaf_cfs_rq() introduced by this commit
is a surprising property that was not considered in followup commits
such as:

  9c2791f936ef ("sched/fair: Fix hierarchical order in rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list")

As Vincent Guittot explains:

 "I think that there is a bigger problem with commit a9e7f6544b9c and
  cfs_rq throttling:

  Let take the example of the following topology TG2 --> TG1 --> root:

   1) The 1st time a task is enqueued, we will add TG2 cfs_rq then TG1
      cfs_rq to leaf_cfs_rq_list and we are sure to do the whole branch in
      one path because it has never been used and can't be throttled so
      tmp_alone_branch will point to leaf_cfs_rq_list at the end.

   2) Then TG1 is throttled

   3) and we add TG3 as a new child of TG1.

   4) The 1st enqueue of a task on TG3 will add TG3 cfs_rq just before TG1
      cfs_rq and tmp_alone_branch will stay  on rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list.

  With commit a9e7f6544b9c, we can del a cfs_rq from rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list.
  So if the load of TG1 cfs_rq becomes NULL before step 2) above, TG1
  cfs_rq is removed from the list.
  Then at step 4), TG3 cfs_rq is added at the beginning of rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list
  but tmp_alone_branch still points to TG3 cfs_rq because its throttled
  parent can't be enqueued when the lock is released.
  tmp_alone_branch doesn't point to rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list whereas it should.

  So if TG3 cfs_rq is removed or destroyed before tmp_alone_branch
  points on another TG cfs_rq, the next TG cfs_rq that will be added,
  will be linked outside rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list - which is bad.

  In addition, we can break the ordering of the cfs_rq in
  rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list but this ordering is used to update and
  propagate the update from leaf down to root."

Instead of trying to work through all these cases and trying to reproduce
the very high loads that produced the lockup to begin with, simplify
the code temporarily by reverting a9e7f6544b9c - which change was clearly
not thought through completely.

This (hopefully) gives us a kernel that doesn't lock up so people
can continue to enjoy their holidays without worrying about regressions. ;-)

1. Functional Analysis

- The function megasas_get_ld_vf_affiliation_111() issues a device‐specific (“DCMD”) command to retrieve or refresh a mapping of logical drives (LDs) to virtual functions (VFs) on a MegaRAID controller.
- It begins by allocating or obtaining a command structure (megasas_cmd) via megasas_get_cmd(). If that fails, it returns –ENOMEM.
- It checks that an existing buffer (instance->vf_affiliation_111) is already set up for the first (“initial”) pass; if not, it bails out.
- On the initial call, it zeroes out the persistent affiliation buffer. On subsequent calls, it allocates a fresh coherent DMA buffer (new_affiliation_111) to hold the firmware’s reply.
- It builds the DCMD frame (dcmd) with the proper opcode (MR_DCMD_LD_VF_MAP_GET_ALL_LDS_111), data transfer length, and a single 32-bit SGE pointing at either the persistent or newly allocated DMA buffer.
- It issues the command synchronously via megasas_issue_blocked_cmd():  
  · On failure, it logs a warning, sets retval=1 to force a later SCSI scan, and jumps to cleanup.  
  · On success and if this is not the initial call, it compares the VF‐policy entries in the old buffer versus the newly fetched buffer. If any policy for the current VF (thisVf) has changed, it copies the new buffer over the old one and sets retval=1.
- Finally, it frees any temporary buffer, returns the command structure, and returns retval (0 if no change, 1 if a change or if the command failed).

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Memory management:  
  · The code checks for allocation failures and returns cleanly on error.  
  · It frees the DMA buffer exactly once in all paths where it was allocated.  
  · It does not dereference new_affiliation_111 except after a successful DMA fetch.
- Bounds and overrun:  
  · The size passed into dma_zalloc_coherent(), data_xfer_len, and memcpy all use sizeof(MR_LD_VF_AFFILIATION_111), so there is no mismatch.  
  · The loop over vdCount only reads entries within the newly fetched struct; both the old and new affiliation arrays are the same size, so there is no out‐of‐bounds access (assuming firmware obeys vdCount ≤ array capacity).
- DMA coherency: using dma_zalloc_coherent() ensures caches are coherent for the device and CPU in one contiguous buffer.
- Race conditions: the function appears to be single‐threaded per instance or protected by higher‐level locking in the driver, so no obvious concurrency bug.
- Command‐issue error paths: the code logs and returns a fallback indication (retval=1) but does not leak memory or leave the hardware in an undefinable state.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any obvious vulnerabilities. It correctly handles resource allocation/frees, size matching, and error paths without buffer overruns or use-after-free.

   - It first checks whether a constant `name` is already defined on `outer` by calling `mrb_const_defined_at(mrb, mrb_obj_value(outer), name)`.

       • Fetches the existing class object via `class_from_sym`.  
       • Marks or records its origin with `MRB_CLASS_ORIGIN(c)`.  
       • If the caller supplied a `super` and it does not match the existing class’s real superclass (`mrb_class_real(c->super)`), it raises a `TypeError` about the superclass mismatch.

     - Allocates a new class object with `mrb_class_new(mrb, super)`.  
     - Hooks it into the `outer` namespace under the given name by calling `setup_class(mrb, outer, c, name)`.  
     - Returns the newly created class.

   - Memory allocation for a new class is done by the VM’s allocator (`mrb_class_new`), and integration into the constant table is done by `setup_class`; both follow standard mruby conventions.  
   - There is no path that mutates memory out of bounds, nor any unchecked format strings (the only formatted output is a `%S`‐based Ruby error).  
   - There is no direct invocation of user‐controlled code at this point—method dispatch and constant lookup are internal.  

3. Decision  
   No, the code does not contain any obvious vulnerability. It safely handles existing definitions, enforces superclass consistency, and creates new classes in a controlled manner.

loop: fix concurrent lo_open/lo_release

范龙飞 reports that KASAN can report a use-after-free in __lock_acquire.
The reason is due to insufficient serialization in lo_release(), which
will continue to use the loop device even after it has decremented the
lo_refcnt to zero.

again as it is being shut down. Confusion ensues.

- First row (y = 0):

    (`*dec += *(dec - 1)`).  
- First column (x = 0):  
  - Starts at `data[3] + linesize` and for each y from 1 to height–1 adds the alpha value from the pixel above  
    (`*dec += *(dec - ls)`).
- Remaining pixels (x ≥ 1, y ≥ 1): applied according to the enum `AlphaFilter m`:  
  - HORIZONTAL: each pixel adds the left neighbor  
  - VERTICAL: each pixel adds the top neighbor  
  - GRADIENT: each pixel adds the sum of left and top minus top-left, then clamps the result to [0..255]

- The loops enforce `x < width` and `y < height`, so there is no out-of-bounds read or write on the alpha buffer.  
- Integer calculations (`y * ls + 1`, pointer offsets) remain in the valid range for typical image dimensions; there is no risk of overflow in these multiplications under realistic constraints.  
- All array accesses use unsigned 8-bit writes or reads; wrapping on addition is intentional except in the gradient case where clamping prevents under/overflow.  
- No unhandled filter values: the switch covers all defined enum cases (any out-of-range value simply skips filtering, not leading to memory corruption).

3. Decision

No, the code correctly bounds its pointer arithmetic and prevents buffer overflows or underflows; it does not contain any exploitable vulnerabilities.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function `asepcos_tlvpath_to_scpath` converts a TLV-encoded input buffer into an `sc_path_t` structure.
- It takes three parameters:
  • `out`: pointer to the output `sc_path_t` structure  
  • `in`: pointer to the input byte array  
  • `in_len`: length of the input array in bytes  
- It zeroes the output structure with `memset`.
- It then enters a loop that processes the input in fixed 4-byte chunks:
  1. If fewer than 4 bytes remain, it returns `SC_ERROR_INTERNAL`.  
  2. It checks that the first byte is the expected tag `0x8B` and the second byte is the expected length `0x02`; if not, it returns `SC_ERROR_INVALID_ASN1_OBJECT`.  
  3. It calls `sc_append_path_id(out, &in[2], 2)` to append the 2-byte file identifier to the path.  
  4. It deducts 4 from `len` and advances `in` by 4 bytes.  
- After all input bytes are consumed, it sets `out->type` to `SC_PATH_TYPE_PATH` and returns `SC_SUCCESS`.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Bounds Checking  
  • The code ensures at each iteration that `len >= 4` before accessing `in[0]` through `in[3]`, preventing out-of-bounds reads.  
- Integer Underflow  
  • `len` is a `size_t` and is only decremented when `len >= 4`, so there is no underflow.  
- Tag/Length Validation  
  • The tag (`0x8B`) and length (`0x02`) bytes are explicitly checked, protecting against malformed TLV records.  
- Dependency on `sc_append_path_id`  
  • The snippet delegates path-entry storage to `sc_append_path_id`. If that function enforces its own limits on the number of entries and the capacity of `sc_path_t`, no buffer overflow or resource exhaustion will occur. If it does not, there is a theoretical risk of overrunning the internal storage of `sc_path_t` when given a large number of chunks.  
- Null-pointer Checks  
  • There is no explicit check for `out == NULL` or `in == NULL`. Passing a null pointer would cause a crash, but in typical internal use the caller is expected to supply valid pointers.

3. Decision

No, the code itself does not introduce exploitable vulnerabilities, assuming that `sc_append_path_id` correctly enforces the capacity limits of `sc_path_t`.

original_information.commit_message:
mm: thp: fix pmd_bad() triggering in code paths holding mmap_sem read mode

commit 1a5a9906d4e8d1976b701f889d8f35d54b928f25 upstream.

In some cases it may happen that pmd_none_or_clear_bad() is called with
the mmap_sem hold in read mode.  In those cases the huge page faults can
allocate hugepmds under pmd_none_or_clear_bad() and that can trigger a
false positive from pmd_bad() that will not like to see a pmd
materializing as trans huge.

It's not khugepaged causing the problem, khugepaged holds the mmap_sem
in write mode (and all those sites must hold the mmap_sem in read mode
to prevent pagetables to go away from under them, during code review it
seems vm86 mode on 32bit kernels requires that too unless it's
restricted to 1 thread per process or UP builds).  The race is only with
the huge pagefaults that can convert a pmd_none() into a
pmd_trans_huge().

Effectively all these pmd_none_or_clear_bad() sites running with
mmap_sem in read mode are somewhat speculative with the page faults, and
the result is always undefined when they run simultaneously.  This is
probably why it wasn't common to run into this.  For example if the
madvise(MADV_DONTNEED) runs zap_page_range() shortly before the page
fault, the hugepage will not be zapped, if the page fault runs first it
will be zapped.

Altering pmd_bad() not to error out if it finds hugepmds won't be enough
to fix this, because zap_pmd_range would then proceed to call
zap_pte_range (which would be incorrect if the pmd become a
pmd_trans_huge()).

The simplest way to fix this is to read the pmd in the local stack
(regardless of what we read, no need of actual CPU barriers, only
compiler barrier needed), and be sure it is not changing under the code
that computes its value.  Even if the real pmd is changing under the
value we hold on the stack, we don't care.  If we actually end up in
zap_pte_range it means the pmd was not none already and it was not huge,
and it can't become huge from under us (khugepaged locking explained
above).

All we need is to enforce that there is no way anymore that in a code
path like below, pmd_trans_huge can be false, but pmd_none_or_clear_bad
can run into a hugepmd.  The overhead of a barrier() is just a compiler
tweak and should not be measurable (I only added it for THP builds).  I
don't exclude different compiler versions may have prevented the race
too by caching the value of *pmd on the stack (that hasn't been
verified, but it wouldn't be impossible considering
pmd_none_or_clear_bad, pmd_bad, pmd_trans_huge, pmd_none are all inlines
and there's no external function called in between pmd_trans_huge and
pmd_none_or_clear_bad).

original_information.Summary: kernel/signal.c in the Linux kernel before 2.6.39 allows local users to spoof the uid and pid of a signal sender via a sigqueueinfo system call.
original_information.commit_message:
Prevent rt_sigqueueinfo and rt_tgsigqueueinfo from spoofing the signal code

Userland should be able to trust the pid and uid of the sender of a
signal if the si_code is SI_TKILL.

Unfortunately, the kernel has historically allowed sigqueueinfo() to
send any si_code at all (as long as it was negative - to distinguish it
from kernel-generated signals like SIGILL etc), so it could spoof a
SI_TKILL with incorrect siginfo values.

Happily, it looks like glibc has always set si_code to the appropriate
SI_QUEUE, so there are probably no actual user code that ever uses
anything but the appropriate SI_QUEUE flag.

So just tighten the check for si_code (we used to allow any negative
value), and add a (one-time) warning in case there are binaries out
there that might depend on using other si_code values.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function `dev_add_pack(struct packet_type *pt)` registers a packet handler into a global list of packet types.  
- It calls `ptype_head(pt)` to pick the appropriate list head based on fields in `pt`.  
- It acquires a spinlock (`ptype_lock`) to serialize writers.  
- It calls `list_add_rcu(&pt->list, head)` to insert `pt->list` at the front of the RCU-protected linked list headed by `head`.  
- It then releases the spinlock.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Concurrency/Race:  
  - Writers are serialized by `spin_lock(&ptype_lock)` / `spin_unlock(&ptype_lock)`.  
  - Readers of the list are expected to use RCU read-side primitives (e.g., `rcu_read_lock()`, `list_for_each_rcu()`). Provided readers obey RCU, there is no iterator invalidation or ABA.  
- Memory safety:  
  - `list_add_rcu()` initializes the new node’s `next`/`prev` pointers; it does not expect them to have been zeroed, so there is no use of uninitialized memory.  
  - The code assumes `pt` and its embedded `pt->list` are already allocated and non-NULL; that precondition must be met by the caller.  
- Double-insertion:  
  - If the same `pt` is passed twice without an intervening removal, the list would become corrupted. However, that is a higher-level logic error, not a flaw in this snippet’s synchronization or pointer handling.  
- Deadlock/Livelock:  
  - Only one spinlock is used, acquired and released unconditionally and for a short critical section. No deadlock risk in this snippet.  

Conclusion: This code correctly synchronizes insertions into an RCU-protected list and does not exhibit any inherent memory-safety or concurrency vulnerabilities in itself.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any vulnerabilities. It safely uses a spinlock plus RCU list insertion under the assumption that readers use the appropriate RCU primitives and that the caller provides a valid, uninserted `pt`.

original_information.commit_message:
net: don't allow CAP_NET_ADMIN to load non-netdev kernel modules

Since a8f80e8ff94ecba629542d9b4b5f5a8ee3eb565c any process with
CAP_NET_ADMIN may load any module from /lib/modules/.  This doesn't mean
that CAP_NET_ADMIN is a superset of CAP_SYS_MODULE as modules are
limited to /lib/modules/**.  However, CAP_NET_ADMIN capability shouldn't
allow anybody load any module not related to networking.

This patch restricts an ability of autoloading modules to netdev modules
with explicit aliases.  This fixes CVE-2011-1019.

Arnd Bergmann suggested to leave untouched the old pre-v2.6.32 behavior
of loading netdev modules by name (without any prefix) for processes
with CAP_SYS_MODULE to maintain the compatibility with network scripts
that use autoloading netdev modules by aliases like "eth0", "wlan0".

Currently there are only three users of the feature in the upstream
kernel: ipip, ip_gre and sit.

Don't allow unhandled POSTs to write to the filesystem by default

- The function mptsas_process_config handles a configuration request (MPIMsgConfig) from a host driver for an MPTSAS (LSI SAS) controller emulation.
- It first fixes up endianness of the incoming request and prepares an empty reply (MPIMsgConfigReply), copying over common fields such as Action, Function, MsgContext, PageType, PageNumber, etc.
- It extracts the page type (and extended page type if applicable) and validates that the requested action is one of the supported configuration actions (read, write, default, header).
- It looks up the requested configuration page descriptor via mptsas_find_config_page(type, page_number).
- For “default” or “header” actions, it calls the page’s build callback with a NULL data pointer to compute the page length, then returns that length in the reply.
- For write actions, it similarly computes the page length and always returns a “can’t commit” status (emulation does not support writes).
- For read actions, it again invokes the page build callback, this time asking it to allocate/fill a data buffer and return the buffer length. It then writes up to the requested DMA length (FlagsLength & MPI_SGE_LENGTH_MASK) into guest memory using pci_dma_write(), capping the transfer with MIN(length, dmalen).
- Finally, it fills in the reply’s length fields (PageLength or ExtPageLength as 32‑bit words), fixes endianness, sends the reply, and frees any allocated data buffer.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Input validation:  
  • PageType and ExtPageType are validated against known masks.  
  • Action is checked against a fixed switch of supported values.  
  • If the page descriptor lookup fails, an appropriate “invalid type/page” status is returned.  
- Memory safety:  
  • The page build callback is first called with a NULL pointer to get the required length; the code checks for negative (error) return values.  
  • For reads, the code uses pci_dma_write(pci, pa, data, MIN(length, dmalen)), ensuring it never writes more than the buffer produced or than the guest claimed it can accept.  
  • The buffer pointer `data` is always passed to g_free() when the function exits, preventing leaks.  
- Integer handling:  
  • The length returned by the page builder is a size_t; it is compared as a signed ssize_t to detect negative-error cases.  
  • The extracted DMA length (dmalen) is masked with MPI_SGE_LENGTH_MASK, preventing use of high bits.  
- Off‑by‑one/bounds:  
  • There is an assert(data[2] == page->number) to check that the page builder set the page number correctly; if that were wrong in debug builds it would abort, but in production the code still caps the transfer.  
- There is no unchecked pointer arithmetic, no copying of unvalidated lengths into fixed-size arrays, and DMA writes are explicitly bounded.

No—the code contains no obvious memory‐safety or logic flaws. It validates inputs, bounds DMA transfers, and manages its buffers correctly.
