1. Functional Analysis

- The function `GetOneAuthenticPixel` retrieves a single “authentic” (precise, unfiltered) pixel at coordinates `(x,y)` from an image.
- It first asserts that:
  - `image` is non-NULL.
  - `image->signature` matches the library’s expected signature.
  - `image->cache` is non-NULL.
  - The cache’s internal signature (`cache_info->signature`) is valid.
- It initializes the output `*pixel` to the image’s `background_color`.
- If the cache provides a custom pixel‐fetch handler (`get_one_authentic_pixel_from_handler`), it calls that handler and returns its result.
- Otherwise it falls back to `GetAuthenticPixelsCache(image, x, y, 1UL, 1UL, exception)`, which:
  - Attempts to map or retrieve a 1×1 pixel region at `(x,y)`.
  - Returns a pointer to the pixel data or NULL on failure.
- If the cache call fails (returns NULL), the function returns `MagickFalse` and leaves `*pixel` set to the background color.
- If the cache call succeeds, it copies the fetched pixel into the user‐supplied `*pixel` and returns `MagickTrue`.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Null Dereferences  
  All input pointers (`image`, `image->cache`) are asserted non-NULL before use. The code never dereferences them without first verifying via `assert`, so in a non‐debug build (where asserts may be disabled) the code would still crash if passed a NULL pointer, but it does not silently continue.
- Signature Checks  
  The function defends against misuse of corrupted or uninitialized `Image` or `CacheInfo` structures by checking `signature` fields.
- Bounds/Overflow  
  The call to `GetAuthenticPixelsCache` is responsible for validating that `(x,y)` is in range and that the cache read of size 1×1 is safe. This wrapper relies on that function’s own safety checks; it does not perform direct arithmetic on image dimensions or buffer pointers.
- Function Pointer Call  
  If a custom handler is set in `cache_info->methods.get_one_authentic_pixel_from_handler`, the code invokes it unchecked. However, that pointer is part of the internal `CacheInfo` structure, which normal library code controls. Unless an attacker can corrupt `cache_info->methods`, they cannot force an arbitrary function call.
- Error Handling  
  On error fetching pixels, `*pixel` remains the background color and the function returns `MagickFalse`. No out‐of‐bounds memory is read or written, and no uninitialized data is exposed.

Conclusion: the code properly validates its inputs via asserts, relies on the downstream cache‐fetch routine for bounds checking, and has controlled use of any function‐pointer hooks. There is no direct buffer overflow, use-after-free, integer overflow, or null-pointer dereference in normal operation.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any evident vulnerabilities. It safely handles null checks, signature validation, and delegates bounds checking to the cache‐fetch routine.

1. Functional Analysis

- skb, fl4, sk, inet setup  
  • skb: the socket‐buffer holding the packet data  
  • fl4: IPv4 flow‐info (source/destination addresses and ports)  
  • sk: socket pointer stored in skb  
  • inet: IPv4‐specific socket data  

- Determine UDP vs. UDP‐Lite  
  • is_udplite = IS_UDPLITE(sk)  

- Calculate transport header offset and payload length  
  • offset = skb_transport_offset(skb)  
  • len = skb->len – offset  

- Build the UDP header  
  • uh = udp_hdr(skb) (pointer into skb data)  
  • uh->source = socket’s source port  
  • uh->dest   = flow’s destination port  
  • uh->len    = htons(total UDP length)  
  • uh->check  = 0 (initially)  

- Compute or disable checksum based on socket flags and hardware offload  
  • If UDP‐Lite: call udplite_csum(skb)  
  • Else if user disabled csum (sk_no_check): mark skb as no checksum and skip further csum  
  • Else if hardware‐offload requested (CHECKSUM_PARTIAL): invoke udp4_hwcsum(…) and skip further csum  
  • Else: compute software UDP checksum via udp_csum(skb)  

- Finalize checksum field  
  • uh->check = csum_tcpudp_magic(src, dst, len, proto, computed_csum)  
  • If result is zero, use special marker (CSUM_MANGLED_0)  

- Transmit the packet  
  • err = ip_send_skb(sock_net(sk), skb)  
  • On ENOBUFS (no buffer) increment SNDBUFERRORS (unless recverr enabled), swallow error  
  • On success increment OUTDATAGRAMS  

- Return err to caller  

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Buffer/length checks  
  • The code derives `len = skb->len - offset` and writes headers at `udp_hdr(skb)`. Upstream callers must ensure `skb` carries sufficient linear data and `offset` is valid. In the standard UDP send path, `skb` always has a correctly reserved transport header area and proper length.  

- Checksum handling  
  • The code cleanly separates software vs. hardware offload and “no‐csum” modes. There is no misuse of uninitialized memory: checksum fields are explicitly zeroed or computed.  

- Integer underflow/overflow  
  • `len` is an `int` and comes from `skb_transport_offset` (non‐negative) and `skb->len` (also non‐negative). A maliciously crafted `skb` with `offset > skb->len` would produce negative `len`, but the kernel’s skb API prevents this in the normal send path—transport offsets are validated on allocation.  

- Race conditions / pointer lifetime  
  • All pointers (`skb`, `sk`, header pointers) are valid in the context of synchronous send. No async re‐use or double‐free issues here.  

- Denial‐of‐service  
  • The function may fail with ENOBUFS, but it handles this gracefully and does not loop or block indefinitely.  

Overall, the code follows expected kernel patterns for UDP packet construction and transmit. No unguarded memory writes, no unchecked copy sizes, and no misuse of user‐supplied pointers occur in this snippet.  

3. Decision

No, this code does not contain any vulnerabilities. It correctly constructs UDP headers, handles all checksum modes, validates lengths via upstream skb APIs, and invokes the IP layer safely.

original_information.commit_message:
Implement a bubble that appears at the top of the screen when a tab enters 
fullscreen mode via webkitRequestFullScreen(), telling the user how to exit 
fullscreen. 

This is implemented as an NSView rather than an NSWindow because the floating 
chrome that appears in presentation mode should overlap the bubble. 

Content-initiated fullscreen mode makes use of 'presentation mode' on the Mac: 
the mode in which the UI is hidden, accessible by moving the cursor to the top 
of the screen. On Snow Leopard, this mode is synonymous with fullscreen mode. 
On Lion, however, fullscreen mode does not imply presentation mode: in 
non-presentation fullscreen mode, the chrome is permanently shown. It is 
possible to switch between presentation mode and fullscreen mode using the 
presentation mode UI control. 

When a tab initiates fullscreen mode on Lion, we enter presentation mode if not 
in presentation mode already. When the user exits fullscreen mode using Chrome 
UI (i.e. keyboard shortcuts, menu items, buttons, switching tabs, etc.) we 
return the user to the mode they were in before the tab entered fullscreen. 

BUG=14471
TEST=Enter fullscreen mode using webkitRequestFullScreen. You should see a bubble pop down from the top of the screen.

+  NSRect bubbleFrame = [[self view] frame];

+- (void)hideTimerFired:(NSTimer*)timer {
+  NSRect endFrame = [[self view] frame];
+  endFrame.origin.y += endFrame.size.height;
+  endFrame.size.height = 0;
+  NSDictionary* dict = [NSDictionary dictionaryWithObjectsAndKeys:
+      [self view], NSViewAnimationTargetKey,
+      [NSValue valueWithRect:endFrame], NSViewAnimationEndFrameKey, nil];

+  NSViewAnimation* animation =

+  [animation gtm_setDuration:kSlideOutDurationMs/1000.0
+                   eventMask:NSLeftMouseUpMask];
+  [animation setDelegate:self];
+  [animation startAnimation];
+  hideAnimation_.reset(animation);

+  [path lineToPoint:topRight];

+    [path addClip];

   - It computes flatness2 as either flatness (fixed point) or flatness² (floating point).  
   - It iterates over the input path’s commands (flags[]) and points (pts[]) by index i, from 0 to path->length–1.  
     - If the current flag has splashPathFirst, it emits a moveTo() on fPath to the corresponding point, then i++.  
     - Otherwise, it checks for splashPathCurve:

     - After either branch, if the flag of the most recently processed point (i–1) has splashPathClosed, it calls fPath->close().  
   - When the loop finishes, fPath contains only moveTo, lineTo, and close operations approximating the original curves, and the function returns fPath.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Out-of-Bounds Access: The code reads path->flags[i] and path->pts[i±k] without explicit bounds checks for i–1, i+1, or i+2. It relies on the invariant that the input path’s length and flag layout guarantee those indices are valid. If path->length or flags[] are inconsistent or corrupted, this can lead to buffer overruns or invalid memory access.

  The function alignContentSpaceBetweenChildren computes spacing between (or around) lines based on available free space and a specified alignment mode:

  - Inputs:  
    • availableFreeSpace (LayoutUnit) – the total extra space to distribute  
    • alignContent (EAlignContent) – an enum indicating the alignment strategy  
    • numberOfLines (unsigned) – how many lines (or rows) of content exist  

  - Behavior:  
    1. If there is positive free space and at least two lines:  
      a. When alignContent == AlignContentSpaceBetween, it divides the free space evenly into (numberOfLines – 1) gaps.  
      b. When alignContent == AlignContentSpaceAround or AlignContentStretch, it divides the free space evenly into numberOfLines gaps.  
    2. In all other cases (no free space, only one line, or an unhandled alignContent value), it returns 0.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

  - Division by zero: The code checks that numberOfLines > 1 before dividing by (numberOfLines – 1) or numberOfLines, so no divide-by-zero can occur.  
  - Integer overflow/underflow: availableFreeSpace is tested for >0; numberOfLines is unsigned but checked >1 before subtraction, avoiding underflow.

original_information.commit_message:
mnt: Correct permission checks in do_remount

While invesgiating the issue where in "mount --bind -oremount,ro ..."
would result in later "mount --bind -oremount,rw" succeeding even if
the mount started off locked I realized that there are several
additional mount flags that should be locked and are not.

In particular MNT_NOSUID, MNT_NODEV, MNT_NOEXEC, and the atime
flags in addition to MNT_READONLY should all be locked.  These
flags are all per superblock, can all be changed with MS_BIND,
and should not be changable if set by a more privileged user.

The following additions to the current logic are added in this patch.
- nosuid may not be clearable by a less privileged user.
- nodev  may not be clearable by a less privielged user.
- noexec may not be clearable by a less privileged user.
- atime flags may not be changeable by a less privileged user.

The logic with atime is that always setting atime on access is a
global policy and backup software and auditing software could break if
atime bits are not updated (when they are configured to be updated),
and serious performance degradation could result (DOS attack) if atime
updates happen when they have been explicitly disabled.  Therefore an
unprivileged user should not be able to mess with the atime bits set
by a more privileged user.

The additional restrictions are implemented with the addition of
MNT_LOCK_NOSUID, MNT_LOCK_NODEV, MNT_LOCK_NOEXEC, and MNT_LOCK_ATIME
mnt flags.

Taken together these changes and the fixes for MNT_LOCK_READONLY
should make it safe for an unprivileged user to create a user
namespace and to call "mount --bind -o remount,... ..." without
the danger of mount flags being changed maliciously.

original_information.commit_message:
sched/fair: Fix infinite loop in update_blocked_averages() by reverting a9e7f6544b9c

Zhipeng Xie, Xie XiuQi and Sargun Dhillon reported lockups in the
scheduler under high loads, starting at around the v4.18 time frame,
and Zhipeng Xie tracked it down to bugs in the rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list
manipulation.

Do a (manual) revert of:

  a9e7f6544b9c ("sched/fair: Fix O(nr_cgroups) in load balance path")

It turns out that the list_del_leaf_cfs_rq() introduced by this commit
is a surprising property that was not considered in followup commits
such as:

  9c2791f936ef ("sched/fair: Fix hierarchical order in rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list")

As Vincent Guittot explains:

 "I think that there is a bigger problem with commit a9e7f6544b9c and
  cfs_rq throttling:

  Let take the example of the following topology TG2 --> TG1 --> root:

   1) The 1st time a task is enqueued, we will add TG2 cfs_rq then TG1
      cfs_rq to leaf_cfs_rq_list and we are sure to do the whole branch in
      one path because it has never been used and can't be throttled so
      tmp_alone_branch will point to leaf_cfs_rq_list at the end.

   2) Then TG1 is throttled

   3) and we add TG3 as a new child of TG1.

   4) The 1st enqueue of a task on TG3 will add TG3 cfs_rq just before TG1
      cfs_rq and tmp_alone_branch will stay  on rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list.

  With commit a9e7f6544b9c, we can del a cfs_rq from rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list.
  So if the load of TG1 cfs_rq becomes NULL before step 2) above, TG1
  cfs_rq is removed from the list.
  Then at step 4), TG3 cfs_rq is added at the beginning of rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list
  but tmp_alone_branch still points to TG3 cfs_rq because its throttled
  parent can't be enqueued when the lock is released.
  tmp_alone_branch doesn't point to rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list whereas it should.

  So if TG3 cfs_rq is removed or destroyed before tmp_alone_branch
  points on another TG cfs_rq, the next TG cfs_rq that will be added,
  will be linked outside rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list - which is bad.

  In addition, we can break the ordering of the cfs_rq in
  rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list but this ordering is used to update and
  propagate the update from leaf down to root."

Instead of trying to work through all these cases and trying to reproduce
the very high loads that produced the lockup to begin with, simplify
the code temporarily by reverting a9e7f6544b9c - which change was clearly
not thought through completely.

This (hopefully) gives us a kernel that doesn't lock up so people
can continue to enjoy their holidays without worrying about regressions. ;-)

1. Functional Analysis

- The function `h2_snd_buf()` is responsible for building and queuing HTTP/2 frames into the provided `buf` for a given HTTP/2 stream (`h2s`), until either  
  a) the HTTP message is fully produced (`h2s->res.state >= HTTP_MSG_DONE`), or  
  b) the output buffer (`buf->o`) no longer has data space, or  
  c) an error or flow-control blocking flag is raised.

- It first marks the stream as having outgoing data if it wasn’t already.  
- It then enters a loop that runs as long as the response is incomplete and there is space in `buf`:  
  • If still producing headers (`state < HTTP_MSG_BODY`), it calls `h2s_frt_make_resp_headers()` to emit header blocks.  
  • Once headers are done but before body trailers (`state < HTTP_MSG_TRAILERS`), it calls `h2s_frt_make_resp_data()` to emit DATA frames.  
  • If it reaches the trailers phase (`state == HTTP_MSG_TRAILERS`), it measures and discards any HTTP/1.x-style trailers in the buffer (it does not forward them over HTTP/2), then marks the message done.  
  • On any fatal error state (`h2s->st >= H2_SS_ERROR`), or if flow-control/blocking flags appear (`H2_SF_BLK_ANY`), it breaks out of the loop.  

- After the main loop, if the stream is in an HTTP/2 error state or an RST was received, it sets `CS_FL_ERROR`, issues an RST_STREAM frame, and closes the stream context.  

- Finally, it updates the connection’s scheduling lists according to any flow-control or blocking flags on the stream, so that streams unblocked by more window or control frames can be reinserted into the send queue.

- The function returns the total number of bytes it appended to `buf`.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Buffer safety:  
  • The code only calls `bo_del(buf, count)` with `count` derived from `h1_measure_trailers(buf)`, which by contract never exceeds the current buffer length (`buf->o`).  
  • The nested calls to remove all remaining bytes (`bo_del(buf, buf->o)`) are likewise bounded by the buffer’s own length field.  
  → No stack or heap overflow risk is apparent from these uses.

- State machine progress and loops:  
  • Each call to `h2s_frt_make_resp_headers()` or `h2s_frt_make_resp_data()` must advance the stream’s state or consume buffer space, and the loop checks for both completion and buffer-space exhaustion.  
  • Blocking flags (`H2_SF_BLK_ANY`) or errors break the loop to prevent infinite spinning.  
  → There is no risk of an infinite loop or CPU spin if the state machine and flow-control flags are implemented correctly.

- Integer overflow/underflow:  
  • The function accumulates return values in `total`, which is an `int`. In typical HTTP/2 frame sizes (tens of kilobytes), this cannot overflow a 32-bit `int`. If someone constructed millions of small frames in one call, it could approach INT_MAX, but practical limits on frame size and buffer size make this infeasible.  
  → No realistic integer-overflow vulnerability.

- Error handling and RST:  
  • On protocol or internal error, the code sends an RST_STREAM and marks the connection error. It does not blindly continue to produce frames after an error.  
  → This is correct according to HTTP/2 specs and prevents malformed states from persisting.

- Flow-control list management:  
  • The code carefully removes and re-adds the stream to the right connection‐level lists depending on window availability.  
  → No use-after-free or list-corruption is visible here.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any obvious buffer overflows, infinite loops, integer overflows, or use-after-free/list corruption vulnerabilities. It properly bounds all buffer removals, advances its state machine, and handles errors/flow-control in accordance with HTTP/2 requirements.

original_information.Summary: An issue was discovered in HAProxy before 1.8.8. The incoming H2 frame length was checked against the max_frame_size setting instead of being checked against the bufsize. The max_frame_size only applies to outgoing traffic and not to incoming, so if a large enough frame size is advertised in the SETTINGS frame, a wrapped frame will be defragmented into a temporary allocated buffer where the second fragment may overflow the heap by up to 16 kB. It is very unlikely that this can be exploited for code execution given that buffers are very short lived and their addresses not realistically predictable in production, but the likelihood of an immediate crash is absolutely certain.

   The function tcp_may_update_window checks whether an incoming TCP segment’s advertised window should be accepted (i.e., “may update” the sender’s notion of the window). It returns true if any of these conditions holds:  
   • after(ack, tp->snd_una)  
     – The incoming ACK number (ack) advances beyond the oldest unacknowledged byte (snd_una), indicating new data has been acknowledged.  
   • after(ack_seq, tp->snd_wl1)  
     – The sequence number of the incoming window advertisement (ack_seq) is greater than the sequence number used for the last window update (snd_wl1), which means it’s a more recent window update.  
   • (ack_seq == tp->snd_wl1 && nwin > tp->snd_wnd)  
     – The sequence number of the incoming window update equals the last one, but the newly advertised window size (nwin) is larger than the current send window (snd_wnd), so the window is growing.

   • Integer overflows: All critical values (ack, ack_seq, nwin, snd_wl1, snd_una, snd_wnd) are 32-bit unsigned; comparisons via after() or simple unsigned comparisons do not introduce undefined behavior or overflow risks.  
   • Logical correctness: The three conditions precisely implement the TCP specification for when a window update is permissible. No invalid memory access or side effects occur.

   - The function ssl3_check_client_certificate(s) returns true (1) if the SSL object s has a client certificate and key suitable for use in the current handshake, or false (0) otherwise.  
   - It first confirms that s->cert, the end-entity X509, and the private key are all present.  
   - If signature algorithms are in use it also checks that a digest method is set on the key.  
   - In “strict TLS” mode it calls tls1_check_chain to verify the certificate chain metadata before proceeding.  
   - It inspects the negotiated key-exchange method via s->s3->tmp.new_cipher->algorithm_mkey.  
   - If the ciphersuite uses static Diffie–Hellman (SSL_kDHr or SSL_kDHd):  
     • It loads the client’s private key and, if that key is of type DH, loads the server’s public DH parameters from the previously established session.  
     • If server parameters are available it compares them to the client’s parameters, failing if they do not match exactly.  
     • Finally, it sets TLS1_FLAGS_SKIP_CERT_VERIFY in s->s3->flags to indicate that the later certificate_verify step may be omitted (because the DH parameters match).  
   - If none of the checks fail, it returns 1; otherwise it returns 0.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Missing Objects Checks: The code correctly rejects s if cert, x509, or privatekey pointers are missing.  
   - Signature-Algorithm Check: When SIGALGS are enabled, the code refuses certificates without a configured digest—this prevents the use of certificates that cannot produce a valid signature under the negotiated hash.  
   - Chain Validation in Strict Mode: The optional tls1_check_chain call ensures in strict mode that the entire certificate chain meets policy before the cert is used.  
   - DH-Parameter Comparison: For static-DH ciphersuites, it refuses a client key if its DH parameters don’t match the server’s.  
     • One minor gap: if peer_cert_type < 0 (no server public key loaded), spkey stays NULL and the parameter check is skipped, but the code still accepts the client DH key and sets SKIP_CERT_VERIFY. In practice peer_cert_type <0 only occurs if the session was not resumed or mis-initialized, so this path will rarely be taken.  
   - SKIP_CERT_VERIFY Flag: The code sets TLS1_FLAGS_SKIP_CERT_VERIFY only after confirming DH-parameter consistency; in all other cases the certificate_verify message will still be required.  

   Overall, no unchecked pointer dereferences or missing length/size validations are present. 1. Functional Analysis

- The function perf_callchain_kernel() collects a kernel-mode call chain (stack of return addresses) into a perf_callchain_entry.
- It begins by reading the stack pointer (sp), return‐address register (ra), and program counter (pc) out of the register context (pt_regs).
- Under CONFIG_KALLSYMS (kernel‐symbol support enabled):
  • If raw_show_trace is set or the current pc is not in the kernel’s text section, it treats this as a “raw” stack dump.  
    – It computes the base of the current task’s stack (task_stack_page), checks that sp lies within [stack_page, stack_page + THREAD_SIZE − 32], and if so calls save_raw_perf_callchain() to record the raw stack contents.  
    – Then it returns without any further unwinding.  
  • Otherwise (standard, symbolized backtrace):  
    – It enters a loop where it stores the current pc in the callchain entry via perf_callchain_store().  
    – It breaks out if it has reached PERF_MAX_STACK_DEPTH.  
    – It calls unwind_stack() to step to the next frame, updating sp/ra/pc, and repeats until pc becomes zero.  
- Without CONFIG_KALLSYMS, it always does the raw stack‑pointer‐based dump via save_raw_perf_callchain().

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Buffer overruns in the callchain entry are prevented:  
  • perf_callchain_store() only appends if entry->nr < PERF_MAX_STACK_DEPTH, and the loop checks nr against that same limit.  
  • save_raw_perf_callchain() is likewise expected to respect the THREAD_SIZE bound.  
- The raw‑dump path checks that sp lies within the current task’s stack page range before reading memory.  
- The symbolized unwind path only proceeds when pc is in kernel text, so it cannot chase into arbitrary user addresses.  
- Control is never transferred to user‐supplied function pointers, nor are there unchecked integer arithmetic operations on user data.  
- The only external inputs are pt_regs (provided by a trap or interrupt) and current task context; neither allows the attacker to force out‑of‑bounds memory reads or buffer overwrites in this code path.  
- unwind_stack() is assumed to validate frame pointers internally; if it did not, one could imagine it walking into invalid memory—but that would be a flaw in the unwinder, not in this function.

3. Decision

No. The code enforces stack‐pointer bounds on raw dumps, limits callchain depth, and restricts unwinding to kernel text addresses, so it does not contain any obvious memory‐safety or control‐flow vulnerabilities.

original_information.commit_message:
perf: Remove the nmi parameter from the swevent and overflow interface

The nmi parameter indicated if we could do wakeups from the current
context, if not, we would set some state and self-IPI and let the
resulting interrupt do the wakeup.

For the various event classes:

  - hardware: nmi=0; PMI is in fact an NMI or we run irq_work_run from
    the PMI-tail (ARM etc.)
  - tracepoint: nmi=0; since tracepoint could be from NMI context.
  - software: nmi=[0,1]; some, like the schedule thing cannot
    perform wakeups, and hence need 0.

As one can see, there is very little nmi=1 usage, and the down-side of
not using it is that on some platforms some software events can have a
jiffy delay in wakeup (when arch_irq_work_raise isn't implemented).

The up-side however is that we can remove the nmi parameter and save a
bunch of conditionals in fast paths.

original_information.commit_message:
KEYS: Fix race between updating and finding a negative key

Consolidate KEY_FLAG_INSTANTIATED, KEY_FLAG_NEGATIVE and the rejection
error into one field such that:

 (1) The instantiation state can be modified/read atomically.

 (2) The error can be accessed atomically with the state.

 (3) The error isn't stored unioned with the payload pointers.

This deals with the problem that the state is spread over three different
objects (two bits and a separate variable) and reading or updating them
atomically isn't practical, given that not only can uninstantiated keys
change into instantiated or rejected keys, but rejected keys can also turn
into instantiated keys - and someone accessing the key might not be using
any locking.

The main side effect of this problem is that what was held in the payload
may change, depending on the state.  For instance, you might observe the
key to be in the rejected state.  You then read the cached error, but if
the key semaphore wasn't locked, the key might've become instantiated
between the two reads - and you might now have something in hand that isn't
actually an error code.

The state is now KEY_IS_UNINSTANTIATED, KEY_IS_POSITIVE or a negative error
code if the key is negatively instantiated.  The key_is_instantiated()
function is replaced with key_is_positive() to avoid confusion as negative
keys are also 'instantiated'.

Additionally, barriering is included:

 (1) Order payload-set before state-set during instantiation.

 (2) Order state-read before payload-read when using the key.

Further separate barriering is necessary if RCU is being used to access the
payload content after reading the payload pointers.

Fixes: 146aa8b1453b ("KEYS: Merge the type-specific data with the payload data")

1. Functional Analysis  
   
   The function `last_fsync_dnode` searches for the most recent “dirty” node-page (a cold data-node) in the F2FS node mapping that belongs to a given inode number `ino`. It proceeds as follows:  
   - Initialize a pagevec to batch page lookups, and set the search range from index 0 to `ULONG_MAX`.  
   - In a loop, call `pagevec_lookup_tag` to fetch up to PAGEVEC_SIZE dirty pages starting at the current index.  
   - For each returned page:  
     • Check for a checkpoint error (`f2fs_cp_error`). If one has occurred, release any held page reference and return an I/O error.  
     • Filter out pages that are not data-nodes (`IS_DNODE`), not marked “cold” (`is_cold_node`), or not belonging to the requested inode (`ino_of_node`).  
     • Lock the page, recheck that its mapping is still the node mapping and the inode number still matches, and verify it remains dirty. If any check fails, unlock and skip it.  
     • If it still qualifies, drop the reference to any previously saved page, increment the refcount of the new page, save it as `last_page`, and unlock it.  
   - After each batch, release the pagevec and call `cond_resched` to allow preemption.  
   - Continue until no more dirty pages are found. Return the last qualifying page (or NULL if none).  
   
2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   
   - Memory safety / reference counting:  
     • Every time a candidate page is replaced as `last_page`, the old page’s reference is dropped (via `f2fs_put_page`). On error, any held `last_page` is put before returning. The final `last_page`, if non-NULL, remains referenced for the caller. No leaks or double‐frees are evident.  
   - Race conditions:  
     • The code rechecks `page->mapping` and `ino_of_node` under the page lock before taking a reference, guarding against races where the page migrates or is freed.  
     • It also rechecks `PageDirty(page)` under lock to avoid racing with an external writer that might have cleaned the page after the initial tag lookup.  
   - Bounds and iteration:  
     • The search range is from 0 to `ULONG_MAX`, but `pagevec_lookup_tag` limits the batch size to PAGEVEC_SIZE, preventing unbounded array accesses.  
   - Error handling:  
     • Checkpoint errors are detected early; the function aborts cleanly, releasing any references and returning an appropriate `ERR_PTR(-EIO)`.  
   - Resource exhaustion or DoS:  
     • The code yields with `cond_resched()` between batches, avoiding excessive CPU hogging, and does no dynamic allocation that could fail under memory pressure.  
   
   Taken together, the code systematically locks pages before revalidating critical invariants, maintains correct refcount discipline, and handles errors and preemption. There are no obvious memory-safety issues, race windows left unprotected, or logic flaws that would expose a vulnerability.  
   
3. Decision  
   
   No, the code does not contain any apparent vulnerabilities; it correctly filters, locks, rechecks, and references pages and cleans up on errors.

original_information.commit_message:
Avoid using forced layout to trigger paint invalidation for SVG containers

Currently, SVG containers in the LayoutObject hierarchy force layout of
their children if the transform changes. The main reason for this is to
trigger paint invalidation of the subtree. In some cases - changes to the
scale factor - there are other reasons to trigger layout, like computing
a new scale factor for <text> or re-layout nodes with non-scaling stroke.

Compute a "scale-factor change" in addition to the "transform change"
already computed, then use this new signal to determine if layout should
be forced for the subtree. Trigger paint invalidation using the
LayoutObject flags instead.

The downside to this is that paint invalidation will walk into "hidden"
containers which rarely require repaint (since they are not technically
visible). This will hopefully be rectified in a follow-up CL.

For the testcase from 603850, this essentially eliminates the cost of
layout (from ~350ms to ~0ms on authors machine; layout cost is related
to text metrics recalculation), bumping frame rate significantly.

original_information.commit_message:
net: Compute protocol sequence numbers and fragment IDs using MD5.

Computers have become a lot faster since we compromised on the
partial MD4 hash which we use currently for performance reasons.

MD5 is a much safer choice, and is inline with both RFC1948 and
other ISS generators (OpenBSD, Solaris, etc.)

Furthermore, only having 24-bits of the sequence number be truly
unpredictable is a very serious limitation.  So the periodic
regeneration and 8-bit counter have been removed.  We compute and
use a full 32-bit sequence number.

For ipv6, DCCP was found to use a 32-bit truncated initial sequence
number (it needs 43-bits) and that is fixed here as well.

ALSA: control: Protect user controls against concurrent access

The user-control put and get handlers as well as the tlv do not protect against
concurrent access from multiple threads. Since the state of the control is not
updated atomically it is possible that either two write operations or a write
and a read operation race against each other. Both can lead to arbitrary memory
disclosure. This patch introduces a new lock that protects user-controls from
concurrent access. Since applications typically access controls sequentially
than in parallel a single lock per card should be fine.

- It first grabs the global MID queue lock (`GlobalMid_Lock`) to check or set the server’s `tcpStatus` to `CifsNeedReconnect`, unless the server is already exiting.
- It then zeroes out `server->maxBuf` and logs that it is reconnecting.
- Under the `cifs_tcp_ses_lock` read lock, it walks the list of SMB sessions (`smb_ses_list`) on this server, marking each session’s `need_reconnect` flag and resetting its `ipc_tid`.  For each session, it also walks its list of tree connects (`tcon_list`) and marks each `tcon->need_reconnect`.
- It takes the server’s `srv_mutex` to serialize socket teardown, then:
  - If there is an existing socket (`ssocket`), it performs a shutdown of writes, releases the socket, and clears `server->ssocket`.
- While still holding `srv_mutex`, it grabs `GlobalMid_Lock` again and scans the pending MID queue (`pending_mid_q`), changing any entries in state `MID_REQUEST_SUBMITTED` to `MID_RETRY_NEEDED`, then releases both locks.
- Finally, it enters a loop that continues until the server’s `tcpStatus` becomes `CifsGood` (or `CifsExiting`):
  - Calls `try_to_freeze()` (for kernel freeze support).
  - Chooses IPv4 or IPv6 connect based on the stored address and attempts `ipv4_connect` or `ipv6_connect`.
  - On failure, logs the error and sleeps 3 seconds, then retries.
  - On success, increments a reconnect counter, sets `tcpStatus` to `CifsGood`, resets `sequence_number`, and wakes up any waiters on `response_q`.
- Returns the last connect return code (`rc`).

  The socket teardown (`kernel_sock_shutdown`/`sock_release`) is protected by `srv_mutex`, and new use of `ssocket` elsewhere is expected to also take that mutex or check `tcpStatus`.  No window appears in which another thread can send on a freed socket.
- MID queue consistency:  
  The pending MID queue is always modified or read under `GlobalMid_Lock`, so entries are not corrupted by concurrent accesses.
- Deadlocks:  
  The code acquires locks in a consistent order (spin lock only briefly, then unlocks before taking the mutex; later it takes the mutex then the spin lock, but no other code holds the mutex and then tries the spin lock at the same time).  There is no inversion seen in this snippet.
- Resource leaks:  
  The old socket is released exactly once and replaced only on a successful connect.  No leaks of sockets are evident.
- Infinite-loop / denial of service:  
  If the server is unreachable, the loop will repeatedly sleep and retry, which is expected reconnect behavior, not a security flaw.
- No buffer overflows or integer overflows are present; no unbounded memory writes or user-controlled length copies occur in this snippet.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any obvious vulnerabilities. It correctly synchronizes socket teardown and reconnection state, protects the MID queue, and handles error retries cleanly.

original_information.commit_message:
coredump: fix race condition between mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm() and core dumping

The core dumping code has always run without holding the mmap_sem for
writing, despite that is the only way to ensure that the entire vma
layout will not change from under it.  Only using some signal
serialization on the processes belonging to the mm is not nearly enough.
This was pointed out earlier.  For example in Hugh's post from Jul 2017:

  https://lkml.kernel.org/r/alpine.LSU.2.11.1707191716030.2055@eggly.anvils

  "Not strictly relevant here, but a related note: I was very surprised
   to discover, only quite recently, how handle_mm_fault() may be called
   without down_read(mmap_sem) - when core dumping. That seems a
   misguided optimization to me, which would also be nice to correct"

In particular because the growsdown and growsup can move the
vm_start/vm_end the various loops the core dump does around the vma will
not be consistent if page faults can happen concurrently.

Pretty much all users calling mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm() and then
taking the mmap_sem had the potential to introduce unexpected side
effects in the core dumping code.

Adding mmap_sem for writing around the ->core_dump invocation is a
viable long term fix, but it requires removing all copy user and page
faults and to replace them with get_dump_page() for all binary formats
which is not suitable as a short term fix.

For the time being this solution manually covers the places that can
confuse the core dump either by altering the vma layout or the vma flags
while it runs.  Once ->core_dump runs under mmap_sem for writing the
function mmget_still_valid() can be dropped.

Allowing mmap_sem protected sections to run in parallel with the
coredump provides some minor parallelism advantage to the swapoff code
(which seems to be safe enough by never mangling any vma field and can
keep doing swapins in parallel to the core dumping) and to some other
corner case.

In order to facilitate the backporting I added "Fixes: 86039bd3b4e6"
however the side effect of this same race condition in /proc/pid/mem
should be reproducible since before 2.6.12-rc2 so I couldn't add any
other "Fixes:" because there's no hash beyond the git genesis commit.

Because find_extend_vma() is the only location outside of the process
context that could modify the "mm" structures under mmap_sem for
reading, by adding the mmget_still_valid() check to it, all other cases
that take the mmap_sem for reading don't need the new check after
mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm().  The expand_stack() in page fault
context also doesn't need the new check, because all tasks under core
dumping are frozen.

original_information.commit_message:
dm snapshot: fix data corruption

This patch fixes a particular type of data corruption that has been
encountered when loading a snapshot's metadata from disk.

When we allocate a new chunk in persistent_prepare, we increment
ps->next_free and we make sure that it doesn't point to a metadata area
by further incrementing it if necessary.

When we load metadata from disk on device activation, ps->next_free is
positioned after the last used data chunk. However, if this last used
data chunk is followed by a metadata area, ps->next_free is positioned
erroneously to the metadata area. A newly-allocated chunk is placed at
the same location as the metadata area, resulting in data or metadata
corruption.

This patch changes the code so that ps->next_free skips the metadata
area when metadata are loaded in function read_exceptions.

The patch also moves a piece of code from persistent_prepare_exception
to a separate function skip_metadata to avoid code duplication.

CVE-2013-4299

   - The function `scopeof` takes a pointer to an IPv6 address (`struct in6_addr *a`) and returns an integer “scope” value according to IPv6 address semantics.  
   - It first checks if the address is a multicast address (`IN6_IS_ADDR_MULTICAST(a)`). If so, it returns the low 4 bits of the second byte (`a->s6_addr[1] & 0x0F`), which is where the IPv6 multicast scope is encoded.  
   - If not multicast, it checks if the address is link‑local or loopback, returning scope `2` for either case.  
   - Next it checks for site‑local addresses and returns scope `5`.  
   - If none of the above conditions match, it treats the address as global and returns scope `14`.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - There is no dynamic memory allocation, no buffer or array writes, and no arithmetic that could overflow; the code only reads a fixed‑size array and performs bit operations.  
   - The only potential issue is that the function does not check for a NULL pointer; if `a` were NULL, it would dereference and crash, but this is not a security vulnerability per se if the caller guarantees a valid pointer.  
   - There are no path conditions that allow out‑of‑bounds access or uninitialized reads.  

3. Decision  
   No, the function does not contain any exploitable vulnerabilities.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function `check_subscription_permission` enforces access control when a client attempts to set up a MIDI (ALSA sequencer) subscription between two ports.
- It takes four arguments:
  • `client`     – the client requesting the subscription  
  • `sport`      – the source port object  
  • `dport`      – the destination port object  
  • `subs`       – subscription parameters (which client is sender/dest)
- First, it checks whether the requesting client is neither the declared sender nor the declared receiver:
  • If it is a “third party” trying to link two other clients’ ports, it checks both ports for the `SNDRV_SEQ_PORT_CAP_NO_EXPORT` flag.  
  • If either port disallows export, it rejects with `-EPERM`.
- Next it enforces read permission on the source port:
  • If the requester is not the sender, it calls `check_port_perm(sport, PERM_RD)` and rejects if that returns false.
- Then it enforces write permission on the destination port:
  • If the requester is not the receiver, it calls `check_port_perm(dport, PERM_WR)` and rejects if that returns false.
- If all checks pass, it returns 0 (success).

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Memory safety: The function only reads pointers passed in; it does not dereference them in an unsafe way or perform any buffer manipulation. There is no obvious buffer overflow, use-after-free, or similar memory vulnerability here.
- Logic/race: All decisions are based on simple integer comparisons and flag checks. A TOCTOU window could exist if port permissions change concurrently, but that would be a broader synchronization concern in the subsystem, not a bug in these straight checks.
- Privilege bypass: The logic ensures that:
  • Third-party connections respect the “no export” flag on both ports.  
  • Direct subscribers have to hold read or write rights unless they are the port owner.  
  There is no branch that inadvertently skips a needed check.
- Information leak: The function returns `-EPERM` generically rather than distinguishing “read vs. write vs. export” failure modes, so it does not reveal extra internal state.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any obvious vulnerabilities. It consistently enforces the intended permission checks without unsafe memory operations or logic gaps.

original_information.Summary: The snd_seq_ioctl_remove_events function in sound/core/seq/seq_clientmgr.c in the Linux kernel before 4.4.1 does not verify FIFO assignment before proceeding with FIFO clearing, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and OOPS) via a crafted ioctl call.
original_information.commit_message:
ALSA: seq: Fix missing NULL check at remove_events ioctl

snd_seq_ioctl_remove_events() calls snd_seq_fifo_clear()
unconditionally even if there is no FIFO assigned, and this leads to
an Oops due to NULL dereference.  The fix is just to add a proper NULL
check.

Reported-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Tested-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>

+		if (client->type == USER_CLIENT && client->data.user.fifo)

- The function starts by initializing a local variable `wordBreakSpacing` with the value of `m_wordSpacingAdjustment`.  
- It then checks whether `m_padding` is greater than zero. If so:  
  - It computes an integer `toPad` by rounding the sum of `m_padPerWordBreak` (a floating‑point per‑break padding amount) and `m_padError` (a running floating‑point error term).  
  - It updates the error accumulator `m_padError` by adding the difference `(m_padPerWordBreak - toPad)`, thereby tracking any fractional remainder for future calls.  
  - If the requested `toPad` exceeds the remaining `m_padding`, it clamps `toPad` to `m_padding`.  
  - It subtracts the (possibly clamped) `toPad` from `m_padding`, reducing the remaining padding budget.  
  - It adds `toPad` to `wordBreakSpacing`.  
- Finally, it returns the computed `wordBreakSpacing`, which combines the base adjustment and any padding applied for this word break.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- There is no direct user input or external data parsing in this function—`m_padding`, `m_padPerWordBreak`, `m_padError`, and `m_wordSpacingAdjustment` are assumed to be internal state.  
- All arithmetic is well‑bounded:  
  - The floating‑to‑integer conversion uses `roundf`, which cannot overflow a typical 32‑bit `int` unless the floats are already extreme (unlikely for padding values).  
  - The clamp `if (m_padding < toPad) toPad = m_padding;` prevents negative or excessive subtraction.  
  - There are no pointers, buffer operations, or dynamic memory manipulations.  
  - No side‑effects leak memory or expose data.  
- Consequently, standard memory corruption (e.g., buffer overflow), integer overflow, format string, or injection vulnerabilities are not present in this snippet.

3. Decision

No, this code does not contain any evident security vulnerabilities; it correctly bounds and updates its internal state.

net: rework recvmsg handler msg_name and msg_namelen logic

This patch now always passes msg->msg_namelen as 0. recvmsg handlers must
set msg_namelen to the proper size <= sizeof(struct sockaddr_storage)
to return msg_name to the user.

recvmsg handlers and makes it harder for new code to accidentally leak
uninitialized memory.

need to copy the address at all, so set it to NULL before invoking the
recvmsg handler. We can do so, because all the recvmsg handlers must
cope with the case a plain read() is called on them. read() also sets
msg_name to NULL.

Miller.

non-null msg_namelen in verify_iovec/verify_compat_iovec. This doesn't
affect sendto as it would bail out earlier while trying to copy-in the
address. It also more naturally reflects the logic by the callers of
verify_iovec.

With this change in place I could remove "
if (!uaddr || msg_sys->msg_namelen == 0)
	msg->msg_name = NULL
".

This change does not alter the user visible error logic as we ignore
msg_namelen as long as msg_name is NULL.

Also remove two unnecessary curly brackets in ___sys_recvmsg and change
comments to netdev style.

original_information.commit_message:
net: sctp: fix ipv6 ipsec encryption bug in sctp_v6_xmit

Alan Chester reported an issue with IPv6 on SCTP that IPsec traffic is not
being encrypted, whereas on IPv4 it is. Setting up an AH + ESP transport
does not seem to have the desired effect:

SCTP + IPv4:

  22:14:20.809645 IP (tos 0x2,ECT(0), ttl 64, id 0, offset 0, flags [DF], proto AH (51), length 116)
    192.168.0.2 > 192.168.0.5: AH(spi=0x00000042,sumlen=16,seq=0x1): ESP(spi=0x00000044,seq=0x1), length 72
  22:14:20.813270 IP (tos 0x2,ECT(0), ttl 64, id 0, offset 0, flags [DF], proto AH (51), length 340)
    192.168.0.5 > 192.168.0.2: AH(spi=0x00000043,sumlen=16,seq=0x1):

SCTP + IPv6:

  22:31:19.215029 IP6 (class 0x02, hlim 64, next-header SCTP (132) payload length: 364)
    fe80::222:15ff:fe87:7fc.3333 > fe80::92e6:baff:fe0d:5a54.36767: sctp
    1) [INIT ACK] [init tag: 747759530] [rwnd: 62464] [OS: 10] [MIS: 10]

Moreover, Alan says:

  This problem was seen with both Racoon and Racoon2. Other people have seen
  this with OpenSwan. When IPsec is configured to encrypt all upper layer
  protocols the SCTP connection does not initialize. After using Wireshark to
  follow packets, this is because the SCTP packet leaves Box A unencrypted and
  Box B believes all upper layer protocols are to be encrypted so it drops
  this packet, causing the SCTP connection to fail to initialize. When IPsec
  is configured to encrypt just SCTP, the SCTP packets are observed unencrypted.

In fact, using `socat sctp6-listen:3333 -` on one end and transferring "plaintext"
string on the other end, results in cleartext on the wire where SCTP eventually
does not report any errors, thus in the latter case that Alan reports, the
non-paranoid user might think he's communicating over an encrypted transport on
SCTP although he's not (tcpdump ... -X):

  ...
  0x0030: 5d70 8e1a 0003 001a 177d eb6c 0000 0000  ]p.......}.l....
  0x0040: 0000 0000 706c 6169 6e74 6578 740a 0000  ....plaintext...

Only in /proc/net/xfrm_stat we can see XfrmInTmplMismatch increasing on the
receiver side. Initial follow-up analysis from Alan's bug report was done by
Alexey Dobriyan. Also thanks to Vlad Yasevich for feedback on this.

SCTP has its own implementation of sctp_v6_xmit() not calling inet6_csk_xmit().
This has the implication that it probably never really got updated along with
changes in inet6_csk_xmit() and therefore does not seem to invoke xfrm handlers.

SCTP's IPv4 xmit however, properly calls ip_queue_xmit() to do the work. Since
a call to inet6_csk_xmit() would solve this problem, but result in unecessary
route lookups, let us just use the cached flowi6 instead that we got through
sctp_v6_get_dst(). Since all SCTP packets are being sent through sctp_packet_transmit(),
we do the route lookup / flow caching in sctp_transport_route(), hold it in
tp->dst and skb_dst_set() right after that. If we would alter fl6->daddr in
sctp_v6_xmit() to np->opt->srcrt, we possibly could run into the same effect
of not having xfrm layer pick it up, hence, use fl6_update_dst() in sctp_v6_get_dst()
instead to get the correct source routed dst entry, which we assign to the skb.

Also source address routing example from 625034113 ("sctp: fix sctp to work with
ipv6 source address routing") still works with this patch! Nevertheless, in RFC5095
it is actually 'recommended' to not use that anyway due to traffic amplification [1].
So it seems we're not supposed to do that anyway in sctp_v6_xmit(). Moreover, if
we overwrite the flow destination here, the lower IPv6 layer will be unable to
put the correct destination address into IP header, as routing header is added in
ipv6_push_nfrag_opts() but then probably with wrong final destination. Things aside,
result of this patch is that we do not have any XfrmInTmplMismatch increase plus on
the wire with this patch it now looks like:

SCTP + IPv6:

  08:17:47.074080 IP6 2620:52:0:102f:7a2b:cbff:fe27:1b0a > 2620:52:0:102f:213:72ff:fe32:7eba:
    AH(spi=0x00005fb4,seq=0x1): ESP(spi=0x00005fb5,seq=0x1), length 72
  08:17:47.074264 IP6 2620:52:0:102f:213:72ff:fe32:7eba > 2620:52:0:102f:7a2b:cbff:fe27:1b0a:
    AH(spi=0x00003d54,seq=0x1): ESP(spi=0x00003d55,seq=0x1), length 296

This fixes Kernel Bugzilla 24412. This security issue seems to be present since
2.6.18 kernels. Lets just hope some big passive adversary in the wild didn't have
its fun with that. lksctp-tools IPv6 regression test suite passes as well with
this patch.

 [1] http://www.secdev.org/conf/IPv6_RH_security-csw07.pdf

  - Call `pf_reset(pf)` and return –1 immediately on failure.
  - If `pf->lun` is set, call `pf_identify(pf)` and return its result.
  - Otherwise loop `pf->lun` from 0 to 7, call `pf_identify(pf)`, returning 0 on first success.
- If no reset or identify succeeds in any path, it returns –1.

- Buffer overflows: None. There are no raw memory copies or string operations.

- The function `get_info` is an ioctl/getsockopt-style handler that returns information about an iptables table (IPv4).
- It takes three arguments:
  • `net`: the network namespace  
  • `user`: a user‐space pointer, which holds both the input name and will receive the output struct  
  • `len`: a pointer to an integer holding the size of the user buffer  
  • `compat`: flag indicating a 32-bit-compat mode call
- Step by step:
  a. Check that the user’s `*len` exactly matches `sizeof(struct ipt_getinfo)`; if not, return –EINVAL.  
  b. Copy up to `XT_TABLE_MAXNAMELEN` bytes from user memory into a local `name[]` buffer; terminate it with `'\0'`.  
  c. If in compat mode, acquire the compat lock for IPv4.  
  d. Lookup and lock the requested table by name via `xt_request_find_table_lock`.  
  e. On success, build a local `struct ipt_getinfo info`:
     - Zero the struct.  
     - Fill in `valid_hooks`, `hook_entry[]`, `underflow[]`, `num_entries`, `size`, and `name`.  
     - In compat mode, translate the internal `xt_table_info` into a temporary compat‐safe copy.  
  f. Copy the filled `info` back to user space via `copy_to_user`.  
  g. Release the table lock, put the module reference, and (if compat) release the compat lock.  
  h. Return 0 on success or the appropriate negative error code.
  
2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Length check: The code rejects any request whose length does not exactly match `sizeof(struct ipt_getinfo)`. This prevents user requests that are too small or too large.  
- Buffer overflow prevention:  
  • `copy_from_user(name, …, sizeof(name))` reads at most `XT_TABLE_MAXNAMELEN` bytes.  
  • `name[XT_TABLE_MAXNAMELEN-1] = '\0'` guarantees NUL termination.  
  • `copy_to_user(user, &info, *len)` copies exactly the verified size.  
- Concurrency and locking:  
  • The code takes the appropriate xtables lock before inspecting `t->private`.  
  • It holds the module reference (`module_put`) until after the copy.  
- Error handling: All `copy_*_user` calls are checked for faults; the table lookup return value is checked with `IS_ERR`/`PTR_ERR`.  
- No unchecked pointers or arithmetic on user data are used; all user‐provided sizes and names are bounded and validated.  
- There is no use of `strcpy` on untrusted strings without size limits (the only `strcpy` copies a guaranteed‐NUL’d local array into a struct field sized the same).  

Conclusion: every external input is range‐checked or bounded; appropriate locks and error checks are in place. There are no evident memory‐safety, buffer‐overflow, integer‐overflow, or use‐after‐free issues.

3. Decision

No, this code does not contain any obvious vulnerabilities. It properly validates sizes, bounds string copies, handles errors, and uses locking/module references correctly.

original_information.commit_message:
netfilter: add back stackpointer size checks

The rationale for removing the check is only correct for rulesets
generated by ip(6)tables.

In iptables, a jump can only occur to a user-defined chain, i.e.
because we size the stack based on number of user-defined chains we
cannot exceed stack size.

However, the underlying binary format has no such restriction,
and the validation step only ensures that the jump target is a
valid rule start point.

IOW, its possible to build a rule blob that has no user-defined
chains but does contain a jump.

If this happens, no jump stack gets allocated and crash occurs
because no jumpstack was allocated.

Fixes: 7814b6ec6d0d6 ("netfilter: xtables: don't save/restore jumpstack offset")

original_information.commit_message:
When opening files for write, ensure they aren't symbolic links

Issue #1048 identified that if, for example, a non privileged user
created a symbolic link from /etc/keepalvied.data to /etc/passwd,
writing to /etc/keepalived.data (which could be invoked via DBus)
would cause /etc/passwd to be overwritten.

This commit stops keepalived writing to pathnames where the ultimate
component is a symbolic link, by setting O_NOFOLLOW whenever opening
a file for writing.

This might break some setups, where, for example, /etc/keepalived.data
was a symbolic link to /home/fred/keepalived.data. If this was the case,
instead create a symbolic link from /home/fred/keepalived.data to
/tmp/keepalived.data, so that the file is still accessible via

Problem is ip_make_skb() calls ip_setup_cork() and

original_information.commit_message:
Btrfs: fix hash overflow handling

The handling for directory crc hash overflows was fairly obscure,
split_leaf returns EOVERFLOW when we try to extend the item and that is
supposed to bubble up to userland.  For a while it did so, but along the
way we added better handling of errors and forced the FS readonly if we
hit IO errors during the directory insertion.

Along the way, we started testing only for EEXIST and the EOVERFLOW case
was dropped.  The end result is that we may force the FS readonly if we
catch a directory hash bucket overflow.

This fixes a few problem spots.  First I add tests for EOVERFLOW in the
places where we can safely just return the error up the chain.

btrfs_rename is harder though, because it tries to insert the new
directory item only after it has already unlinked anything the rename
was going to overwrite.  Rather than adding very complex logic, I added
a helper to test for the hash overflow case early while it is still safe
to bail out.

Snapshot and subvolume creation had a similar problem, so they are using
the new helper now too.

Signed-off-by: Chris Mason <chris.mason@fusionio.com>
Reported-by: Pascal Junod <pascal@junod.info>

original_information.commit_message:
Avoid using forced layout to trigger paint invalidation for SVG containers

Currently, SVG containers in the LayoutObject hierarchy force layout of
their children if the transform changes. The main reason for this is to
trigger paint invalidation of the subtree. In some cases - changes to the
scale factor - there are other reasons to trigger layout, like computing
a new scale factor for <text> or re-layout nodes with non-scaling stroke.

Compute a "scale-factor change" in addition to the "transform change"
already computed, then use this new signal to determine if layout should
be forced for the subtree. Trigger paint invalidation using the
LayoutObject flags instead.

The downside to this is that paint invalidation will walk into "hidden"
containers which rarely require repaint (since they are not technically
visible). This will hopefully be rectified in a follow-up CL.

For the testcase from 603850, this essentially eliminates the cost of
layout (from ~350ms to ~0ms on authors machine; layout cost is related
to text metrics recalculation), bumping frame rate significantly.

socket: close race condition between sock_close() and sockfs_setattr()

fchownat() doesn't even hold refcnt of fd until it figures out
fd is really needed (otherwise is ignored) and releases it after
it resolves the path. This means sock_close() could race with
sockfs_setattr(), which leads to a NULL pointer dereference
since typically we set sock->sk to NULL in ->release().

As pointed out by Al, this is unique to sockfs. So we can fix this
in socket layer by acquiring inode_lock in sock_close() and
checking against NULL in sockfs_setattr().

sock_release() is called in many places, only the sock_close()
path matters here. And fortunately, this should not affect normal
sock_close() as it is only called when the last fd refcnt is gone.
It only affects sock_close() with a parallel sockfs_setattr() in
progress, which is not common.

Separate repaint and layout requirements of StyleDifference (Step 1)

Previously StyleDifference was an enum that proximately bigger values
imply smaller values (e.g. StyleDifferenceLayout implies
StyleDifferenceRepaint). This causes unnecessary repaints in some cases
on layout change.

Convert StyleDifference to a structure containing relatively independent
flags.

repaint optimizations possible.

Step 1 doesn't change any functionality. RenderStyle still generate the
legacy StyleDifference enum when comparing styles and convert the result
to the new StyleDifference. Implicit requirements are not handled during
the conversion.

Converted call sites to use the new StyleDifference according to the
following conversion rules:
- diff == StyleDifferenceEqual (&& !context) => diff.hasNoChange()
- diff == StyleDifferenceRepaint => diff.needsRepaintObjectOnly()
- diff == StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsRepaintLayer()
- diff == StyleDifferenceRepaint || diff == StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsRepaintLayer()
- diff >= StyleDifferenceRepaint => diff.needsRepaint() || diff.needsLayout()
- diff >= StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsRepaintLayer() || diff.needsLayout()
- diff > StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsLayout()
- diff == StyleDifferencePositionedMovementLayoutOnly => diff.needsPositionedMovementLayoutOnly()
- diff == StyleDifferenceLayout => diff.needsFullLayout()

  - starttime: Requested ticket start time  
  - endtime: Requested ticket expiration time (client’s “until”)  
  - till: Optional administrative override for “until” (0 means “no override”)  
  - client, server: Database entries that may impose per-principal maximum lifetimes  
  - out_endtime: Output pointer for the computed expiration  

- Step by step  
  1. If till is zero, replace it with kdc_infinity (i.e., no practical limit).  
  2. Compute until = min(till, endtime).  This is the latest allowed expiry before consulting principal/realm limits.  
  3. Compute life = until – starttime.  This is the raw requested ticket lifetime.  
  4. If the client entry has a nonzero max_life, clamp life to that.  
  5. Clamp life to the server’s max_life if nonzero.  
  6. Clamp life to the realm’s realm_maxlife if nonzero.  
  7. Set *out_endtime = starttime + life.  

Overall, the code enforces a ticket expiration that cannot exceed any of: the client’s request, an administrative “till” override, or the max_life settings in the client, server, or realm objects.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Integer Overflow/Underflow  
  • Subtracting starttime from until yields a signed result (“life”). Because timestamps in Kerberos (krb5_timestamp) are signed, this subtraction can produce a negative value if starttime > until. The code never wraps unsigned, so there’s no silent underflow.  
  • Adding life back to starttime yields until (in the negative‐life case). There is no overflow unless life or starttime are so large that the signed addition exceeds the range of krb5_timestamp. In practice all max_life values are administratively constrained well below INT_MAX, so overflow is not a realistic concern.  

- Logical Errors  
  • If starttime > until, life becomes negative and the resulting *out_endtime equals until, which is earlier than starttime. This simply produces an immediately expired ticket rather than enabling any privilege escalation.  

- Memory Safety  
  • There is no buffer manipulation or pointer arithmetic beyond writing the final timestamp.  

- Authorization Bypass  
  • All relevant limits (client, server, realm, request parameters) are checked in turn. No stage can extend the ticket beyond the tightest ceiling.  

Conclusion: The function correctly computes an expiration time bounded by all configured limits. There is no exploitable integer wrap‐around or logical flaw that would allow a user to extend a ticket’s life.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain a vulnerability. It properly bounds the ticket lifetime by all requested and configured limits.

original_information.commit_message:
bpf: fix branch pruning logic

when the verifier detects that register contains a runtime constant
and it's compared with another constant it will prune exploration
of the branch that is guaranteed not to be taken at runtime.
This is all correct, but malicious program may be constructed
in such a way that it always has a constant comparison and
the other branch is never taken under any conditions.
In this case such path through the program will not be explored
by the verifier. It won't be taken at run-time either, but since
all instructions are JITed the malicious program may cause JITs
to complain about using reserved fields, etc.
To fix the issue we have to track the instructions explored by
the verifier and sanitize instructions that are dead at run time
with NOPs. We cannot reject such dead code, since llvm generates
it for valid C code, since it doesn't do as much data flow
analysis as the verifier does.

Fixes: 17a5267067f3 ("bpf: verifier (add verifier core)")

  It stores the (big-endian) payload length in `ipv6_hdr(skb)->payload_len`.  
- Record header offset for extension-header parsing  
  `IP6CB(skb)->nhoff` is set to the offset of the `nexthdr` field within the IPv6 header.  
- Handle L3-master enslaved devices  
  `l3mdev_ip6_out()` is called to let any L3-master device (e.g. VRF) rewrite or drop the packet. A NULL return implies the packet was consumed or dropped.  
- Set ETH protocol  
  On success, it marks `skb->protocol = htons(ETH_P_IPV6)` to indicate this is an IPv6 frame.  
- Invoke Netfilter and output  
  Finally it calls `nf_hook()` with `NF_INET_LOCAL_OUT`, handing the SKB to any IPv6 netfilter hooks and then to `dst_output` (the routing output function).

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Integer underflow of `len`  
  If `skb->len < sizeof(struct ipv6hdr)`, `len` becomes negative. This negative value is not clamped to zero and ends up cast via `htons()` into a large unsigned 16-bit payload length. In practice, however, SKBs passed here always contain at least the IPv6 header, so this path is not reachable under normal use.  
- Integer overflow above maximum length  
  The code does check `len > IPV6_MAXPLEN` and resets to zero, preventing an excessively large advertised payload.  
- Memory safety  
  The routine only writes into the existing `ipv6hdr` within the SKB. There is no buffer allocation or indexing beyond the header bounds, so there is no out-of-bounds memory access.  
- Null-pointer and device checks  
  The only pointer check is `if (!skb)` after `l3mdev_ip6_out()`. `skb_dst(skb)->dev` is used without a further null check, but SKBs at this stage always have a valid `dst` and `dev` set by the routing code.  
- Other attack vectors (e.g. UAF, use-after-free, data races)  
  This is purely local-output path code operating on a single SKB in process context; there are no obvious concurrency or lifetime–management issues here.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any exploitable vulnerabilities. While there is a theoretical integer underflow of `len` when `skb->len` is too small, such a condition cannot occur in the normal packet-creation path, and no other buffer-overruns or dangerous dereferences are present.

original_information.Summary: The IPv6 fragmentation implementation in the Linux kernel through 4.11.1 does not consider that the nexthdr field may be associated with an invalid option, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read and BUG) or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted socket and send system calls.
original_information.commit_message:
ipv6: Prevent overrun when parsing v6 header options

The KASAN warning repoted below was discovered with a syzkaller
program.  The reproducer is basically:
  int s = socket(AF_INET6, SOCK_RAW, NEXTHDR_HOP);
  send(s, &one_byte_of_data, 1, MSG_MORE);
  send(s, &more_than_mtu_bytes_data, 2000, 0);

The socket() call sets the nexthdr field of the v6 header to
NEXTHDR_HOP, the first send call primes the payload with a non zero
byte of data, and the second send call triggers the fragmentation path.

The fragmentation code tries to parse the header options in order
to figure out where to insert the fragment option.  Since nexthdr points
to an invalid option, the calculation of the size of the network header
can made to be much larger than the linear section of the skb and data
is read outside of it.

This fix makes ip6_find_1stfrag return an error if it detects
running out-of-bounds.

original_information.commit_message:
Make MediaStreamDispatcherHost per-request instead of per-frame.

Instead of having RenderFrameHost own a single MSDH to handle all
requests from a frame, MSDH objects will be owned by a strong binding.

A consequence of this is that an additional requester ID is added to
requests to MediaStreamManager, so that an MSDH is able to cancel only
requests generated by it.

In practice, MSDH will continue to be per frame in most cases since
each frame normally makes a single request for an MSDH object.

This fixes a lifetime issue caused by the IO thread executing tasks
after the RenderFrameHost dies.

   - It takes these parameters:  
     • `net`: the network namespace to check in.  
     • `addr`: the IPv6 address to look up.  
     • `dev`: (optional) a specific network device to restrict the lookup to.  
     • `strict`: when zero, relaxes the match criteria for certain scoped addresses if no device is specified.  
     • `banned_flags`: a bitmask of address flags which, if set on the candidate address, disqualify the match.  
   - The code computes a hash of the target address, then enters an RCU-protected read section (`rcu_read_lock_bh`).  
   - It iterates over all `inet6_ifaddr` entries in the corresponding hash bucket. For each entry (`ifp`):  
     • Skips entries in a different network namespace.  
     • Builds a local copy of the address flags (`ifp_flags`), explicitly stripping `IFA_F_TENTATIVE` if the address is marked `IFA_F_OPTIMISTIC`.  
     • Checks if the stored address equals `addr`, that none of the `banned_flags` are set in `ifp_flags`, and that either:  
         – No device restriction was given; or  
         – The entry’s device matches `dev`; or  
         – The entry’s scope is neither link-local nor host-local and `strict` is false.  
     • If all conditions pass, it exits RCU, returns 1 (found).  
   - If no entry matches, it exits RCU and returns 0 (not found).

   - Concurrency/Race: The code uses RCU (`rcu_read_lock_bh`/`rcu_read_unlock_bh`), which is the standard mechanism in the Linux IPv6 stack for safely walking a shared address list under concurrent updates. No use-after-free or lock inversion is apparent.

   - Hash collision: The initial hash bucket selection is just for performance; incorrect bucket choice cannot cause out‐of‐bounds memory access.  
   - Flag logic: The code explicitly normalizes optimistic addresses by stripping `IFA_F_TENTATIVE`, then enforces `banned_flags`. This is intentional policy, not a logic flaw.  
   - No user‐supplied data is dereferenced as a pointer or used to compute offsets. The only inputs are an `in6_addr`, a pointer to a device, flags, and an integer `strict`; these do not yield memory corruption vectors.  
   - Overall, there is no buffer overflow, use-after-free, integer overflow, or other memory‐safety issue; nor is there an apparent privilege bypass or side‐channel concern in this code path.

3. Decision  
   No, the code does not contain any observable vulnerabilities. It correctly protects concurrent access with RCU, applies its matching logic safely, and makes no unsafe pointer assumptions.

original_information.Summary: net/ipv6/addrconf.c in the IPv6 stack in the Linux kernel before 4.0 does not validate attempted changes to the MTU value, which allows context-dependent attackers to cause a denial of service (packet loss) via a value that is (1) smaller than the minimum compliant value or (2) larger than the MTU of an interface, as demonstrated by a Router Advertisement (RA) message that is not validated by a daemon, a different vulnerability than CVE-2015-0272.  NOTE: the scope of CVE-2015-0272 is limited to the NetworkManager product.
original_information.commit_message:
ipv6: addrconf: validate new MTU before applying it

Currently we don't check if the new MTU is valid or not and this allows
one to configure a smaller than minimum allowed by RFCs or even bigger
than interface own MTU, which is a problem as it may lead to packet
drops.

If you have a daemon like NetworkManager running, this may be exploited
by remote attackers by forging RA packets with an invalid MTU, possibly
leading to a DoS. (NetworkManager currently only validates for values
too small, but not for too big ones.)

The fix is just to make sure the new value is valid. That is, between
IPV6_MIN_MTU and interface's MTU.

Note that similar check is already performed at
ndisc_router_discovery(), for when kernel itself parses the RA.

   - The method `Document::SendSensitiveInputVisibility()` is responsible for scheduling a task that will eventually invoke `SendSensitiveInputVisibilityInternal()` on the same `Document` instance.  
   - It first checks whether there is already an active “sensitive input visibility” task (`sensitive_input_visibility_task_.IsActive()`). If so, it bails out immediately to avoid posting duplicate tasks.  
   - If no task is active, it acquires a task runner for the category `TaskType::kUnspecedLoading`, then calls `PostCancellableTask(...)`, passing in a bound callback to `Document::SendSensitiveInputVisibilityInternal` wrapped with a weak‐persistent reference to `this`.

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Use‐After‐Free: The code wraps `this` in `WrapWeakPersistent()`, ensuring that if the `Document` object is destroyed before the task runs, the callback no‐ops instead of dereferencing a dangling pointer.

1. Functional Analysis

• The function’s purpose is to write a chunk of data into a guest physical page (identified by its guest-frame-number) within a given KVM memory slot.  
• It takes as input:  
  – A memslot pointer (describing a contiguous region of guest memory backed by host pages)  
  – A guest-frame-number (gfn) that selects which 4K page in that slot to modify  
  – A pointer to the source data, plus an offset within the page and a length to copy  
• First it calls gfn_to_hva_memslot(memslot, gfn) to translate the gfn into a host-virtual address (HVA) pointing to the start of the target guest page in kernel space.  
• If that translation fails (gfn out of range or slot inactive), it returns –EFAULT.  
• Otherwise it copies ‘len’ bytes from the caller’s buffer ‘data’ into the guest page at HVA+offset, using the low-level __copy_to_user primitive.  
• If the copy routine reports any fault (nonzero return), it returns –EFAULT.  
• Finally, on success it marks the page dirty in the memslot (so that KVM knows it was written) and returns 0.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

• Out-of-bounds within a page?  
  – There is no explicit check that offset+len ≤ PAGE_SIZE. If a caller passed an offset or length that overran the page boundary, the copy routine would write past the intended 4K page into adjacent pages in the same memslot mapping. That could corrupt guest memory outside the intended page.  
  – Mitigation: Typically callers of __kvm_write_guest_page (e.g. KVM’s MMU or device-emulation code) ensure 0 ≤ offset < PAGE_SIZE and len ≤ PAGE_SIZE–offset.  
• Use of __copy_to_user vs memcpy:  
  – __copy_to_user is the raw copy primitive that does not run the usual “is this a user pointer?” checks. It simply performs the memory write in kernel mode, so writing to any kernel address is permitted and any fault triggers an EFAULT return.  
  – Here that allows the direct write into the kernel-mapped guest page. There is no ring-0→ring-3 protection bypass because the destination is a kernel mapping of guest RAM, not arbitrary host memory.  
• Host memory safety:  
  – gfn_to_hva_memslot already bounds the gfn inside the memslot’s backed range, so the HVA you get is guaranteed to point to memory that belongs to that guest region. There’s no way here to trick it into returning a kernel function pointer or other critical data.  
• Partial writes on fault:  
  – If the copy faults midway, __copy_to_user returns the number of bytes not written. This code then returns –EFAULT but any bytes already copied remain in place. That could leave the guest page partially corrupted, but recovering atomicity is up to higher-level logic.

3. Decision

No, the snippet itself does not contain a direct arbitrary-write or privilege-escalation bug. The only caveat is the lack of an explicit page-bounds check (offset+len), but in KVM’s usage the caller must ensure those constraints. There is no vulnerability in this function as it stands.

original_information.Summary: The Btrfs implementation in the Linux kernel before 3.19 does not ensure that the visible xattr state is consistent with a requested replacement, which allows local users to bypass intended ACL settings and gain privileges via standard filesystem operations (1) during an xattr-replacement time window, related to a race condition, or (2) after an xattr-replacement attempt that fails because the data does not fit.
original_information.commit_message:
Btrfs: make xattr replace operations atomic

Replacing a xattr consists of doing a lookup for its existing value, delete
the current value from the respective leaf, release the search path and then
finally insert the new value. This leaves a time window where readers (getxattr,
listxattrs) won't see any value for the xattr. Xattrs are used to store ACLs,
so this has security implications.

This change also fixes 2 other existing issues which were:

*) Deleting the old xattr value without verifying first if the new xattr will
   fit in the existing leaf item (in case multiple xattrs are packed in the
   same item due to name hash collision);

*) Returning -EEXIST when the flag XATTR_CREATE is given and the xattr doesn't
   exist but we have have an existing item that packs muliple xattrs with
   the same name hash as the input xattr. In this case we should return ENOSPC.

A test case for xfstests follows soon.

Thanks to Alexandre Oliva for reporting the non-atomicity of the xattr replace
implementation.

original_information.commit_message:
perf: Fix race in swevent hash

There's a race on CPU unplug where we free the swevent hash array
while it can still have events on. This will result in a
use-after-free which is BAD.

Simply do not free the hash array on unplug. This leaves the thing
around and no use-after-free takes place.

When the last swevent dies, we do a for_each_possible_cpu() iteration
anyway to clean these up, at which time we'll free it, so no leakage
will occur.

The Git protocol does not specify what should happen in the case
of an empty packet line (that is a packet line "0004"). We

original_information.commit_message:
posix-timer: Properly check sigevent->sigev_notify

timer_create() specifies via sigevent->sigev_notify the signal delivery for
the new timer. The valid modes are SIGEV_NONE, SIGEV_SIGNAL, SIGEV_THREAD
and (SIGEV_SIGNAL | SIGEV_THREAD_ID).

The sanity check in good_sigevent() is only checking the valid combination
for the SIGEV_THREAD_ID bit, i.e. SIGEV_SIGNAL, but if SIGEV_THREAD_ID is
not set it accepts any random value.

This has no real effects on the posix timer and signal delivery code, but
it affects show_timer() which handles the output of /proc/$PID/timers. That
function uses a string array to pretty print sigev_notify. The access to
that array has no bound checks, so random sigev_notify cause access beyond
the array bounds.

Add proper checks for the valid notify modes and remove the SIGEV_THREAD_ID
masking from various code pathes as SIGEV_NONE can never be set in
combination with SIGEV_THREAD_ID.
