+install-binSCRIPTS: $(bin_SCRIPTS)
+	@$(NORMAL_INSTALL)
+	@list='$(bin_SCRIPTS)'; test -n "$(bindir)" || list=; \
+	if test -n "$$list"; then \
+	  echo " $(MKDIR_P) '$(DESTDIR)$(bindir)'"; \
+	  $(MKDIR_P) "$(DESTDIR)$(bindir)" || exit 1; \
+	fi; \
+	for p in $$list; do \
+	  if test -f "$$p"; then d=; else d="$(srcdir)/"; fi; \
+	  if test -f "$$d$$p"; then echo "$$d$$p"; echo "$$p"; else :; fi; \
+	done | \
+	sed -e 'p;s,.*/,,;n' \
+	    -e 'h;s|.*|.|' \
+	    -e 'p;x;s,.*/,,;$(transform)' | sed 'N;N;N;s,\n, ,g' | \
+	$(AWK) 'BEGIN { files["."] = ""; dirs["."] = 1; } \
+	  { d=$$3; if (dirs[d] != 1) { print "d", d; dirs[d] = 1 } \
+	    if ($$2 == $$4) { files[d] = files[d] " " $$1; \
+	      if (++n[d] == $(am__install_max)) { \
+		print "f", d, files[d]; n[d] = 0; files[d] = "" } } \
+	    else { print "f", d "/" $$4, $$1 } } \
+	  END { for (d in files) print "f", d, files[d] }' | \
+	while read type dir files; do \
+	     if test "$$dir" = .; then dir=; else dir=/$$dir; fi; \
+	     test -z "$$files" || { \
+	       echo " $(INSTALL_SCRIPT) $$files '$(DESTDIR)$(bindir)$$dir'"; \
+	       $(INSTALL_SCRIPT) $$files "$(DESTDIR)$(bindir)$$dir" || exit $$?; \
+	     } \
+	; done

+# This directory's subdirectories are mostly independent; you can cd
+# into them and run 'make' without going through this Makefile.
+# To change the values of 'make' variables: instead of editing Makefiles,
+# (1) if the variable is set in 'config.status', edit 'config.status'

+$(am__recursive_targets):
+	@fail=; \
+	if $(am__make_keepgoing); then \
+	  failcom='fail=yes'; \
+	else \
+	  failcom='exit 1'; \
+	fi; \
+	dot_seen=no; \
+	target=`echo $@ | sed s/-recursive//`; \
+	case "$@" in \
+	  distclean-* | maintainer-clean-*) list='$(DIST_SUBDIRS)' ;; \
+	  *) list='$(SUBDIRS)' ;; \
+	esac; \
+	for subdir in $$list; do \
+	  echo "Making $$target in $$subdir"; \
+	  if test "$$subdir" = "."; then \
+	    dot_seen=yes; \
+	    local_target="$$target-am"; \
+	  else \
+	    local_target="$$target"; \
+	  fi; \
+	  ($(am__cd) $$subdir && $(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) $$local_target) \
+	  || eval $$failcom; \
+	done; \
+	if test "$$dot_seen" = "no"; then \
+	  $(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) "$$target-am" || exit 1; \
+	fi; test -z "$$fail"

+tags-am: $(TAGS_DEPENDENCIES) $(am__tagged_files)

+	  include_option=--etags-include; \
+	  empty_fix=.; \
+	else \
+	  include_option=--include; \

+	fi; \
+	list='$(SUBDIRS)'; for subdir in $$list; do \

+	if test -z "$(ETAGS_ARGS)$$*$$unique"; then :; else \

+	test -d "$(distdir)" || mkdir "$(distdir)"
+	@srcdirstrip=`echo "$(srcdir)" | sed 's/[].[^$$\\*]/\\\\&/g'`; \
+	topsrcdirstrip=`echo "$(top_srcdir)" | sed 's/[].[^$$\\*]/\\\\&/g'`; \
+	list='$(DISTFILES)'; \
+	  dist_files=`for file in $$list; do echo $$file; done | \
+	  sed -e "s|^$$srcdirstrip/||;t" \
+	      -e "s|^$$topsrcdirstrip/|$(top_builddir)/|;t"`; \
+	case $$dist_files in \
+	  */*) $(MKDIR_P) `echo "$$dist_files" | \
+			   sed '/\//!d;s|^|$(distdir)/|;s,/[^/]*$$,,' | \
+			   sort -u` ;; \
+	esac; \
+	for file in $$dist_files; do \
+	  if test -f $$file || test -d $$file; then d=.; else d=$(srcdir); fi; \
+	  if test -d $$d/$$file; then \
+	    dir=`echo "/$$file" | sed -e 's,/[^/]*$$,,'`; \
+	    if test -d "$(distdir)/$$file"; then \
+	      find "$(distdir)/$$file" -type d ! -perm -700 -exec chmod u+rwx {} \;; \
+	    fi; \
+	    if test -d $(srcdir)/$$file && test $$d != $(srcdir); then \
+	      cp -fpR $(srcdir)/$$file "$(distdir)$$dir" || exit 1; \
+	      find "$(distdir)/$$file" -type d ! -perm -700 -exec chmod u+rwx {} \;; \
+	    fi; \
+	    cp -fpR $$d/$$file "$(distdir)$$dir" || exit 1; \
+	  else \
+	    test -f "$(distdir)/$$file" \
+	    || cp -p $$d/$$file "$(distdir)/$$file" \
+	    || exit 1; \
+	  fi; \
+	done
+	@list='$(DIST_SUBDIRS)'; for subdir in $$list; do \
+	  if test "$$subdir" = .; then :; else \
+	    $(am__make_dryrun) \
+	      || test -d "$(distdir)/$$subdir" \
+	      || $(MKDIR_P) "$(distdir)/$$subdir" \
+	      || exit 1; \
+	    dir1=$$subdir; dir2="$(distdir)/$$subdir"; \
+	    $(am__relativize); \
+	    new_distdir=$$reldir; \
+	    dir1=$$subdir; dir2="$(top_distdir)"; \
+	    $(am__relativize); \
+	    new_top_distdir=$$reldir; \
+	    echo " (cd $$subdir && $(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) top_distdir="$$new_top_distdir" distdir="$$new_distdir" \\"; \
+	    echo "     am__remove_distdir=: am__skip_length_check=: am__skip_mode_fix=: distdir)"; \
+	    ($(am__cd) $$subdir && \
+	      $(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) \
+	        top_distdir="$$new_top_distdir" \
+	        distdir="$$new_distdir" \
+		am__remove_distdir=: \
+		am__skip_length_check=: \
+		am__skip_mode_fix=: \
+	        distdir) \
+	      || exit 1; \
+	  fi; \
+	done
+	$(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) \
+	  top_distdir="$(top_distdir)" distdir="$(distdir)" \
+	  dist-hook
+	-test -n "$(am__skip_mode_fix)" \
+	|| find "$(distdir)" -type d ! -perm -755 \

+	  ! -type d ! -perm -444 -exec $(install_sh) -c -m a+r {} {} \; \
+	|| chmod -R a+r "$(distdir)"

+
+        NOTES relative to the implementation
+	====================================
+
+xsl:stylesheet:
+
+  all children except xsl:import can be in any order, so this
+can be stored as one big structure.
+
+xsl:include:
+  
+  this is really similar to XInclude, can be implemented as a
+nearly separate processing just after the XML stylesheet has been
+parsed.
+  Detect loops using a limited stack ...
+
+xsl:import:
+
+  seems this should be really implemented as having a stylesheet
+sublist being itself an import list
+
+  add the list at the end
+  when doing a resolution explore child before siblings in the list
+
+3 Data Model, we should operate on parsed trees
+
+3.1 No problem
+
+3.2 use the XML Base call, XSLT-1.1 references it
+
+3.4 Whitespace Stripping
+
+  Seems one may have to do a bit of preprocessing on both the
+stylesheet trees and the source trees.
+
+4 Expressions
+
+  looks okay, wondering about variable bindings though...
+  default namespace not in scope
+
+5.1 Processing Model
+
+  look in Michael Kay's book about how to efficiently find the
+template applying to a node. Might influence the in-memory stylesheet
+representation
+
+5.2 Patterns
+
+  the end of that section suggest that the expression could be computed in
+a simpler way. Maybe templates needs to be evaluated differently than
+through the normal XPath processing. This can be implemented separately
+or build an expression tree in the XPath module and use a different 
+evaluation mechanism. Not sure this is best.
+
+5.4 Applying Template Rules
+
+  xsl:apply-templates is the recurstion mechanism, note the select
+mechanism.
+
+  detection of loop: once the applied nodeset has been computed,
+check that none of the elements is part of the existing set in use, this
+may be costly and should be triggered only at a certain depth.
+
+5.5 Conflict Resolution for Template Rules
+
+  Sounds again that evaluation of a pattern rule should provide one
+more information not provided by the standard XPath evaluation
+
+5.6 Overriding Template Rules
+
+  another recursion mechanism, confirm that it is needed to separate
+the imported stylesheets.
+
+5.7 Modes
+
+  Confusing ??? need an example.
+
+6 Named Templates
+
+  No big deal it seems
+
+7.1.1 Literal Result Elements
+
+  cleanup of the namespace template should be done initially at stylesheet
+parsing.
+
+7.1.2 Creating Elements with xsl:element
+
+   okay, I bet it's usually used with { } expression computations
+
+7.1.3 Creating Attributes with xsl:attribute
+
+   need some running code to better understand all the subtilties
+
+7.1.4 Named Attribute Sets
+
+   Okay just a way to mimick param entities use fo attrib groups in Dtd's
+
+7.2 Creating Text
+
+   adjacent text nodes are merged ... okay
+   output escapeing might need a libxml API extension
+
+7.3 Creating Processing Instructions
+7.4 Creating Comments
+
+   RAS, one just need to make a couple of trivial checks
+
+7.5 Copying
+
+   Okay will need some testing
+
+7.6.1 Generating Text with xsl:value-of
+
+   will be a good test for XPath string() function
+   note in the example that the text nodes are coalesced
+
+7.6.2 Attribute Value Templates
+
+   hum, this is 
+    - contextual
+    - uses XPath
+
+  best seems to parse, generate an evaluation tree then evaluate
+when accessed. Note that multipe expressions can be associated to 
+a single attribute. Sounds like i will have to introduce a new
+element type inserted in the attribute nodelist. dohh ...
+
+7.7 Numbering
+
+  sounds interesting for users but might be costly, we will see ...
+
+7.7.1 Number to String Conversion Attributes
+
+   format="..." :-( it's gonna be painful ...
+
+8 Repetition
+9 Conditional Processing
+
+  doesn't sounds hard to implement since we are at an interpreter
+level but really useful in practice. Will be simple once the overall
+framework is set-up.
+
+10 Sorting
+
+  Okay applied to the node list of an xsl:apply-templates or xsl:for-each
+
+  The NOTEs are a bit scary ...
+
+11 Variables and Parameters
+
+   Variables can only be afttected at the top level, so it
+seems they act only as global variables ...
+   But this is by regions .... so some of the statements within
+a stylesheet my use a different set than others ... in practice
+it turns to be nearly like loacal variables ....
+  Need more thinking on this to handle it properly.
+  Might explain on of TOM's requests w.r.t. variable resolution
+
+11.1 Result Tree Fragments
+
+  Dohhh a new type ...
+  actually it's just a node set restricted type
+
+11.2 Values of Variables and Parameters
+
+  okay, real problem is scoping ...
+
+11.3 Using Values of Variables and Parameters with xsl:copy-of 
+
+  No surprize
+
+11.4 Top-level Variables and Parameters
+
+   It is an error if a stylesheet contains more than one binding
+   of a top-level variable with the same name and same import precedence
+
+   => ah ah, so it seems one can associate the variable bindings
+to a stylesheet and if needed recurse down the import list if not
+found, would simplify things a lot !
+
+   If the template or expression specifying the value of a global variable
+x references a global variable y, then the value for y must be computed
+before the value of x.
+
+   => Values can probably be computed dynamically at reference
+time, if this generate a loop, then it's an error. Lazy computations
+are great ...
+
+11.5 Variables and Parameters within Templates
+
+   
+   xsl:variable is allowed anywhere within a template that an instruction
+is allowed. In this case, the binding is visible for all following siblings
+and their descendants.
+   It is an error if a binding established by an xsl:variable or xsl:param
+element within a template shadows another binding established by an
+xsl:variable or xsl:param element also within the template.
+
+  => the example seems to imply that we can simply keep a list of
+     local variable binding to a template ... sounds fine.
+
+11.6 Passing Parameters to Templates
+
+  => Okay the parameter overrides the local binding
+
+12.1 Multiple Source Documents
+12.2 Keys
+
+  skipped for now
+
+12.3 Number Formatting
+
+  reimplementing Java formatting in C is gonna be a pain !
+
+12.4 Miscellaneous Additional Functions
+
+  current() => trivial
+
+  unparsed-entity-uri() => support in uri.c should do
+
+  generate-id() => use the in-memory address of the node ???
+
+  system-property() => sounds simple
+
+13 Messages
+
+  trivial I/Os
+
+14 Extensions
+15 Fallback
+
+   skipped for now
+
+16 Output
+
+16.1 XML Output Method
+
+  sounds that calling directly libxml output on the result tree
+should do it with a few caveats, for example one need to be
+able to parametrize the output
+
+16.2 HTML Output Method
+
+  sounds that calling libxml HTML output should do it too
+
+16.3 Text Output Method
+
+  doesn't sounds too hard ...
+
+16.4 Disabling Output Escaping
+
+  hum ... might be a bit painful to implement with the current framework."}<_**next**_>{"sha": "056d1961ee974f708960dfb3e8524b75c4a9c0f4", "filename": "third_party/libxslt/README.chromium", "status": "modified", "additions": 12, "deletions": 7, "changes": 19, "blob_url": "https://github.com/chromium/chromium/blob/96dbafe288dbe2f0cc45fa3c39daf6d0c37acbab/third_party/libxslt/README.chromium", "raw_url": "https://github.com/chromium/chromium/raw/96dbafe288dbe2f0cc45fa3c39daf6d0c37acbab/third_party/libxslt/README.chromium", "contents_url": "https://api.github.com/repos/chromium/chromium/contents/third_party/libxslt/README.chromium?ref=96dbafe288dbe2f0cc45fa3c39daf6d0c37acbab", "patch": "@@ -1,6 +1,6 @@

+	@$(NORMAL_INSTALL)
+	@list1=''; \
+	list2='$(man_MANS)'; \
+	test -n "$(man3dir)" \
+	  && test -n "`echo $$list1$$list2`" \
+	  || exit 0; \
+	echo " $(MKDIR_P) '$(DESTDIR)$(man3dir)'"; \
+	$(MKDIR_P) "$(DESTDIR)$(man3dir)" || exit 1; \
+	{ for i in $$list1; do echo "$$i"; done;  \
+	if test -n "$$list2"; then \
+	  for i in $$list2; do echo "$$i"; done \
+	    | sed -n '/\.3[a-z]*$$/p'; \
+	fi; \
+	} | while read p; do \
+	  if test -f $$p; then d=; else d="$(srcdir)/"; fi; \
+	  echo "$$d$$p"; echo "$$p"; \
+	done | \
+	sed -e 'n;s,.*/,,;p;h;s,.*\.,,;s,^[^3][0-9a-z]*$$,3,;x' \
+	      -e 's,\.[0-9a-z]*$$,,;$(transform);G;s,\n,.,' | \
+	sed 'N;N;s,\n, ,g' | { \
+	list=; while read file base inst; do \
+	  if test "$$base" = "$$inst"; then list="$$list $$file"; else \
+	    echo " $(INSTALL_DATA) '$$file' '$(DESTDIR)$(man3dir)/$$inst'"; \
+	    $(INSTALL_DATA) "$$file" "$(DESTDIR)$(man3dir)/$$inst" || exit $$?; \
+	  fi; \
+	done; \
+	for i in $$list; do echo "$$i"; done | $(am__base_list) | \
+	while read files; do \
+	  test -z "$$files" || { \
+	    echo " $(INSTALL_DATA) $$files '$(DESTDIR)$(man3dir)'"; \
+	    $(INSTALL_DATA) $$files "$(DESTDIR)$(man3dir)" || exit $$?; }; \

+xsltPreCompEval(xsltTransformContextPtr ctxt, xmlNodePtr node,

+    xmlXPathObjectPtr res;

+
+    xpctxt->node = node;
+#ifdef XSLT_REFACTORED

+        xpctxt->namespaces = comp->inScopeNs->list;
+        xpctxt->nsNr = comp->inScopeNs->xpathNumber;

+    xpctxt->namespaces = comp->nsList;

+
+    xpctxt->node = oldXPContextNode;
+    xpctxt->proximityPosition = oldXPProximityPosition;
+    xpctxt->contextSize = oldXPContextSize;
+    xpctxt->nsNr = oldXPNsNr;
+    xpctxt->namespaces = oldXPNamespaces;
+
+    return(res);

+	  $(MKDIR_P) "$(DESTDIR)$(bindir)" || exit 1; \
+	fi; \
+	for p in $$list; do \

+	  if test -f "$$d$$p"; then echo "$$d$$p"; echo "$$p"; else :; fi; \
+	done | \

+	    -e 'h;s|.*|.|' \
+	    -e 'p;x;s,.*/,,;$(transform)' | sed 'N;N;N;s,\n, ,g' | \
+	$(AWK) 'BEGIN { files["."] = ""; dirs["."] = 1; } \
+	  { d=$$3; if (dirs[d] != 1) { print "d", d; dirs[d] = 1 } \
+	    if ($$2 == $$4) { files[d] = files[d] " " $$1; \
+	      if (++n[d] == $(am__install_max)) { \
+		print "f", d, files[d]; n[d] = 0; files[d] = "" } } \
+	    else { print "f", d "/" $$4, $$1 } } \
+	  END { for (d in files) print "f", d, files[d] }' | \
+	while read type dir files; do \
+	     if test "$$dir" = .; then dir=; else dir=/$$dir; fi; \
+	     test -z "$$files" || { \
+	       echo " $(INSTALL_SCRIPT) $$files '$(DESTDIR)$(bindir)$$dir'"; \

+# This directory's subdirectories are mostly independent; you can cd

+$(am__recursive_targets):

+	if $(am__make_keepgoing); then \
+	  failcom='fail=yes'; \
+	else \
+	  failcom='exit 1'; \
+	fi; \
+	dot_seen=no; \
+	target=`echo $@ | sed s/-recursive//`; \
+	case "$@" in \
+	  distclean-* | maintainer-clean-*) list='$(DIST_SUBDIRS)' ;; \
+	  *) list='$(SUBDIRS)' ;; \
+	esac; \
+	for subdir in $$list; do \
+	  echo "Making $$target in $$subdir"; \
+	  if test "$$subdir" = "."; then \
+	    dot_seen=yes; \
+	    local_target="$$target-am"; \
+	  else \
+	    local_target="$$target"; \
+	  fi; \
+	  ($(am__cd) $$subdir && $(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) $$local_target) \
+	  || eval $$failcom; \
+	done; \
+	if test "$$dot_seen" = "no"; then \
+	  $(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) "$$target-am" || exit 1; \
+	fi; test -z "$$fail"

+	    fi; \

+import io
+import os
+import sys
+import difflib
+
+from os import path
+from subprocess import Popen, PIPE
+
+xsltproc = path.join(os.getcwd(), "win32", "bin.msvc", "xsltproc.exe")
+if not path.isfile(xsltproc):
+    raise FileNotFoundError(xsltproc)
+
+def runtests(xsl_dir, xml_dir="."):
+    old_dir = os.getcwd()
+    os.chdir(xsl_dir)
+
+    for xsl_file in os.listdir():
+        if not xsl_file.endswith(".xsl"):
+            continue
+        xsl_path = "./" + xsl_file
+        name = path.splitext(xsl_file)[0]
+
+        xml_path = path.join(xml_dir + "/" + name + ".xml")
+        if not path.isfile(xml_path):
+            continue
+
+        args = [ xsltproc, xsl_path, xml_path ]
+        p = Popen(args, stdout=PIPE, stderr=PIPE)
+        out_path = path.join(xml_dir, name + ".out")
+        err_path = path.join(xml_dir, name + ".err")
+        out_diff = diff(p.stdout, "<stdout>", name + ".out")
+        err_diff = diff(p.stderr, "<stderr>", name + ".err")
+
+        if (len(out_diff) or len(err_diff)):
+            sys.stdout.writelines(out_diff)
+            sys.stdout.writelines(err_diff)
+            print()
+
+    os.chdir(old_dir)
+
+def diff(got_stream, got_name, expected_path):
+    text_stream = io.TextIOWrapper(got_stream, encoding="latin_1")
+    got_lines = text_stream.readlines()
+
+    if path.isfile(expected_path):
+        file = open(expected_path, "r", encoding="latin_1")
+        expected_lines = file.readlines()
+    else:
+        expected_lines = []
+
+    diff = difflib.unified_diff(expected_lines, got_lines,
+                                fromfile=expected_path,
+                                tofile=got_name)
+    return list(diff)
+
+print("## Running REC tests")
+runtests("tests/REC")
+
+print("## Running general tests")
+runtests("tests/general", "./../docs")
+
+print("## Running exslt common tests")
+runtests("tests/exslt/common")
+
+print("## Running exslt functions tests")
+runtests("tests/exslt/functions")
+
+print("## Running exslt math tests")
+runtests("tests/exslt/math")
+
+print("## Running exslt sets tests")
+runtests("tests/exslt/sets")
+
+print("## Running exslt strings tests")
+runtests("tests/exslt/strings")
+
+print("## Running exslt dynamic tests")
+runtests("tests/exslt/dynamic")
+
+print("## Running exslt date tests")
+runtests("tests/exslt/date")
+"}<_**next**_>{"sha": "45c3e28f2f12f86861102f3b0f3f2367f5b1a3cc", "filename": "third_party/libxslt/xslt-config.in", "status": "removed", "additions": 0, "deletions": 137, "changes": 137, "blob_url": "https://github.com/chromium/chromium/blob/5d32c4d7ac9cd3e4a45a5cc1fc547103b66816c7/third_party/libxslt/xslt-config.in", "raw_url": "https://github.com/chromium/chromium/raw/5d32c4d7ac9cd3e4a45a5cc1fc547103b66816c7/third_party/libxslt/xslt-config.in", "contents_url": "https://api.github.com/repos/chromium/chromium/contents/third_party/libxslt/xslt-config.in?ref=5d32c4d7ac9cd3e4a45a5cc1fc547103b66816c7", "patch": "@@ -1,137 +0,0 @@

-/*
- * Entity loading control and customization.
- */
-static
-void parsePath(const xmlChar *path) {
-    const xmlChar *cur;
-
-    if (path == NULL)
-	return;
-    while (*path != 0) {
-	if (nbpaths >= MAX_PATHS) {
-	    fprintf(stderr, "MAX_PATHS reached: too many paths\n");
-	    return;
-	}
-	cur = path;
-	while ((*cur == ' ') || (*cur == ':'))
-	    cur++;
-	path = cur;
-	while ((*cur != 0) && (*cur != ' ') && (*cur != ':'))
-	    cur++;
-	if (cur != path) {
-	    paths[nbpaths] = xmlStrndup(path, cur - path);
-	    if (paths[nbpaths] != NULL)
-		nbpaths++;
-	    path = cur;
-	}
-    }
-}

-static xmlParserInputPtr
-xsltprocExternalEntityLoader(const char *URL, const char *ID,
-			     xmlParserCtxtPtr ctxt) {
-    xmlParserInputPtr ret;
-    warningSAXFunc warning = NULL;
-
-    int i;
-    const char *lastsegment = URL;
-    const char *iter = URL;
-
-    if (nbpaths > 0) {
-	while (*iter != 0) {
-	    if (*iter == '/')
-		lastsegment = iter + 1;
-	    iter++;
-	}
-    }
-
-    if ((ctxt != NULL) && (ctxt->sax != NULL)) {
-	warning = ctxt->sax->warning;
-	ctxt->sax->warning = NULL;
-    }
-
-    if (defaultEntityLoader != NULL) {
-	ret = defaultEntityLoader(URL, ID, ctxt);
-	if (ret != NULL) {
-	    if (warning != NULL)
-		ctxt->sax->warning = warning;
-	    if (load_trace) {
-		fprintf \
-			(stderr,
-			 "Loaded URL=\"%s\" ID=\"%s\"\n",
-			 URL ? URL : "(null)",
-			 ID ? ID : "(null)");
-	    }
-	    return(ret);
-	}
-    }
-    for (i = 0;i < nbpaths;i++) {
-	xmlChar *newURL;
-
-	newURL = xmlStrdup((const xmlChar *) paths[i]);
-	newURL = xmlStrcat(newURL, (const xmlChar *) "/");

-/*
- * Internal timing routines to remove the necessity to have unix-specific
- * function calls
- */
-#ifndef HAVE_GETTIMEOFDAY
-#ifdef HAVE_SYS_TIMEB_H
-#ifdef HAVE_SYS_TIME_H
-#ifdef HAVE_FTIME
-
-int
-my_gettimeofday(struct timeval *tvp, void *tzp)
-{
-	struct timeb timebuffer;
-
-	ftime(&timebuffer);
-	if (tvp) {
-		tvp->tv_sec = timebuffer.time;
-		tvp->tv_usec = timebuffer.millitm * 1000L;
-	}
-	return (0);
-}
-#define HAVE_GETTIMEOFDAY 1
-#define gettimeofday my_gettimeofday
-
-#endif /* HAVE_FTIME */
-#endif /* HAVE_SYS_TIME_H */
-#endif /* HAVE_SYS_TIMEB_H */
-#endif /* !HAVE_GETTIMEOFDAY */
-
-#if defined(HAVE_GETTIMEOFDAY)
-static struct timeval begin, endtime;
-/*
- * startTimer: call where you want to start timing
- */
-static void startTimer(void)
-{
-    gettimeofday(&begin,NULL);
-}
-/*
- * endTimer: call where you want to stop timing and to print out a
- *           message about the timing performed; format is a printf
- *           type argument
- */
-static void endTimer(const char *format, ...)
-{
-    long msec;
-    va_list ap;
-
-    gettimeofday(&endtime, NULL);
-    msec = endtime.tv_sec - begin.tv_sec;
-    msec *= 1000;
-    msec += (endtime.tv_usec - begin.tv_usec) / 1000;
-
-#ifndef HAVE_STDARG_H
-#error "endTimer required stdarg functions"
-#endif
-    va_start(ap, format);
-    vfprintf(stderr,format,ap);
-    va_end(ap);
-
-    fprintf(stderr, " took %ld ms\n", msec);
-}
-#elif defined(HAVE_TIME_H)
-/*
- * No gettimeofday function, so we have to make do with calling clock.
- * This is obviously less accurate, but there's little we can do about
- * that.
- */
-#ifndef CLOCKS_PER_SEC
-#define CLOCKS_PER_SEC 100
-#endif
-
-clock_t begin, endtime;
-static void startTimer(void)
-{
-    begin=clock();
-}
-static void endTimer(char *format, ...)
-{
-    long msec;
-    va_list ap;
-
-    endtime=clock();
-    msec = ((endtime-begin) * 1000) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC;
-
-#ifndef HAVE_STDARG_H
-#error "endTimer required stdarg functions"
-#endif
-    va_start(ap, format);
-    vfprintf(stderr,format,ap);
-    va_end(ap);
-    fprintf(stderr, " took %ld ms\n", msec);
-}
-#else
-/*
- * We don't have a gettimeofday or time.h, so we just don't do timing
- */
-static void startTimer(void)
-{
-  /*
-   * Do nothing
-   */
-}
-static void endTimer(char *format, ...)
-{
-  /*
-   * We cannot do anything because we don't have a timing function
-   */
-#ifdef HAVE_STDARG_H
-    va_start(ap, format);
-    vfprintf(stderr,format,ap);
-    va_end(ap);
-    fprintf(stderr, " was not timed\n", msec);
-#else
-  /* We don't have gettimeofday, time or stdarg.h, what crazy world is
-   * this ?!
-   */
-#endif
-}
-#endif

-	xmlFreeDoc(res);

original_information.commit_message:
af_netlink: force credentials passing [CVE-2012-3520]

Pablo Neira Ayuso discovered that avahi and
potentially NetworkManager accept spoofed Netlink messages because of a
kernel bug.  The kernel passes all-zero SCM_CREDENTIALS ancillary data
to the receiver if the sender did not provide such data, instead of not
including any such data at all or including the correct data from the
peer (as it is the case with AF_UNIX).

This bug was introduced in commit 16e572626961
(af_unix: dont send SCM_CREDENTIALS by default)

This patch forces passing credentials for netlink, as
before the regression.

Another fix would be to not add SCM_CREDENTIALS in
netlink messages if not provided by the sender, but it
might break some programs.

With help from Florian Weimer & Petr Matousek

This issue is designated as CVE-2012-3520

1. Functional Analysis  
   - The function `jpc_ft_fwdlift_colgrp` performs the forward lifting (wavelet) transform on a column group of fixed-point samples.  
   - It takes as input:  
     • `a[]`: a linear buffer of samples  
     • `numrows`: the total number of rows in the column group  
     • `stride`: the distance in the buffer between successive rows  
     • `parity`: determines whether the first sample belongs to the high‑pass or low‑pass subband  
   - It first computes `llen`, the number of low‑pass samples:  
     `llen = (numrows + 1 – parity) >> 1;`  
   - If `numrows > 1`, it applies two lifting steps over the high‑pass and low‑pass samples:  
     1) Predict (first lifting step): for each high sample, subtracts a combination of its low‑neighbours (special‑casing start/end if parity differs from `(numrows&1)`).  
     2) Update (second lifting step): for each low sample, adds a combination of its high‑neighbours (again special‑casing edges).  
   - If `numrows <= 1` and `parity == 1`, it simply scales the lone sample by a left shift.  
   - Internally it relies only on pointer arithmetic, a fixed kernel size `JPC_QMFB_COLGRPSIZE`, and inlined fixed‑point shifts (`jpc_fix_asr` and `jpc_fix_asl`).

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Buffer overruns: the code indexes `a` only via pointers `lptr`, `hptr` computed as `&a[0]` or `&a[llen*stride]`, then walks forward at most `JPC_QMFB_COLGRPSIZE` elements per iteration. If the caller supplies inconsistent or out‑of‑range values for `numrows` or `stride`, out‑of‑bounds access could occur—but that is true of any low‑level C routine without explicit bounds checks. Within its intended use (with correctly computed `numrows` and `stride`), no indexing escapes the allocated buffer.  
   - Integer overflow/divide‑by‑zero:  
     • Shifts (`jpc_fix_asr`, `jpc_fix_asl`) do not divide by a variable or run any modulo operations, so there is no risk of division by zero.  
     • The intermediate computation of `llen = (numrows+1–parity)>>1` can only overflow if `numrows` itself is near `INT_MAX`, which is not expected in image dimensions.  
   - Arithmetic overflow: fixed‑point additions/subtractions could overflow the underlying integer type if sample magnitudes are extreme, but that again is a domain constraint on input data, not a code bug.  
   - No use of dynamic allocation, no format strings, no system calls—no classic heap or format‑string vulnerabilities.  

3. Decision  
   No, under its intended use—with valid `numrows`, `stride`, and sample buffer—the code contains no inherent vulnerabilities.

original_information.commit_message:
Implement a bubble that appears at the top of the screen when a tab enters 
fullscreen mode via webkitRequestFullScreen(), telling the user how to exit 
fullscreen. 

This is implemented as an NSView rather than an NSWindow because the floating 
chrome that appears in presentation mode should overlap the bubble. 

Content-initiated fullscreen mode makes use of 'presentation mode' on the Mac: 
the mode in which the UI is hidden, accessible by moving the cursor to the top 
of the screen. On Snow Leopard, this mode is synonymous with fullscreen mode. 
On Lion, however, fullscreen mode does not imply presentation mode: in 
non-presentation fullscreen mode, the chrome is permanently shown. It is 
possible to switch between presentation mode and fullscreen mode using the 
presentation mode UI control. 

When a tab initiates fullscreen mode on Lion, we enter presentation mode if not 
in presentation mode already. When the user exits fullscreen mode using Chrome 
UI (i.e. keyboard shortcuts, menu items, buttons, switching tabs, etc.) we 
return the user to the mode they were in before the tab entered fullscreen.

+- (id)initWithOwner:(BrowserWindowController*)owner browser:(Browser*)browser {

+- (void)positionInWindowAtTop:(CGFloat)maxY width:(CGFloat)maxWidth {
+  NSRect bubbleFrame = [[self view] frame];
+  bubbleFrame.origin.x = (int)(maxWidth/2 - NSWidth(bubbleFrame)/2);
+  bubbleFrame.origin.y = maxY - NSHeight(bubbleFrame);

+// Called when someone clicks on the embedded link.

+- (void)hideTimerFired:(NSTimer*)timer {
+  NSRect endFrame = [[self view] frame];
+  endFrame.origin.y += endFrame.size.height;
+  endFrame.size.height = 0;
+  NSDictionary* dict = [NSDictionary dictionaryWithObjectsAndKeys:
+      [self view], NSViewAnimationTargetKey,
+      [NSValue valueWithRect:endFrame], NSViewAnimationEndFrameKey, nil];

+  NSViewAnimation* animation =
+      [[NSViewAnimation alloc]
+        initWithViewAnimations:[NSArray arrayWithObjects:dict, nil]];
+  [animation gtm_setDuration:kSlideOutDurationMs/1000.0
+                   eventMask:NSLeftMouseUpMask];
+  [animation setDelegate:self];
+  [animation startAnimation];
+  hideAnimation_.reset(animation);

+  }

+- (void)initializeLabel {

+  exitLabel_.reset([[HyperlinkTextView alloc]

+  [[exitLabelPlaceholder_ superview]
+      replaceSubview:exitLabelPlaceholder_ with:exitLabel_.get()];
+  exitLabelPlaceholder_ = nil;  // Now released.
+  [exitLabel_.get() setDelegate:self];
+
+  NSString *message = l10n_util::GetNSStringF(IDS_EXIT_FULLSCREEN_MODE,
+      base::SysNSStringToUTF16([[self class] keyCommandString]));

+  [(HyperlinkTextView*)exitLabel_.get()
+        setMessageAndLink:@""
+                 withLink:message

+             messageColor:[NSColor whiteColor]
+                linkColor:[NSColor whiteColor]];
+
+  [exitLabel_.get() sizeToFit];

+  NSSize textSize = textFrame.size;
+  frame.size.width = textSize.width + 2 * kPaddingPx;
+  [[self view] setFrame:frame];
+  textFrame.origin.x = textFrame.origin.y = kPaddingPx;
+  [exitLabel_.get() setFrame:textFrame];

+// This looks at the Main Menu and determines what the user has set as the

++ (ui::AcceleratorCocoa)acceleratorForToggleFullscreen {
+  NSMenu* mainMenu = [NSApp mainMenu];
+  // Get the application menu (i.e. Chromium).
+  for (NSMenuItem* menu in [mainMenu itemArray]) {
+    for (NSMenuItem* item in [[menu submenu] itemArray]) {
+      // Find the toggle presentation mode item.
+      if ([item tag] == IDC_PRESENTATION_MODE) {
+        return ui::AcceleratorCocoa([item keyEquivalent],
+                                    [item keyEquivalentModifierMask]);
+      }
+    }
+  }
+  // Default to Cmd+Shift+F.
+  return ui::AcceleratorCocoa(@"f", NSCommandKeyMask|NSShiftKeyMask);
+}

   This function, `ec_asn1_group2fieldid`, takes an EC_GROUP object (an elliptic-curve group) and fills in an X9_62_FIELDID ASN.1 structure with the appropriate field identifier parameters for that curve. Broadly speaking it:

   • Validates inputs: returns 0 if either pointer is NULL.  
   • Clears any existing contents of the `field` structure by freeing `fieldType` and `p.other` if they are non-NULL.  
   • Determines the underlying field type (prime or characteristic-two) by calling `EC_METHOD_get_field_type`.  
   • Sets `field->fieldType` to the corresponding OID object (`OBJ_nid2obj(nid)`).  
   • If it’s a prime field:
     – Allocates a temporary BIGNUM.  
     – Retrieves the curve parameter p into that BIGNUM.  
     – Converts the BIGNUM to an ASN1_INTEGER and stores it in `field->p.prime`.  
   • If it’s a characteristic-two field:
     – Allocates and initializes an X9_62_CHARACTERISTIC_TWO structure.  
     – Retrieves the field degree m and stores it.  
     – Queries the basis type (trinomial, pentanomial, or optimal normal basis).  
     – For trinomial basis, gets k and wraps it in an ASN1_INTEGER.  
     – For pentanomial basis, gets k1,k2,k3 and stores them in an X9_62_PENTANOMIAL sub-structure.  
     – For ONB, simply creates an ASN1_NULL object.  
   • Frees the temporary BIGNUM and returns 1 on success, or jumps to an error label that also frees the BIGNUM, returning 0 on failure.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

   • Memory-allocation failures are checked after each `new` or conversion call; on failure the code jumps to the `err` label, frees the temporary BIGNUM, reports an error, and returns 0.  
   • There are no uses of fixed-size buffers or unchecked pointer arithmetic, so classic buffer overflows are not present.  
   • All ASN.1 and BIGNUM conversions go through the library’s APIs, which do their own internal validation.  
   • Error paths properly free the temporary BIGNUM, avoiding a use-after-free; however, if an error occurs after allocating `field->p.char_two`, that substructure is not freed on the way out—this is a memory leak rather than a security vulnerability.  
   • There is no opportunity here for integer underflow/overflow beyond what BN or ASN1_INTEGER handles internally, nor is there any injection risk because the inputs are library objects, not external data buffers.  
   • No NULL-dereference paths exist, as all pointers are checked immediately after allocation and before use.

   No, this code does not contain vulnerabilities. It correctly checks for allocation failures, uses safe library APIs for big-number and ASN.1 operations, and handles error reporting cleanly. There is a minor memory-leak on some error paths but no exploitable security flaw.

original_information.Summary: The inode_init_owner function in fs/inode.c in the Linux kernel through 4.17.4 allows local users to create files with an unintended group ownership, in a scenario where a directory is SGID to a certain group and is writable by a user who is not a member of that group. Here, the non-member can trigger creation of a plain file whose group ownership is that group. The intended behavior was that the non-member can trigger creation of a directory (but not a plain file) whose group ownership is that group. The non-member can escalate privileges by making the plain file executable and SGID.
original_information.commit_message:
Fix up non-directory creation in SGID directories

sgid directories have special semantics, making newly created files in
the directory belong to the group of the directory, and newly created
subdirectories will also become sgid.  This is historically used for
group-shared directories.

But group directories writable by non-group members should not imply
that such non-group members can magically join the group, so make sure
to clear the sgid bit on non-directories for non-members (but remember
that sgid without group execute means "mandatory locking", just to
confuse things even more).

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Cc: Andy Lutomirski <luto@kernel.org>
Cc: Al Viro <viro@zeniv.linux.org.uk>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

The function DetermineFrameLoadType inspects various aspects of the current frame, the incoming load request, and navigation history state to decide which load type enum to return. In detail:

• Child‑frame initialization  
  - If the frame has a parent AND the loader has not yet committed its first “real” document load, return kFrameLoadTypeInitialInChildFrame.  

• Top‑level fresh navigation  
  - If the frame has no parent (i.e. it is top‑level) AND there is no back‑forward history:  
    – If there is an opener and the requested URL is empty, return kFrameLoadTypeReplaceCurrentItem (i.e. replace the current history item).  
    – Otherwise, return kFrameLoadTypeStandard.  

• Reload based on cache mode  
  - If the request’s cache mode is kValidateCache, return kFrameLoadTypeReload.  
  - If the request’s cache mode is kBypassCache, return kFrameLoadTypeReloadBypassingCache.  

• Replace current history item on explicit request or blank‑page substitute  
  - If request.ReplacesCurrentItem() is true OR  
    (no multiple real loads have committed yet AND the current document URL is “about:blank”),  
    return kFrameLoadTypeReplaceCurrentItem.  

• Same‑URL navigation  
  - If the requested URL equals the loader’s history URL:  
    – If the HTTP method is POST, treat it as a standard navigation.  
    – Else if there is no origin document (i.e. a direct navigation with no referring document), return kFrameLoadTypeReload.  
    – Otherwise, return kFrameLoadTypeReplaceCurrentItem.  

• Reload on failing substitute data  
  - If the request’s substitute data “failing URL” matches the loader’s history URL AND the loader’s recorded load type is already kFrameLoadTypeReload, return kFrameLoadTypeReload.  

• Empty‑URL direct replace  
  - If both the resource request URL and the substitute data failing URL are empty, return kFrameLoadTypeReplaceCurrentItem.  

• Origin‑document history restrictions  
  - If there is an origin document AND that document cannot create a history entry, return kFrameLoadTypeReplaceCurrentItem.  

• Default  
  - In all other cases, return kFrameLoadTypeStandard.

• Invocation of OS or shell commands  
• Arithmetic or pointer arithmetic on untrusted data  
• Bypasses of security checks or authorization decisions based on tainted input  

All comparisons are equality checks or enum tests. URL and method strings are compared but never used in a way that could introduce injection or overflow within this function. No mutable global state is written, and no unchecked memory accesses occur.  

Therefore, there are no obvious security vulnerabilities (e.g. injection, buffer overflow, use‑after‑free) in this snippet.

- If the `fopen` fails (e.g. because the file doesn’t exist), it simply returns without printing anything.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Boundary checks / buffer overflows: There is no fixed‐size buffer into which data is being read, so there is no risk of a stack or heap buffer overflow from the file’s contents.
- Format‐string vulnerabilities: The code uses `putchar(c)` rather than `printf` or `puts`, so there is no format‐string issue.
- Path and file‐access issues: The path is a compile‐time constant (`_PATH_NOLOGIN`), so there is no user‐controlled pathname injection or directory traversal.  
- Symlink / TOCTTOU: Because the function only opens the file for reading and does not make any privilege decisions based on its contents, a malicious symlink or race does not lead to code execution or privilege escalation; at worst it might display unexpected content but does not itself introduce a security vulnerability.
- Resource exhaustion: Reading and outputting one character at a time is not an exploitable denial‐of‐service vector in typical use.

Conclusion: The code correctly handles the read‐print‐close sequence without introducing any standard C I/O vulnerabilities.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any vulnerabilities based on the above analysis.

1. Functional Analysis

• The function nf_tables_abort_release takes a pointer to an nft_trans structure (trans).  
• It switches on trans->msg_type to determine what kind of Netfilter‐table object was being created in the aborted transaction.  
  – If the transaction was creating a new table (NFT_MSG_NEWTABLE), it calls nf_tables_table_destroy(&trans->ctx).  
  – If it was creating a new chain (NFT_MSG_NEWCHAIN), it calls nf_tables_chain_destroy(trans->ctx.chain).  
  – If it was creating a new rule (NFT_MSG_NEWRULE), it calls nf_tables_rule_destroy(&trans->ctx, nft_trans_rule(trans)).  
  – If it was creating a new set (NFT_MSG_NEWSET), it calls nft_set_destroy(nft_trans_set(trans)).  
• After cleaning up the specific object, it frees the memory for the transaction itself by calling kfree(trans).

2. Vulnerability Analysis

• null-pointer dereference  
  – The code unconditionally dereferences trans and trans->ctx.*. It does not check whether trans is NULL. In practice, callers should ensure trans is non-NULL before invoking this cleanup, so a null-pointer dereference would indicate a bug in the caller, not this function.  
• use-after-free or double-free  
  – Each destroy function is called exactly once for the matching msg_type. There is no path here that frees the same internal resource twice. After the switch, kfree(trans) frees only the transaction structure itself. There is no further use of trans or its fields.  
• uninitialized data  
  – It’s assumed that ctx and the pointers inside it (e.g., chain) are properly initialized when trans was allocated for those msg types. If a previous step stored garbage in trans->ctx.chain, chain_destroy could operate on an invalid pointer, but that would again be a bug in the transaction setup, not this cleanup.  
• missing default case  
  – If msg_type is not one of the listed values, no destroy function runs and the code just kfree’s trans. That may leak the internal resources if some other type slipped through. In a well-typed implementation, msg_type will always be one of the known values; otherwise the caller is at fault.

Overall, this function simply dispatches to the correct destroy routine and frees the transaction. It makes no unchecked assumptions beyond trans being non-NULL and its ctx fields having been properly initialized by the matching “new” operation.

3. Decision

No, the code does not itself contain any exploitable vulnerability. It correctly cleans up per the transaction type and then frees the transaction structure.

1. Functional Analysis  
   - The function `errParseTest` runs a parse test on an XML (or HTML) file named by `filename`, comparing its serialized output against the expected output file `result` and any parser/warning output against `err`.  
   - It increments a global test counter (`nb_tests`).  
   - Based on the `options` bits it chooses one of three flows:  
     • If HTML parsing is enabled and requested, it calls `htmlReadFile`.  
     • Else if XInclude is requested, it calls `xmlReadFile` and then `xmlXIncludeProcessFlags`.  
     • Otherwise it turns on warnings by setting `xmlGetWarningsDefaultValue = 1` and calls `xmlReadFile`.  
   - It then resets `xmlGetWarningsDefaultValue = 0`.  
   - If an expected-result file is provided (`result != NULL`), it serializes the document (`xmlDocDumpMemory` or `htmlDocDumpMemory`) into a memory buffer, compares that buffer to the contents of `result` via `compareFileMem`, and returns –1 on mismatch.  
   - It frees the serialized buffer and the parsed document if they were allocated.  
   - If an expected-error file is provided (`err != NULL`), it compares the collected errors (`testErrors`) to that file and returns –1 on mismatch.  
   - If DTD validation was requested (`XML_PARSE_DTDVALID`) but no expected-error file is given, it emits an error if any validation warnings/errors were collected.  
   - On success it returns 0.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Input Validation: The function passes `filename` directly to the underlying parser functions (`xmlReadFile`/`htmlReadFile`) without sanitization. In a production context that could allow attackers to choose arbitrary file paths, but in a controlled test harness it’s expected behavior.  
   - Buffer Handling: The code uses library serialization routines that allocate the output buffer and then frees it. There is no overflow risk here since the parser handles its own allocations.  
   - Null checks: After reading the file, `doc` may be NULL but the code guards against dereferencing it. The code sets `base=""` when `doc` is NULL so calling the comparator with a zero-length buffer is safe.  
   - Error Injection / XML External Entity (XXE): Unless the parser is explicitly configured to disable external entity loading, an untrusted XML input could trigger external resource fetches. That is a property of how `xmlReadFile` is configured globally, not a bug in this wrapper.  
   - Memory leaks: All allocated resources (`base`, `doc`) are freed on the success path. On early returns after a compare failure, the function returns immediately without freeing the parsed document or buffer. That could leak memory in a long-running test suite when a test fails—but that’s test harness behavior, not a security flaw per se.  

3. Decision  
No, the code itself does not introduce a security vulnerability. It is a test harness that correctly handles its allocations and comparisons, though test failures will leak memory if not cleaned up.

original_information.Summary: parser.c in libxml2 before 2.9.5 mishandles parameter-entity references because the NEXTL macro calls the xmlParserHandlePEReference function in the case of a '%' character in a DTD name.
original_information.commit_message:
Fix handling of parameter-entity references

There were two bugs where parameter-entity references could lead to an
unexpected change of the input buffer in xmlParseNameComplex and
xmlDictLookup being called with an invalid pointer.

Percent sign in DTD Names
=========================

The NEXTL macro used to call xmlParserHandlePEReference. When parsing
"complex" names inside the DTD, this could result in entity expansion
which created a new input buffer. The fix is to simply remove the call
to xmlParserHandlePEReference from the NEXTL macro. This is safe because
no users of the macro require expansion of parameter entities.

- xmlParseNameComplex
- xmlParseNCNameComplex
- xmlParseNmtoken

The percent sign is not allowed in names, which are grammatical tokens.

- xmlParseEntityValue

Parameter-entity references in entity values are expanded but this
happens in a separate step in this function.

- xmlParseSystemLiteral

Parameter-entity references are ignored in the system literal.

- xmlParseAttValueComplex
- xmlParseCharDataComplex
- xmlParseCommentComplex
- xmlParsePI
- xmlParseCDSect

Parameter-entity references are ignored outside the DTD.

- xmlLoadEntityContent

This function is only called from xmlStringLenDecodeEntities and
entities are replaced in a separate step immediately after the function
call.

This bug could also be triggered with an internal subset and double
entity expansion.

This fixes bug 766956 initially reported by Wei Lei and independently by
Chromium's ClusterFuzz, Hanno Böck, and Marco Grassi. Thanks to everyone
involved.

xmlParseNameComplex with XML_PARSE_OLD10
========================================

When parsing Names inside an expanded parameter entity with the
XML_PARSE_OLD10 option, xmlParseNameComplex would call xmlGROW via the
GROW macro if the input buffer was exhausted. At the end of the
parameter entity's replacement text, this function would then call
xmlPopInput which invalidated the input buffer.

There should be no need to invoke GROW in this situation because the
buffer is grown periodically every XML_PARSER_CHUNK_SIZE characters and,
at least for UTF-8, in xmlCurrentChar. This also matches the code path
executed when XML_PARSE_OLD10 is not set.

This fixes bugs 781205 (CVE-2017-9049) and 781361 (CVE-2017-9050).
Thanks to Marcel Böhme and Thuan Pham for the report.

Additional hardening
====================

A separate check was added in xmlParseNameComplex to validate the
buffer size.

1. Functional Analysis  
   This function computes the ARIA text alternative (accessible name) for an element, returning it as a String and recording where it came from. Its main steps are:  
   a. Initialize an empty result string `textAlternative` and record whether this element was already in the `visited` set; then insert it.  
   b. If we’re not already traversing an `aria-labelledby` chain and the element is considered hidden for text-alternative purposes, mark “found” and return empty.  
   c. If we’re not in an `aria-labelledby` traversal and haven’t yet visited this node:  
      - Decide whether to use `aria-labelledby` or the legacy `aria_labelledby`.  
      - Record the source type (`AXNameFromRelatedElement`) in `nameFrom` and, if requested, append a `NameSource` entry.  
      - Read the attribute’s value; if non‑null, recurse (copying the visited set) via `textFromAriaLabelledby` to collect text from referenced elements.  
      - If that yields non‑null text, record it in the source list or return it immediately; otherwise mark that source invalid.  
   d. Next, fall back to `aria-label` (queried via AOM or legacy ARIA), set `nameFrom = AXNameFromAttribute`, push a new `NameSource` if needed, read the label, and if nonempty record or return it.  
   e. If neither approach produced a label-or text, return the (still-empty) `textAlternative`.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - No unbounded recursion: every recursive call carries a copy of `visited`, and the root call itself marks the node visited. That structural guard prevents infinite loops via circular `aria-labelledby`.  
   - No injection risk: the method merely reads attribute text and returns it; it does not insert it into executable contexts or build HTML/JS. Rendering or scripting layers that consume this string are responsible for their own escaping and sanitization.  
   - No memory-unsafe operations: only high‑level String and container manipulations occur—no raw pointers or buffer arithmetic.  
   - Performance is at worst proportional to the number of related nodes times the cost of copying a small set; while not trivial, it’s not a security vulnerability.  

3. Decision  
   No, the code does not contain any security vulnerabilities. It correctly guards against infinite recursion, uses no unsafe memory operations, and does not introduce injection threats.

1. Functional Analysis  
   - The function `segmented_write_std` is designed to write a block of data to memory using a segmented address.  
   - It takes as input:  
     • `ctxt`: the CPU-emulation context,  
     • `addr`: a struct describing a segment:offset address,  
     • `data`: pointer to the bytes to write,  
     • `size`: number of bytes to write.  
   - It calls `linearize(ctxt, addr, size, true, &linear)` to convert the segment:offset pair into a flat (linear) address, performing all the usual segment‑limit and privilege checks.  
   - If `linearize` reports an error (anything other than `X86EMUL_CONTINUE`), the function immediately returns that code and does not attempt the write.  
   - If the address is valid, it then invokes the backend’s `write_std` operation via `ctxt->ops->write_std(ctxt, linear, data, size, &ctxt->exception)`. This is the routine that actually performs the memory write and may itself raise an exception if, for example, the target pages are not present or are read‑only.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Buffer Overflow / Out-of-Bounds Write:  
     The call to `linearize` is responsible for ensuring that the full range `[linear, linear+size)` lies within the segment’s limits. If `linearize` is correctly implemented, it will reject any request that would wrap around or exceed the segment.  
   - Use-after-free / Invalid Pointer:  
     The function merely forwards a user-supplied `data` pointer to `write_std`; there is no manipulation of that pointer here, so any risk in abusing `data` must lie in the caller or in `write_std` itself.  
   - Privilege / Protection Checks:  
     The code honors the segment’s access rights (via `linearize`) and relies on the backend to enforce page‑level permissions, so it does not bypass any intended protection.  
   - Exception Safety:  
     Both `linearize` and `write_std` report any fault through well‑defined return codes or by setting `ctxt->exception`. The function does not swallow errors and always propagates them.  

   In short, this wrapper enforces segment bounds and delegates low‑level validation and write logic to trusted components. There is no sign here of unchecked pointer arithmetic or missing validation steps.  

3. Decision  
   No, the code does not contain a vulnerability—it correctly bounds‐checks the segmented range before writing and propagates any errors generated during the process.

original_information.Summary: The load_segment_descriptor implementation in arch/x86/kvm/emulate.c in the Linux kernel before 4.9.5 improperly emulates a *MOV SS, NULL selector* instruction, which allows guest OS users to cause a denial of service (guest OS crash) or gain guest OS privileges via a crafted application.
original_information.commit_message:
KVM: x86: fix emulation of "MOV SS, null selector"

This is CVE-2017-2583.  On Intel this causes a failed vmentry because
SS's type is neither 3 nor 7 (even though the manual says this check is
only done for usable SS, and the dmesg splat says that SS is unusable!).
On AMD it's worse: svm.c is confused and sets CPL to 0 in the vmcb.

The fix fabricates a data segment descriptor when SS is set to a null
selector, so that CPL and SS.DPL are set correctly in the VMCS/vmcb.
Furthermore, only allow setting SS to a NULL selector if SS.RPL < 3;
this in turn ensures CPL < 3 because RPL must be equal to CPL.

Thanks to Andy Lutomirski and Willy Tarreau for help in analyzing
the bug and deciphering the manuals.

- The method begins by acquiring a mutex lock to protect shared state.
- It checks if an extractor (`mImpl`) is already set; if so, returns an error.
- It constructs a `DataSource` from the given URI (path) and optional HTTP headers.  
  - If this fails, it returns “no such file or directory” (ENOENT).
- It initializes a flag `mIsWidevineExtractor` to false.
- It tests whether the path starts with “widevine://” (case-insensitive).  
  - If so, it calls `SniffWVM` to confirm the content is Widevine media; if that fails or the MIME type is not WVM, it returns “unsupported format.”  
  - On success, it creates a `WVMExtractor`, enables adaptive streaming mode, and marks it as the implementation.
- If the path is not Widevine, it calls `MediaExtractor::Create` to pick an appropriate extractor based on the data source.
- If no extractor results, it returns “unsupported format.”
- It retrieves the extractor’s metadata.  
  - If the container MIME type is “video/wvm,” it enables crypto‐plugin mode on the `WVMExtractor`.  
  - Otherwise, if the extractor reports DRM content, it gives up and returns “unsupported format.”
- It calls `updateDurationAndBitrate()` to finalize media properties. On success, it holds onto the data source (`mDataSource`).
- Finally, it returns OK.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Buffer overflows: None. The only string comparison is `strncasecmp` on a fixed 11‐byte prefix.
- Injection (SQL, code, command): None. The path is passed to a well‑defined URI parser (`CreateFromURI`); no unsanitized shell or SQL contexts.
- Race conditions: The method uses a mutex to serialize access, avoiding concurrent-init races.
- Resource leaks: Unused extractors are cleared on failure; the data source is stored only after successful initialization.
- DRM checks: Widevine sniffing and DRM flags are explicitly checked and disallowed where unsupported.
- Denial‑of‑service: The method does not spawn unbounded threads or loops; failure paths return promptly.

3. Decision

No, the code contains no evident vulnerabilities. It performs standard URI handling, extractor selection, and DRM checks in a thread‑safe manner.

1. Functional Analysis

   The function `file_signextend` takes three inputs:
   - `ms`: a pointer to a `magic_set` structure (used for error reporting and flags).
   - `m`: a pointer to a `magic` structure, which describes a data item’s type and whether it should be treated as unsigned.
   - `v`: a 64‑bit unsigned integer value read from some data source.

   The function does the following:
   - Checks if the `UNSIGNED` flag is not set in `m->flag`. If the data is unsigned, it simply returns `v` unchanged.
   - If the data is signed, it switches on `m->type` to determine the intended width of the value:
     • For `FILE_BYTE`, it casts `v` to `signed char` and reassigns it to `v`.  
     • For 16‑bit types (`FILE_SHORT`, `FILE_BESHORT`, `FILE_LESHORT`), it casts `v` to `short`.  
     • For 32‑bit types (`FILE_LONG`, various date and float variants), it casts `v` to `int32_t`.  
     • For 64‑bit types (`FILE_QUAD`, `FILE_DOUBLE`, and their variants), it casts `v` to `int64_t`.  
     • For all string, regex, search, and other non‑numeric types, it leaves `v` unchanged.  
     • If `m->type` is not recognized, and verbose checking (`MAGIC_CHECK`) is enabled, it emits a warning, then returns `~0U` (all ones in 32 bits, zero‑extended to 64 bits).
   - Finally, it returns the possibly sign‑extended (or unchanged) value `v`.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

   - Integer Casting & Sign Extension  
     The function intentionally casts the 64‑bit input to smaller signed types (8, 16, 32 bits) when appropriate, then promotes back to 64 bits. This is exactly how C achieves proper sign extension, so no arithmetic or logic error is introduced by the casts themselves.
   - Control Flow  
     The `switch` covers each known numeric type. Non‑numeric and end‑user types are explicitly skipped, which is correct because sign‑extension is irrelevant there.
   - Default Case  
     Unrecognized `m->type` values trigger a warning (if enabled) and return `~0U`. This is a safe “fail‑fast” indicator rather than silently misprocessing data.
   - Memory Safety  
     There are no buffer accesses or pointer arithmetic here, so no buffer overflow or out‑of‑bounds issues.
   - Other Common Integer Vulnerabilities  
     No divisions, no pointer arithmetic, no user‑supplied array indices. The code only manipulates a local integer and returns it.

   Overall, the code correctly implements sign‑extension on a 64‑bit value based on the specified data width, with appropriate handling of unsigned types and unrecognized types. There is no evident integer overflow, underflow, out‑of‑bounds memory access, or other exploitable flaw in this snippet.

3. Decision

   No, the code is not vulnerable. It correctly performs safe sign extension without introducing integer or memory errors.

		case FILE_BYTE:

   The function `file_or_fd` is designed to identify the “type” of some input data, either from a file name (`inname`) or an existing file descriptor (`fd`). Its workflow is roughly as follows:  
   
   a. Initialization and buffer allocation  
   - Calls `file_reset(ms)` to clear any previous state.  
   - Allocates a buffer of size HOWMANY + SLOP, where SLOP provides space for a terminating NUL and a small overlap for matching data near EOF.  
   
   b. Filesystem-based “magic” test  
   - Calls `file_fsmagic(ms, inname, &sb)` to see if the file name or path attributes alone determine its type (e.g., block device, symlink).  
     - On match, the type is printed and the function returns that result.  
     - On error, it skips ahead to cleanup.  
   
   c. Preparing to read raw data  
   - On Windows, if reading from STDIN, switches it to binary mode.  
   - If `inname` is NULL, assumes the caller provided a valid `fd` and:  
     - Uses `fstat` to check if it’s a pipe; if not, remembers the current `lseek` position.  
   - If `inname` is non-NULL, opens the file for reading (in binary mode on Windows), possibly in nonblocking mode for FIFOs, then clears the nonblocking flag again.  
   - If the open fails but the stat said the file existed, reports “unreadable” info and returns.  
   
   d. Reading up to HOWMANY bytes  
   - If it’s a pipe or FIFO, uses `sread` in a small-loop read to accumulate data until EOF or until at most HOWMANY bytes.  
   - Otherwise, does a single `read`, shrinking HOWMANY on large Windows consoles to 8 KiB if needed.  
   - On read error, reports it and jumps to cleanup.  
   - Pads the buffer’s tail with zeros for safe pattern matching.  
   
   e. Passing data to the “buffer” magic test  
   - Calls `file_buffer(ms, fd, inname, buf, nbytes)` to run the in-buffer magic rules.  
   - On success, sets `rv = 0`.  
   
   f. Cleanup and return  
   - Frees the buffer.  
   - If it saved a file position, seeks back to it.  
   - Calls `close_and_restore(ms, inname, fd, &sb)` to close the FD if it opened it and restore any modes.  
   - Returns either the detected-type string (`file_getbuffer(ms)`) on success, or NULL on failure.  
   
2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   
   Buffer management  
   - The buffer is allocated as `HOWMANY + SLOP` bytes. All reads into the buffer are strictly limited to `HOWMANY` bytes, and the extra `SLOP` bytes are explicitly zeroed to guard against overruns near EOF. There is no unbounded copy or read beyond the allocated buffer.  
   
   File-descriptor handling

This opens a small race window, but the code treats failure to open robustly by reporting it as “unreadable” rather than proceeding with unsafe assumptions. - It retrieves the current thread’s credentials via `current_cred()` into `cred`.  
- If the caller has already supplied a non-null `dest_keyring`, it simply takes an extra reference on that keyring by calling `key_get(dest_keyring)`.  
- If no keyring was supplied, it looks at `cred->jit_keyring` (the “just-in-time” default keyring selector) and falls through a series of cases, trying in turn:  
  • The requestor’s authorization keyring (`request_key_auth`) if present and not revoked—this involves:  
    – Locking the key’s semaphore (`down_read`)  
    – Checking the `KEY_FLAG_REVOKED` bit  
    – Retrieving its payload (a `request_key_auth` structure) and from that the `dest_keyring`  
    – Unlocking the semaphore (`up_read`)  
  • The thread keyring (`cred->thread_keyring`)  
  • The process keyring (`cred->process_keyring`)  
  • The session keyring (via RCU-protected dereference of `cred->session_keyring`)  
  • The user session keyring (`cred->user->session_keyring`)  
  • The user keyring (`cred->user->uid_keyring`)  
- On the first successful retrieval (i.e., `key_get()` returns non-null), the switch breaks and that keyring is used.  
- If none of the cases returns a valid ring, the default label (`KEY_REQKEY_DEFL_GROUP_KEYRING` or any unknown value) hits a `BUG()` (kernel panic).  
- Finally, the chosen keyring pointer (possibly null if `BUG()` did not fire but all `key_get()` calls returned null) is stored back into `*_dest_keyring`, and the function returns.

- Reference counting: every time a keyring pointer is selected, `key_get()` is invoked, which increments the key’s reference count under appropriate internal protection. This prevents use-after-free on a keyring returned here.  
- Revocation check: when looking at the requestor’s auth keyring, the code holds the key’s read semaphore while checking the `REVOKED` flag, ensuring it does not use a revoked keyring.  
- RCU protection: reading `cred->session_keyring` is wrapped in `rcu_read_lock()`/`rcu_read_unlock()`, which safely handles concurrent updates to that pointer.  
- For `cred->user->session_keyring` and `cred->user->uid_keyring`, the code does not explicitly take RCU locks at that point, but the `struct cred` is pinned for the duration of the syscall and the `key_get()` call ensures the key object remains valid once obtained.

- The use of `BUG()` on an unexpected selector is deliberate kernel behavior to catch logic errors rather than a security vulnerability.

Conclusion: the code correctly sequences reference-counting, locking, and RCU protection. It prevents use-after-free, avoids races on revocation, and only panics on truly out‑of‑range defaults.

3. Decision

original_information.commit_message:
net: sctp: fix ipv6 ipsec encryption bug in sctp_v6_xmit

Alan Chester reported an issue with IPv6 on SCTP that IPsec traffic is not
being encrypted, whereas on IPv4 it is. Setting up an AH + ESP transport
does not seem to have the desired effect:

SCTP + IPv4:

  22:14:20.809645 IP (tos 0x2,ECT(0), ttl 64, id 0, offset 0, flags [DF], proto AH (51), length 116)
    192.168.0.2 > 192.168.0.5: AH(spi=0x00000042,sumlen=16,seq=0x1): ESP(spi=0x00000044,seq=0x1), length 72
  22:14:20.813270 IP (tos 0x2,ECT(0), ttl 64, id 0, offset 0, flags [DF], proto AH (51), length 340)
    192.168.0.5 > 192.168.0.2: AH(spi=0x00000043,sumlen=16,seq=0x1):

SCTP + IPv6:

  22:31:19.215029 IP6 (class 0x02, hlim 64, next-header SCTP (132) payload length: 364)
    fe80::222:15ff:fe87:7fc.3333 > fe80::92e6:baff:fe0d:5a54.36767: sctp
    1) [INIT ACK] [init tag: 747759530] [rwnd: 62464] [OS: 10] [MIS: 10]

Moreover, Alan says:

  This problem was seen with both Racoon and Racoon2. Other people have seen
  this with OpenSwan. When IPsec is configured to encrypt all upper layer
  protocols the SCTP connection does not initialize. After using Wireshark to
  follow packets, this is because the SCTP packet leaves Box A unencrypted and
  Box B believes all upper layer protocols are to be encrypted so it drops
  this packet, causing the SCTP connection to fail to initialize. When IPsec
  is configured to encrypt just SCTP, the SCTP packets are observed unencrypted.

In fact, using `socat sctp6-listen:3333 -` on one end and transferring "plaintext"
string on the other end, results in cleartext on the wire where SCTP eventually
does not report any errors, thus in the latter case that Alan reports, the
non-paranoid user might think he's communicating over an encrypted transport on
SCTP although he's not (tcpdump ... -X):

  ...
  0x0030: 5d70 8e1a 0003 001a 177d eb6c 0000 0000  ]p.......}.l....
  0x0040: 0000 0000 706c 6169 6e74 6578 740a 0000  ....plaintext...

Only in /proc/net/xfrm_stat we can see XfrmInTmplMismatch increasing on the
receiver side. Initial follow-up analysis from Alan's bug report was done by
Alexey Dobriyan. Also thanks to Vlad Yasevich for feedback on this.

SCTP has its own implementation of sctp_v6_xmit() not calling inet6_csk_xmit().
This has the implication that it probably never really got updated along with
changes in inet6_csk_xmit() and therefore does not seem to invoke xfrm handlers.

SCTP's IPv4 xmit however, properly calls ip_queue_xmit() to do the work. Since
a call to inet6_csk_xmit() would solve this problem, but result in unecessary
route lookups, let us just use the cached flowi6 instead that we got through
sctp_v6_get_dst(). Since all SCTP packets are being sent through sctp_packet_transmit(),
we do the route lookup / flow caching in sctp_transport_route(), hold it in
tp->dst and skb_dst_set() right after that. If we would alter fl6->daddr in
sctp_v6_xmit() to np->opt->srcrt, we possibly could run into the same effect
of not having xfrm layer pick it up, hence, use fl6_update_dst() in sctp_v6_get_dst()
instead to get the correct source routed dst entry, which we assign to the skb.

Also source address routing example from 625034113 ("sctp: fix sctp to work with
ipv6 source address routing") still works with this patch! Nevertheless, in RFC5095
it is actually 'recommended' to not use that anyway due to traffic amplification [1].
So it seems we're not supposed to do that anyway in sctp_v6_xmit(). Moreover, if
we overwrite the flow destination here, the lower IPv6 layer will be unable to
put the correct destination address into IP header, as routing header is added in
ipv6_push_nfrag_opts() but then probably with wrong final destination. Things aside,
result of this patch is that we do not have any XfrmInTmplMismatch increase plus on
the wire with this patch it now looks like:

SCTP + IPv6:

  08:17:47.074080 IP6 2620:52:0:102f:7a2b:cbff:fe27:1b0a > 2620:52:0:102f:213:72ff:fe32:7eba:
    AH(spi=0x00005fb4,seq=0x1): ESP(spi=0x00005fb5,seq=0x1), length 72
  08:17:47.074264 IP6 2620:52:0:102f:213:72ff:fe32:7eba > 2620:52:0:102f:7a2b:cbff:fe27:1b0a:
    AH(spi=0x00003d54,seq=0x1): ESP(spi=0x00003d55,seq=0x1), length 296

This fixes Kernel Bugzilla 24412. This security issue seems to be present since
2.6.18 kernels. Lets just hope some big passive adversary in the wild didn't have
its fun with that. lksctp-tools IPv6 regression test suite passes as well with
this patch.

 [1] http://www.secdev.org/conf/IPv6_RH_security-csw07.pdf

The function `pfkey_spdadd` processes a PF_KEY “add policy” request (SADB_X_SPDADD or SPDUPDATE) over a netlink socket.  Its main steps are:

 a. Extract and validate the required headers from the incoming PF_KEY message:  
    – The source and destination address extensions must both be present and of the same address family.  
    – The policy extension must be present.  

 b. Validate the policy parameters:  
    – The policy type must be either “IPSEC” or “DISCARD.”  
    – The policy direction must be in the valid range (1 … IPSEC_DIR_MAX−1).  

 c. Allocate a new `xfrm_policy` structure (`xp`) with `xfrm_policy_alloc()`.  

 d. Initialize the new policy:  
    – Set `xp->action` to either BLOCK or ALLOW based on the policy type.  
    – Copy the priority from the PF_KEY data.  
    – Convert the PF_KEY source address into `xp->selector.saddr` and set the family, prefix length, protocol, and source port (and mask).  
    – Convert the PF_KEY destination address into `xp->selector.daddr` and set the prefix length, protocol, and destination port (and mask).  

 e. If a security context extension is supplied, convert it to the kernel’s internal form and attach it to `xp->security` via `security_xfrm_policy_alloc()`.  

 f. Initialize the policy’s lifetime fields (`xp->lft`) to infinite, then override them if “hard” or “soft” lifetime extensions are present.  

 g. If this is an IPSEC-type policy, parse the list of IPSEC requests (transform specifications) into the policy via `parse_ipsecrequests()`.  

 h. Insert the policy into the system with `xfrm_policy_insert()`.  Audit the addition, generate the appropriate netlink event (`NEWPOLICY` or `UPDPOLICY`), and notify listeners.  

 i. On success, release the local reference to the policy (`xfrm_pol_put()`) and return 0.  On any failure, clean up the partially built policy and return the corresponding error code.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

– Memory safety / bounds checking  
  • The code validates that the required extensions exist before dereferencing them.  
  • The index arithmetic (`ext_hdrs[SADB_EXT_ADDRESS_SRC-1]`, etc.) is based on well‑defined SADB extension IDs and is safe if `ext_hdrs` is sized to the maximum extension ID, which is the standard PF_KEY helper convention.  
  • All allocations are checked for failure; on failure the code returns `-ENOBUFS` or propagates other errors without dereferencing a NULL pointer.

– Integer under/overflow  
  • The conversions of lifetimes use the `_KEY2X()` macro; no arithmetic is done here in the snippet that could overflow unchecked.  Any special handling of extremely large values is left to the `_KEY2X` definition and the `xfrm_policy` lifetime fields, which accept up to `XFRM_INF`.

– Resource leaks  
  • All allocated resources (`xfrm_policy`, the temporary user‑sec‑ctx) are freed or consumed on every exit path (successful or error).  

– Use-after-free and reference counting  
  • On insertion success, the function drops its local reference with `xfrm_pol_put()`.  Pending netlink notifications hold their own references.  
  • On failure, the code marks the policy as dead and calls `xfrm_policy_destroy()`, preventing any live use of the partial object.

– Privilege checks / access control  
  • The code relies on PF_KEY’s higher‑level dispatch to ensure only privileged users can issue these messages.  It does not itself recheck capabilities, which is the normal design in Linux’s PF_KEY handler.

No buffer overflows, no unchecked pointer arithmetic, and no logic that would allow an attacker to subvert control flow or corrupt kernel memory are visible in this snippet.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any obvious vulnerabilities.

1. Functional Analysis

1.1 Parameter Copying  
- Copies the new association’s configuration and peer parameters (congestion control pointer, receive window, SACK flag, auth capability, initial TSN and mapping state) into the existing association.  
- Re-initializes the peer’s TSN map with the new initial TSN.

1.2 Peer Address Synchronization  
- Iterates the existing association’s peer-address list.  
- For each transport “trans” not present in the new association, removes it from the old one.  
- If the association is already established, resets each surviving transport’s state.

1.3 TSN and Queue Handling for Established Associations  
- If `asoc->state >= SCTP_STATE_ESTABLISHED`, treats this as an association restart:  
  • Adopts the new TSN, cumulative TSN ACK, and advertised peer ACK point.  
  • Clears all stream-sequence numbering state.  
  • Flushes the upper-layer reassembly/ordered queue.  
  • Resets the overall error count to prevent immediate teardown.

1.4 Address Addition for Pre-established Associations  
- Otherwise (state not yet established), treats this as the initial establishment:  
  • Adds any peer addresses present in the new association but missing from the old one.  
  • Sets ACK points to “next_tsn – 1.”  
  • If no SSN map exists yet, steals the new association’s SSN map.  
  • If no association ID has been assigned, allocates one.

1.5 Authentication State Migration  
- Frees the old peer-random, peer-chunks, and peer-HMAC lists and replaces them with the ones from the new association (nulling them out in `new` to avoid double-free).  
- Drops the current shared key reference and re-initializes the active authentication key.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

2.1 Memory Safety  
- All list removals use the safe iterator (`list_for_each_safe`).  
- Pointer moves for `peer_random`, `peer_chunks`, and `peer_hmacs` are preceded by `kfree` of the old contents and followed by nulling out in the source, avoiding both leaks and double-frees.  
- SSN map is only moved when the destination has none; otherwise the new one is left in `new` (potentially a leak but not a corrupt/free-after-use).  
- No raw buffer accesses or integer indexing is present, so buffer overflows or out-of-bounds writes do not appear.

2.2 Logical Correctness and State Handling  
- The code unconditionally treats any `asoc->state >= SCTP_STATE_ESTABLISHED` as a full restart. If one sub-case meant to preserve retransmission state (case B in the comment), this branch instead resets it all. That may cause valid state to be dropped unexpectedly, but not a memory-corruption vulnerability.  
- When adding new peer addresses, the code only does so in the “not yet established” branch; established associations will not pick up new addresses from `new`. This is a protocol-logic issue but not a security exploit per se.

2.3 Race or Concurrency Risks  
- All allocations use `GFP_ATOMIC`, implying the callers hold the necessary locks or are in atomic context. No unprotected shared-data access patterns stand out.

original_information.Summary: The sctp_assoc_lookup_asconf_ack function in net/sctp/associola.c in the SCTP implementation in the Linux kernel through 3.17.2 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (panic) via duplicate ASCONF chunks that trigger an incorrect uncork within the side-effect interpreter.
original_information.commit_message:
net: sctp: fix panic on duplicate ASCONF chunks

When receiving a e.g. semi-good formed connection scan in the
form of ...

  -------------- INIT[ASCONF; ASCONF_ACK] ------------->
  <----------- INIT-ACK[ASCONF; ASCONF_ACK] ------------
  -------------------- COOKIE-ECHO -------------------->
  <-------------------- COOKIE-ACK ---------------------
  ---------------- ASCONF_a; ASCONF_b ----------------->

... where ASCONF_a equals ASCONF_b chunk (at least both serials
need to be equal), we panic an SCTP server!

The problem is that good-formed ASCONF chunks that we reply with
ASCONF_ACK chunks are cached per serial. Thus, when we receive a
same ASCONF chunk twice (e.g. through a lost ASCONF_ACK), we do
not need to process them again on the server side (that was the
idea, also proposed in the RFC). Instead, we know it was cached
and we just resend the cached chunk instead. So far, so good.

Where things get nasty is in SCTP's side effect interpreter, that
is, sctp_cmd_interpreter():

While incoming ASCONF_a (chunk = event_arg) is being marked
!end_of_packet and !singleton, and we have an association context,
we do not flush the outqueue the first time after processing the
ASCONF_ACK singleton chunk via SCTP_CMD_REPLY. Instead, we keep it
queued up, although we set local_cork to 1. Commit 2e3216cd54b1
changed the precedence, so that as long as we get bundled, incoming
chunks we try possible bundling on outgoing queue as well. Before
this commit, we would just flush the output queue.

Now, while ASCONF_a's ASCONF_ACK sits in the corked outq, we
continue to process the same ASCONF_b chunk from the packet. As
we have cached the previous ASCONF_ACK, we find it, grab it and
do another SCTP_CMD_REPLY command on it. So, effectively, we rip
the chunk->list pointers and requeue the same ASCONF_ACK chunk
another time. Since we process ASCONF_b, it's correctly marked
with end_of_packet and we enforce an uncork, and thus flush, thus
crashing the kernel.

Fix it by testing if the ASCONF_ACK is currently pending and if
that is the case, do not requeue it. When flushing the output
queue we may relink the chunk for preparing an outgoing packet,
but eventually unlink it when it's copied into the skb right
before transmission.

Joint work with Vlad Yasevich.

Fixes: 2e3216cd54b1 ("sctp: Follow security requirement of responding with 1 packet")

Signed-off-by: Vlad Yasevich <vyasevich@gmail.com>

original_information.commit_message:
Btrfs: make xattr replace operations atomic

Replacing a xattr consists of doing a lookup for its existing value, delete
the current value from the respective leaf, release the search path and then
finally insert the new value. This leaves a time window where readers (getxattr,
listxattrs) won't see any value for the xattr. Xattrs are used to store ACLs,
so this has security implications.

This change also fixes 2 other existing issues which were:

*) Deleting the old xattr value without verifying first if the new xattr will
   fit in the existing leaf item (in case multiple xattrs are packed in the
   same item due to name hash collision);

*) Returning -EEXIST when the flag XATTR_CREATE is given and the xattr doesn't
   exist but we have have an existing item that packs muliple xattrs with
   the same name hash as the input xattr. In this case we should return ENOSPC.

A test case for xfstests follows soon.

Thanks to Alexandre Oliva for reporting the non-atomicity of the xattr replace
implementation.

Separate repaint and layout requirements of StyleDifference (Step 1)

Previously StyleDifference was an enum that proximately bigger values
imply smaller values (e.g. StyleDifferenceLayout implies
StyleDifferenceRepaint). This causes unnecessary repaints in some cases
on layout change.

Convert StyleDifference to a structure containing relatively independent
flags.

This change doesn't directly improve the result, but can make further
repaint optimizations possible.

Step 1 doesn't change any functionality. RenderStyle still generate the
legacy StyleDifference enum when comparing styles and convert the result
to the new StyleDifference. Implicit requirements are not handled during
the conversion.

Converted call sites to use the new StyleDifference according to the
following conversion rules:
- diff == StyleDifferenceEqual (&& !context) => diff.hasNoChange()
- diff == StyleDifferenceRepaint => diff.needsRepaintObjectOnly()
- diff == StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsRepaintLayer()
- diff == StyleDifferenceRepaint || diff == StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsRepaintLayer()
- diff >= StyleDifferenceRepaint => diff.needsRepaint() || diff.needsLayout()
- diff >= StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsRepaintLayer() || diff.needsLayout()
- diff > StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsLayout()
- diff == StyleDifferencePositionedMovementLayoutOnly => diff.needsPositionedMovementLayoutOnly()
