Prevent rt_sigqueueinfo and rt_tgsigqueueinfo from spoofing the signal code

Userland should be able to trust the pid and uid of the sender of a
signal if the si_code is SI_TKILL.

Unfortunately, the kernel has historically allowed sigqueueinfo() to
send any si_code at all (as long as it was negative - to distinguish it
from kernel-generated signals like SIGILL etc), so it could spoof a
SI_TKILL with incorrect siginfo values.

Happily, it looks like glibc has always set si_code to the appropriate
SI_QUEUE, so there are probably no actual user code that ever uses
anything but the appropriate SI_QUEUE flag.

So just tighten the check for si_code (we used to allow any negative
value), and add a (one-time) warning in case there are binaries out
there that might depend on using other si_code values.

1. Functional Analysis

- Clearing segment registers  
  The code begins by zeroing out the user-supplied DS, ES, FS (and, unless lazy‑GS is enabled, GS) to prevent a user from carrying over unintended segment bases into VM86 mode.

- Sanitizing EFLAGS  
  It reads the user’s requested flags into a temporary (VEFLAGS), then strips out any bits not allowed by SAFE_MASK, restores the host’s safe bits (the inverse of SAFE_MASK), and finally forces the VM86 bit (X86_VM_MASK) on.

- Configuring v86mask based on CPU level  
  Depending on whether the CPU is a 286, 386, 486, or newer, it sets `tsk->thread.v86mask` to control which EFLAGS bits (NT, IOPL, AC, ID) will trap back to the kernel when running in VM86 mode.

- Saving host state and preparing for VM86  
  It stores the old kernel stack pointer (sp0), the old FS/GS selectors, sets the return value in AX to VM86_SIGNAL, then switches sp0 to point at the VM86 save area within `info`.

- Per-CPU TSS setup  
  It fetches the per‑CPU initial TSS, patches its RSP0 with the new v86 stack area, disables SYSENTER_CS if SYSENTER is supported, and writes the new sp0 into the TSS.

- Optional screen bitmap protection  
  If the VM86_SCREEN_BITMAP flag is set, the address bitmap mapping I/O ports is recorded and the pages are marked read‑only to catch user writes to the I/O bitmap.

- Auditing exit  
  If Linux auditing is enabled, it calls `__audit_syscall_exit` to record that the syscall is doing a non‑standard exit path.

- Final context switch into VM86  
  An inline assembly block loads the user’s saved registers block as ESP, the thread_info as EBP (and possibly GS), then jumps directly to the shared resume_userspace entry point. Execution never returns here.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Segment register zeroization  
  By forcing DS/ES/FS/GS to zero, the code blocks any attempt by user code to drag in arbitrary segment bases into VM86, so no privilege escalation via bogus segments is possible.

- EFLAGS sanitization  
  The combination of SAFE_MASK clearing and host-flag OR’ing prevents a malicious user from setting interrupt‑disable, IOPL, or other privileged flags themselves, while still preserving the kernel’s original interrupt state. The code then forces the VM86 bit, so the CPU really runs in v86 mode.

- v86mask trapping  
  By choosing the correct mask for the CPU generation, the kernel guarantees that attempts to use instructions or flags not permitted in VM86 will generate a fault that the kernel can handle, preventing escape from the virtual‑8086 sandbox.

- TSS and stack setup  
  The code correctly writes the new stack pointer into the per‑CPU TSS and updates the thread state. It uses `get_cpu()/put_cpu()` around the per‑CPU TSS, avoiding races. There is no user influence over which TSS or which CPU is used.

- Screen bitmap handling  
  If the screen‑bitmap feature is requested, pages are marked read‑only so that any illegal writes to the I/O permission bitmap fault back to the kernel rather than corrupting kernel memory.

- Inline assembly switch  
  The final asm block is minimal, only touching general-purpose registers and the stack. It does not expose any kernel pointers to the user space or rely on user-supplied pointers beyond the already validated `info`.

No steps assume unchecked user pointers or trust user‑supplied privileged fields. All user inputs that could affect privilege (segment selectors, EFLAGS, I/O bitmap) are sanitized or trapped.

3. Decision

No, the code contains no obvious vulnerabilities—it properly sanitizes user inputs, confines execution in VM86 mode, and sets up kernel state safely.

restricted to 1 thread per process or UP builds).  The race is only with
the huge pagefaults that can convert a pmd_none() into a
pmd_trans_huge().

Effectively all these pmd_none_or_clear_bad() sites running with
mmap_sem in read mode are somewhat speculative with the page faults, and
the result is always undefined when they run simultaneously.  This is
probably why it wasn't common to run into this.  For example if the
madvise(MADV_DONTNEED) runs zap_page_range() shortly before the page
fault, the hugepage will not be zapped, if the page fault runs first it
will be zapped.

Altering pmd_bad() not to error out if it finds hugepmds won't be enough
to fix this, because zap_pmd_range would then proceed to call
zap_pte_range (which would be incorrect if the pmd become a
pmd_trans_huge()).

The simplest way to fix this is to read the pmd in the local stack
(regardless of what we read, no need of actual CPU barriers, only
compiler barrier needed), and be sure it is not changing under the code
that computes its value.  Even if the real pmd is changing under the
value we hold on the stack, we don't care.  If we actually end up in
zap_pte_range it means the pmd was not none already and it was not huge,
and it can't become huge from under us (khugepaged locking explained
above).

All we need is to enforce that there is no way anymore that in a code
path like below, pmd_trans_huge can be false, but pmd_none_or_clear_bad
can run into a hugepmd.  The overhead of a barrier() is just a compiler
tweak and should not be measurable (I only added it for THP builds).  I
don't exclude different compiler versions may have prevented the race
too by caching the value of *pmd on the stack (that hasn't been
verified, but it wouldn't be impossible considering
pmd_none_or_clear_bad, pmd_bad, pmd_trans_huge, pmd_none are all inlines
and there's no external function called in between pmd_trans_huge and
pmd_none_or_clear_bad).

- It starts by ensuring there is at most one of `source_instance` or `dest_instance` non-null, and retrieves the current `SiteInstance` from the active `RenderFrameHost`.
- If the current site URL uses a special “guest” scheme, it immediately reuses the current instance.
- It looks up the browser context and computes the “effective” current URL, preferring the last successful load if available.
- It checks whether the current page is in view‑source mode via the last committed navigation entry.
- It calls `ShouldSwapBrowsingInstancesForNavigation` to decide if a forced cross‑instance swap is needed, based on the current versus destination effective URLs, view‑source modes, and any existing `dest_instance`.
- By default, it starts with a descriptor for the current instance, but if cross‑site transitions or a force‑swap are indicated, it invokes `DetermineSiteInstanceForURL` to pick or create a more appropriate `SiteInstanceDescriptor`.
- It converts that descriptor (and possibly a `candidate_instance` hint) into an actual `SiteInstance`.
- If a force‑swap was requested, it asserts that the new instance is not the same as the old.
- If no new instance was needed (the navigation can stay in‑process), it cleans up any spare renderer process host.
- It asserts the returned instance is in the same browser context.
- For non‑main frames whose new `SiteInstance` does not yet have a process but requires a dedicated one, it tweaks its process reuse policy to ensure isolation.
- Finally, it returns the chosen `SiteInstance`.

- The code makes decisions about process isolation and site instance reuse based solely on well‑defined, internal functions (`ShouldSwapBrowsingInstancesForNavigation`, `DetermineSiteInstanceForURL`, etc.) and on parsed URL origins.
- There is no direct user input being executed, no serialization or deserialization of attacker‑controlled data, no unsafe casts, and no buffer operations.

- All assertions (DCHECK/CHECK) guard internal invariants that would catch logical flaws during testing or debugging.
- There is no use of untrusted data to bypass security checks or to cause out‑of‑bounds memory access or code injection.
- No vulnerability patterns (e.g., use‑after‑free, integer overflow, command injection) are present in this snippet.

No, this code does not contain any evident security vulnerabilities. It correctly enforces site isolation policies and safely manages renderer process assignments.

1. Functional Analysis

   The function `xid_map_find` looks up an RPC transaction in a fixed-size circular table (`xid_map`).  It takes:

   • `rp`        – the incoming RPC message structure, from which it extracts the 32‑bit XID.  
   • `bp`        – a pointer to an IP (v4 or v6) packet header.  
   • `proc, vers`– output pointers to return the matched RPC procedure and version.  

   Steps:

   a.  Copy `rp->rm_xid` into a local `uint32_t xid`.  
   b.  Start scanning `xid_map` at the index held in the global hint `xid_map_hint`.  It will wrap around modulo `XIDMAPSIZE` and stop once it returns to the starting hint.  
   c.  For each entry `xmep` in the map:
       - First compare `xmep->ipver` against the packet’s IP version and `xmep->xid` against the copied `xid`.
       - If those match, switch on the version:
         • IPv4: compare the packet’s source/destination 32‑bit addresses (`ip->ip_src`/`ip_dst`) against the stored server/client addresses in `xmep`.  
         • IPv6: compare the 128‑bit addresses (`ip6->ip6_src`/`ip6->ip6_dst`) similarly.  
       - If both address comparisons also match, we have found the right entry.  The function sets the global hint to this index, stores `xmep->proc` and `xmep->vers` in the output pointers, and returns 0.  
       - Otherwise it moves to the next index, wrapping to 0 after `XIDMAPSIZE-1`.  

   d.  If the scan returns to the starting hint without a match, the function returns –1.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

   • Buffer overruns: The code assumes that `bp` points to at least the size of an IP or IPv6 header.  If the caller always passes a full packet buffer, no out‑of‑bounds read occurs.  The function itself does not allocate or write beyond fixed-size arrays.  
   • Infinite loops: The loop is a bounded circular scan over `XIDMAPSIZE` entries.  It always terminates after at most `XIDMAPSIZE` iterations.  
   • Integer overflows: No arithmetic on untrusted values that could overflow array indices.  
   • Unaligned memory access: The code uses special UNALIGNED_ macros to safely copy or compare possibly unaligned fields; no undefined behavior.  
   • Race conditions: If multiple threads call this concurrently and update the global `xid_map_hint`, there could be a minor lost update on the hint, but no memory corruption or out‑of‑bounds.  At worst the hint becomes slightly less optimal.  

   No paths in this code snippet read or write out‑of‑bounds, nor do they expose sensitive data via unvalidated pointers.  Assuming well‑formed inputs and a proper surrounding framework, this code does not introduce buffer overflows, infinite loops, or other standard C vulnerabilities.

3. Decision

   No, this code does not contain any obvious vulnerabilities; it safely bounds its search, uses unaligned‐safe access macros, and terminates correctly after scanning a fixed-size table.

1. Functional Analysis  
   - The function virDomainGetSecurityLabelList takes two parameters: a domain pointer and a pointer-to-virSecurityLabelPtr where the labels will be returned.  
   - It logs a debug message showing the seclabels pointer.  
   - It resets any prior libvirt error state.  
   - It verifies that the domain argument is valid (non-NULL and properly initialized). If the check fails, it returns –1.  
   - It verifies that the seclabels output pointer is non-NULL. If it is NULL, it jumps to the error handling block.  
   - It retrieves the connection object from the domain.  
   - If the underlying driver provides its own domainGetSecurityLabelList implementation, it calls that driver function with the same arguments.  
     – If the driver call returns a negative value, it jumps to error handling.  
     – Otherwise it returns the driver’s return code (presumably the number of labels).  
   - If the driver does not support this operation, it reports “unsupported” and flows to the error block.  
   - The error block dispatches an error on the connection and returns –1.

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Null-pointer checks are in place for both the domain parameter and the seclabels output pointer, preventing dereferencing NULL.  
   - No direct memory copies, format-string uses, integer overflows, or buffer-length calculations are performed here; all logic is a thin wrapper that delegates to the driver implementation.  
   - Error paths do not expose internal state or allow control-flow hijacking; they consistently jump to a known error dispatcher.  
   - There is no user-controlled format string or unbounded copy in this snippet.  
   - Any security-critical behavior (allocation, bounds checking on the returned list, etc.) is deferred to driver code. This wrapper does not introduce new vulnerabilities.

3. Decision  
   No, this snippet does not contain any direct vulnerabilities. It performs standard null checks and delegates to the driver, handling errors cleanly.

   - There is no exposure to format‐string, SQL injection, or other logic‐level injection attacks in this snippet.

1. Functional Analysis  
   The function WebContext::setCookies takes a QUrl and a list of QNetworkCookie objects, and schedules each cookie to be set in an underlying net::CookieStore asynchronously.  
   - It first allocates a unique request_id and a SetCookiesContext (ctxt) to track results.  
   - It iterates over each QNetworkCookie:  
     • If the cookie name is empty, it records it in ctxt->failed and skips it.  
     • Otherwise it computes an optional expiry time from the cookie’s expirationDate().  
     • It increments ctxt->remaining and invokes cookie_store->SetCookieWithDetailsAsync, passing:  
       – The URL (converted to a GURL)  
       – The cookie’s name, value, domain, path  
       – Creation time (now), expiry (if any), last-access time (now)  
       – Secure and HttpOnly flags, default SameSite policy, default priority, and a callback bound to WebContext::SetCookieCallback.  
   - After the loop, if no cookies required setting (remaining == 0), it posts a task to immediately call DeliverSetCookiesResponse, which finalizes delivery back to the caller.  
   - Finally it returns request_id to the caller.

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   • Input Validation / Domain Enforcement  
     – The code forwards the QNetworkCookie’s domain directly into SetCookieWithDetailsAsync without checking that it matches or is a subdomain of the provided URL. If an untrusted caller can supply arbitrary QNetworkCookie objects, they could attempt to set cookies for domains outside the URL’s origin. In practice, Chrome’s cookie store enforces domain validity and will reject cookies whose domain is not a suffix of the request URL’s host.  
   • String Conversions  
     – Conversions from QString/QByteArray to std::string use toStdString() and constData(), which perform UTF‑8 or local‐8bit conversions. There is no path for buffer overflow here, because std::string constructors copy and bound-check.  
   • Secure/HttpOnly Flags  
     – The code simply passes cookie.isSecure() and cookie.isHttpOnly() through. There is no attempt to override or downgrade flags. Both Chrome’s cookie store and the browser’s network stack will enforce that Secure cookies are only sent on HTTPS, and HttpOnly cookies are inaccessible to scripts.  
   • Race Conditions / Use-After-Free  
     – The scoped_refptr to SetCookiesContext and the weak pointer mechanism prevent use-after-free in the async callback. The code also handles the zero-cookie case by posting a task rather than calling the callback inline.  
   • Injection Attacks  
     – No SQL, HTML, or command‐line contexts are constructed here; these are opaque cookie attributes handed to a well‑contained cookie API.  

   In summary, the only potential concern would be trusting the caller not to supply a mismatched domain, but the underlying cookie store enforces that domain restrictions are met. 

3. Decision  
   No, the code does not contain a vulnerability. It properly delegates policy enforcement (domain, secure, HttpOnly) to the cookie store, handles empty names, and avoids buffer or memory-safety issues.

+# This directory's subdirectories are mostly independent; you can cd
+# into them and run 'make' without going through this Makefile.
+# To change the values of 'make' variables: instead of editing Makefiles,

+$(am__recursive_targets):
+	@fail=; \
+	if $(am__make_keepgoing); then \
+	  failcom='fail=yes'; \
+	else \
+	  failcom='exit 1'; \
+	fi; \
+	dot_seen=no; \
+	target=`echo $@ | sed s/-recursive//`; \
+	case "$@" in \
+	  distclean-* | maintainer-clean-*) list='$(DIST_SUBDIRS)' ;; \
+	  *) list='$(SUBDIRS)' ;; \
+	esac; \
+	for subdir in $$list; do \
+	  echo "Making $$target in $$subdir"; \
+	  if test "$$subdir" = "."; then \
+	    dot_seen=yes; \
+	    local_target="$$target-am"; \
+	  else \
+	    local_target="$$target"; \
+	  fi; \
+	  ($(am__cd) $$subdir && $(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) $$local_target) \
+	  || eval $$failcom; \
+	done; \
+	if test "$$dot_seen" = "no"; then \
+	  $(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) "$$target-am" || exit 1; \
+	fi; test -z "$$fail"

+	test -d "$(distdir)" || mkdir "$(distdir)"
+	@srcdirstrip=`echo "$(srcdir)" | sed 's/[].[^$$\\*]/\\\\&/g'`; \
+	topsrcdirstrip=`echo "$(top_srcdir)" | sed 's/[].[^$$\\*]/\\\\&/g'`; \
+	list='$(DISTFILES)'; \
+	  dist_files=`for file in $$list; do echo $$file; done | \
+	  sed -e "s|^$$srcdirstrip/||;t" \
+	      -e "s|^$$topsrcdirstrip/|$(top_builddir)/|;t"`; \
+	case $$dist_files in \
+	  */*) $(MKDIR_P) `echo "$$dist_files" | \
+			   sed '/\//!d;s|^|$(distdir)/|;s,/[^/]*$$,,' | \
+			   sort -u` ;; \
+	esac; \
+	for file in $$dist_files; do \
+	  if test -f $$file || test -d $$file; then d=.; else d=$(srcdir); fi; \
+	  if test -d $$d/$$file; then \
+	    dir=`echo "/$$file" | sed -e 's,/[^/]*$$,,'`; \
+	    if test -d "$(distdir)/$$file"; then \
+	      find "$(distdir)/$$file" -type d ! -perm -700 -exec chmod u+rwx {} \;; \
+	    fi; \
+	    if test -d $(srcdir)/$$file && test $$d != $(srcdir); then \
+	      cp -fpR $(srcdir)/$$file "$(distdir)$$dir" || exit 1; \
+	      find "$(distdir)/$$file" -type d ! -perm -700 -exec chmod u+rwx {} \;; \
+	    fi; \
+	    cp -fpR $$d/$$file "$(distdir)$$dir" || exit 1; \
+	  else \
+	    test -f "$(distdir)/$$file" \
+	    || cp -p $$d/$$file "$(distdir)/$$file" \
+	    || exit 1; \
+	  fi; \
+	done
+	@list='$(DIST_SUBDIRS)'; for subdir in $$list; do \
+	  if test "$$subdir" = .; then :; else \
+	    $(am__make_dryrun) \
+	      || test -d "$(distdir)/$$subdir" \
+	      || $(MKDIR_P) "$(distdir)/$$subdir" \
+	      || exit 1; \
+	    dir1=$$subdir; dir2="$(distdir)/$$subdir"; \
+	    $(am__relativize); \

+	    dir1=$$subdir; dir2="$(top_distdir)"; \
+	    $(am__relativize); \
+	    new_top_distdir=$$reldir; \
+	    echo " (cd $$subdir && $(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) top_distdir="$$new_top_distdir" distdir="$$new_distdir" \\"; \
+	    echo "     am__remove_distdir=: am__skip_length_check=: am__skip_mode_fix=: distdir)"; \
+	    ($(am__cd) $$subdir && \
+	      $(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) \
+	        top_distdir="$$new_top_distdir" \
+	        distdir="$$new_distdir" \
+		am__remove_distdir=: \
+		am__skip_length_check=: \
+		am__skip_mode_fix=: \
+	        distdir) \
+	      || exit 1; \
+	  fi; \
+	done
+	$(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) \
+	  top_distdir="$(top_distdir)" distdir="$(distdir)" \
+	  dist-hook
+	-test -n "$(am__skip_mode_fix)" \

+# it guarantees that the distribution is self-contained by making another

+distcheck: dist
+	case '$(DIST_ARCHIVES)' in \
+	*.tar.gz*) \
+	  GZIP=$(GZIP_ENV) gzip -dc $(distdir).tar.gz | $(am__untar) ;;\
+	*.tar.bz2*) \
+	  bzip2 -dc $(distdir).tar.bz2 | $(am__untar) ;;\
+	*.tar.lz*) \
+	  lzip -dc $(distdir).tar.lz | $(am__untar) ;;\
+	*.tar.xz*) \
+	  xz -dc $(distdir).tar.xz | $(am__untar) ;;\
+	*.tar.Z*) \
+	  uncompress -c $(distdir).tar.Z | $(am__untar) ;;\
+	*.shar.gz*) \
+	  GZIP=$(GZIP_ENV) gzip -dc $(distdir).shar.gz | unshar ;;\
+	*.zip*) \
+	  unzip $(distdir).zip ;;\
+	esac
+	chmod -R a-w $(distdir)
+	chmod u+w $(distdir)
+	mkdir $(distdir)/_build $(distdir)/_inst
+	chmod a-w $(distdir)
+	test -d $(distdir)/_build || exit 0; \
+	dc_install_base=`$(am__cd) $(distdir)/_inst && pwd | sed -e 's,^[^:\\/]:[\\/],/,'` \
+	  && dc_destdir="$${TMPDIR-/tmp}/am-dc-$$$$/" \
+	  && am__cwd=`pwd` \

+	    $(DISTCHECK_CONFIGURE_FLAGS) \
+	    --srcdir=.. --prefix="$$dc_install_base" \
+	  && $(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) \
+	  && $(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) dvi \
+	  && $(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) check \
+	  && $(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) install \
+	  && $(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) installcheck \
+	  && $(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) uninstall \
+	  && $(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) distuninstallcheck_dir="$$dc_install_base" \
+	        distuninstallcheck \
+	  && chmod -R a-w "$$dc_install_base" \
+	  && ({ \
+	       (cd ../.. && umask 077 && mkdir "$$dc_destdir") \
+	       && $(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) DESTDIR="$$dc_destdir" install \
+	       && $(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) DESTDIR="$$dc_destdir" uninstall \
+	       && $(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) DESTDIR="$$dc_destdir" \

+	  list='$(DIST_ARCHIVES)'; for i in $$list; do echo $$i; done) | \

+
+        NOTES relative to the implementation
+	====================================
+
+xsl:stylesheet:
+
+  all children except xsl:import can be in any order, so this
+can be stored as one big structure.
+
+xsl:include:
+  
+  this is really similar to XInclude, can be implemented as a
+nearly separate processing just after the XML stylesheet has been
+parsed.
+  Detect loops using a limited stack ...
+
+xsl:import:
+
+  seems this should be really implemented as having a stylesheet
+sublist being itself an import list
+
+  add the list at the end
+  when doing a resolution explore child before siblings in the list
+
+3 Data Model, we should operate on parsed trees
+
+3.1 No problem
+
+3.2 use the XML Base call, XSLT-1.1 references it
+
+3.4 Whitespace Stripping
+
+  Seems one may have to do a bit of preprocessing on both the
+stylesheet trees and the source trees.
+
+4 Expressions
+
+  looks okay, wondering about variable bindings though...
+  default namespace not in scope
+
+5.1 Processing Model
+
+  look in Michael Kay's book about how to efficiently find the
+template applying to a node. Might influence the in-memory stylesheet
+representation
+
+5.2 Patterns
+
+  the end of that section suggest that the expression could be computed in
+a simpler way. Maybe templates needs to be evaluated differently than
+through the normal XPath processing. This can be implemented separately
+or build an expression tree in the XPath module and use a different 
+evaluation mechanism. Not sure this is best.
+
+5.4 Applying Template Rules
+
+  xsl:apply-templates is the recurstion mechanism, note the select
+mechanism.
+
+  detection of loop: once the applied nodeset has been computed,
+check that none of the elements is part of the existing set in use, this
+may be costly and should be triggered only at a certain depth.
+
+5.5 Conflict Resolution for Template Rules
+
+  Sounds again that evaluation of a pattern rule should provide one
+more information not provided by the standard XPath evaluation
+
+5.6 Overriding Template Rules
+
+  another recursion mechanism, confirm that it is needed to separate
+the imported stylesheets.
+
+5.7 Modes
+
+  Confusing ??? need an example.
+
+6 Named Templates
+
+  No big deal it seems
+
+7.1.1 Literal Result Elements
+
+  cleanup of the namespace template should be done initially at stylesheet
+parsing.
+
+7.1.2 Creating Elements with xsl:element
+
+   okay, I bet it's usually used with { } expression computations
+
+7.1.3 Creating Attributes with xsl:attribute
+
+   need some running code to better understand all the subtilties
+
+7.1.4 Named Attribute Sets
+
+   Okay just a way to mimick param entities use fo attrib groups in Dtd's
+
+7.2 Creating Text
+
+   adjacent text nodes are merged ... okay
+   output escapeing might need a libxml API extension
+
+7.3 Creating Processing Instructions
+7.4 Creating Comments
+
+   RAS, one just need to make a couple of trivial checks
+
+7.5 Copying
+
+   Okay will need some testing
+
+7.6.1 Generating Text with xsl:value-of
+
+   will be a good test for XPath string() function
+   note in the example that the text nodes are coalesced
+
+7.6.2 Attribute Value Templates
+
+   hum, this is 
+    - contextual
+    - uses XPath
+
+  best seems to parse, generate an evaluation tree then evaluate
+when accessed. Note that multipe expressions can be associated to 
+a single attribute. Sounds like i will have to introduce a new
+element type inserted in the attribute nodelist. dohh ...
+
+7.7 Numbering
+
+  sounds interesting for users but might be costly, we will see ...
+
+7.7.1 Number to String Conversion Attributes
+
+   format="..." :-( it's gonna be painful ...
+
+8 Repetition
+9 Conditional Processing
+
+  doesn't sounds hard to implement since we are at an interpreter
+level but really useful in practice. Will be simple once the overall
+framework is set-up.
+
+10 Sorting
+
+  Okay applied to the node list of an xsl:apply-templates or xsl:for-each
+
+  The NOTEs are a bit scary ...
+
+11 Variables and Parameters
+
+   Variables can only be afttected at the top level, so it
+seems they act only as global variables ...
+   But this is by regions .... so some of the statements within
+a stylesheet my use a different set than others ... in practice
+it turns to be nearly like loacal variables ....
+  Need more thinking on this to handle it properly.
+  Might explain on of TOM's requests w.r.t. variable resolution
+
+11.1 Result Tree Fragments
+
+  Dohhh a new type ...
+  actually it's just a node set restricted type
+
+11.2 Values of Variables and Parameters
+
+  okay, real problem is scoping ...
+
+11.3 Using Values of Variables and Parameters with xsl:copy-of 
+
+  No surprize
+
+11.4 Top-level Variables and Parameters
+
+   It is an error if a stylesheet contains more than one binding
+   of a top-level variable with the same name and same import precedence
+
+   => ah ah, so it seems one can associate the variable bindings
+to a stylesheet and if needed recurse down the import list if not
+found, would simplify things a lot !
+
+   If the template or expression specifying the value of a global variable
+x references a global variable y, then the value for y must be computed
+before the value of x.
+
+   => Values can probably be computed dynamically at reference
+time, if this generate a loop, then it's an error. Lazy computations
+are great ...
+
+11.5 Variables and Parameters within Templates
+
+   
+   xsl:variable is allowed anywhere within a template that an instruction
+is allowed. In this case, the binding is visible for all following siblings
+and their descendants.
+   It is an error if a binding established by an xsl:variable or xsl:param
+element within a template shadows another binding established by an
+xsl:variable or xsl:param element also within the template.
+
+  => the example seems to imply that we can simply keep a list of
+     local variable binding to a template ... sounds fine.
+
+11.6 Passing Parameters to Templates
+
+  => Okay the parameter overrides the local binding
+
+12.1 Multiple Source Documents
+12.2 Keys
+
+  skipped for now
+
+12.3 Number Formatting
+
+  reimplementing Java formatting in C is gonna be a pain !
+
+12.4 Miscellaneous Additional Functions
+
+  current() => trivial
+
+  unparsed-entity-uri() => support in uri.c should do
+
+  generate-id() => use the in-memory address of the node ???
+
+  system-property() => sounds simple
+
+13 Messages
+
+  trivial I/Os
+
+14 Extensions
+15 Fallback
+
+   skipped for now
+
+16 Output
+
+16.1 XML Output Method
+
+  sounds that calling directly libxml output on the result tree
+should do it with a few caveats, for example one need to be
+able to parametrize the output
+
+16.2 HTML Output Method
+
+  sounds that calling libxml HTML output should do it too
+
+16.3 Text Output Method
+
+  doesn't sounds too hard ...
+
+16.4 Disabling Output Escaping
+
+  hum ... might be a bit painful to implement with the current framework."}<_**next**_>{"sha": "056d1961ee974f708960dfb3e8524b75c4a9c0f4", "filename": "third_party/libxslt/README.chromium", "status": "modified", "additions": 12, "deletions": 7, "changes": 19, "blob_url": "https://github.com/chromium/chromium/blob/96dbafe288dbe2f0cc45fa3c39daf6d0c37acbab/third_party/libxslt/README.chromium", "raw_url": "https://github.com/chromium/chromium/raw/96dbafe288dbe2f0cc45fa3c39daf6d0c37acbab/third_party/libxslt/README.chromium", "contents_url": "https://api.github.com/repos/chromium/chromium/contents/third_party/libxslt/README.chromium?ref=96dbafe288dbe2f0cc45fa3c39daf6d0c37acbab", "patch": "@@ -1,6 +1,6 @@

+	$(AWK) 'BEGIN { files["."] = ""; dirs["."] = 1; } \
+	  { d=$$3; if (dirs[d] != 1) { print "d", d; dirs[d] = 1 } \

+	    local_target="$$target-am"; \

+	  ($(am__cd) $$subdir && $(MAKE) $(AM_MAKEFLAGS) $$local_target) \
+	  || eval $$failcom; \

+install-man3: $(man_MANS)
+	@$(NORMAL_INSTALL)
+	@list1=''; \
+	list2='$(man_MANS)'; \
+	test -n "$(man3dir)" \
+	  && test -n "`echo $$list1$$list2`" \
+	  || exit 0; \
+	echo " $(MKDIR_P) '$(DESTDIR)$(man3dir)'"; \
+	$(MKDIR_P) "$(DESTDIR)$(man3dir)" || exit 1; \
+	{ for i in $$list1; do echo "$$i"; done;  \
+	if test -n "$$list2"; then \
+	  for i in $$list2; do echo "$$i"; done \
+	    | sed -n '/\.3[a-z]*$$/p'; \
+	fi; \
+	} | while read p; do \
+	  if test -f $$p; then d=; else d="$(srcdir)/"; fi; \
+	  echo "$$d$$p"; echo "$$p"; \
+	done | \
+	sed -e 'n;s,.*/,,;p;h;s,.*\.,,;s,^[^3][0-9a-z]*$$,3,;x' \
+	      -e 's,\.[0-9a-z]*$$,,;$(transform);G;s,\n,.,' | \
+	sed 'N;N;s,\n, ,g' | { \
+	list=; while read file base inst; do \
+	  if test "$$base" = "$$inst"; then list="$$list $$file"; else \
+	    echo " $(INSTALL_DATA) '$$file' '$(DESTDIR)$(man3dir)/$$inst'"; \
+	    $(INSTALL_DATA) "$$file" "$(DESTDIR)$(man3dir)/$$inst" || exit $$?; \
+	  fi; \
+	done; \
+	for i in $$list; do echo "$$i"; done | $(am__base_list) | \
+	while read files; do \
+	  test -z "$$files" || { \
+	    echo " $(INSTALL_DATA) $$files '$(DESTDIR)$(man3dir)'"; \
+	    $(INSTALL_DATA) $$files "$(DESTDIR)$(man3dir)" || exit $$?; }; \
+	done; }

+Summary: Library providing the GNOME XSLT engine

+Prefix: %{_prefix}

+
+%description
+This C library allows to transform XML files into other XML files
+(or HTML, text, ...) using the standard XSLT stylesheet transformation
+mechanism. To use it you need to have a version of libxml2 >= 2.6.27
+installed. The xsltproc command is a command line interface to the XSLT engine
+

+(or HTML, text, ...) using the standard XSLT stylesheet transformation
+mechanism. To use it you need to have a version of libxml2 >= 2.6.27
+installed.
+

+Group: Development/Libraries
+Requires: libxslt = %{version}-%{release}
+Requires: libxml2 >= 2.6.27
+Requires: libxml2-python >= 2.6.27

+The libxslt-python package contains a module that permits applications
+written in the Python programming language to use the interface
+supplied by the libxslt library to apply XSLT transformations.
+
+This library allows to parse sytlesheets, uses the libxml2-python
+to load and save XML and HTML files. Direct access to XPath and
+the XSLT transformation context are possible to extend the XSLT language
+with XPath functions written in Python.

+install-man3: $(man_MANS)
+	@$(NORMAL_INSTALL)
+	@list1=''; \
+	list2='$(man_MANS)'; \
+	test -n "$(man3dir)" \
+	  && test -n "`echo $$list1$$list2`" \
+	  || exit 0; \
+	echo " $(MKDIR_P) '$(DESTDIR)$(man3dir)'"; \
+	$(MKDIR_P) "$(DESTDIR)$(man3dir)" || exit 1; \
+	{ for i in $$list1; do echo "$$i"; done;  \
+	if test -n "$$list2"; then \
+	  for i in $$list2; do echo "$$i"; done \
+	    | sed -n '/\.3[a-z]*$$/p'; \
+	fi; \
+	} | while read p; do \
+	  if test -f $$p; then d=; else d="$(srcdir)/"; fi; \
+	  echo "$$d$$p"; echo "$$p"; \
+	done | \
+	sed -e 'n;s,.*/,,;p;h;s,.*\.,,;s,^[^3][0-9a-z]*$$,3,;x' \
+	      -e 's,\.[0-9a-z]*$$,,;$(transform);G;s,\n,.,' | \
+	sed 'N;N;s,\n, ,g' | { \
+	list=; while read file base inst; do \
+	  if test "$$base" = "$$inst"; then list="$$list $$file"; else \
+	    echo " $(INSTALL_DATA) '$$file' '$(DESTDIR)$(man3dir)/$$inst'"; \
+	    $(INSTALL_DATA) "$$file" "$(DESTDIR)$(man3dir)/$$inst" || exit $$?; \
+	  fi; \
+	done; \
+	for i in $$list; do echo "$$i"; done | $(am__base_list) | \
+	while read files; do \
+	  test -z "$$files" || { \
+	    echo " $(INSTALL_DATA) $$files '$(DESTDIR)$(man3dir)'"; \
+	    $(INSTALL_DATA) $$files "$(DESTDIR)$(man3dir)" || exit $$?; }; \
+	done; }
+

+	@list=''; test -n "$(man3dir)" || exit 0; \
+	files=`{ for i in $$list; do echo "$$i"; done; \
+	l2='$(man_MANS)'; for i in $$l2; do echo "$$i"; done | \
+	  sed -n '/\.3[a-z]*$$/p'; \
+	} | sed -e 's,.*/,,;h;s,.*\.,,;s,^[^3][0-9a-z]*$$,3,;x' \

+import io
+import os
+import sys
+import difflib
+
+from os import path
+from subprocess import Popen, PIPE
+
+xsltproc = path.join(os.getcwd(), "win32", "bin.msvc", "xsltproc.exe")
+if not path.isfile(xsltproc):
+    raise FileNotFoundError(xsltproc)
+
+def runtests(xsl_dir, xml_dir="."):
+    old_dir = os.getcwd()
+    os.chdir(xsl_dir)
+
+    for xsl_file in os.listdir():
+        if not xsl_file.endswith(".xsl"):
+            continue
+        xsl_path = "./" + xsl_file
+        name = path.splitext(xsl_file)[0]
+
+        xml_path = path.join(xml_dir + "/" + name + ".xml")
+        if not path.isfile(xml_path):
+            continue
+
+        args = [ xsltproc, xsl_path, xml_path ]
+        p = Popen(args, stdout=PIPE, stderr=PIPE)
+        out_path = path.join(xml_dir, name + ".out")
+        err_path = path.join(xml_dir, name + ".err")
+        out_diff = diff(p.stdout, "<stdout>", name + ".out")
+        err_diff = diff(p.stderr, "<stderr>", name + ".err")
+
+        if (len(out_diff) or len(err_diff)):
+            sys.stdout.writelines(out_diff)
+            sys.stdout.writelines(err_diff)
+            print()
+
+    os.chdir(old_dir)
+
+def diff(got_stream, got_name, expected_path):
+    text_stream = io.TextIOWrapper(got_stream, encoding="latin_1")
+    got_lines = text_stream.readlines()
+
+    if path.isfile(expected_path):
+        file = open(expected_path, "r", encoding="latin_1")
+        expected_lines = file.readlines()
+    else:
+        expected_lines = []
+
+    diff = difflib.unified_diff(expected_lines, got_lines,
+                                fromfile=expected_path,
+                                tofile=got_name)
+    return list(diff)
+
+print("## Running REC tests")
+runtests("tests/REC")
+
+print("## Running general tests")
+runtests("tests/general", "./../docs")
+
+print("## Running exslt common tests")
+runtests("tests/exslt/common")
+
+print("## Running exslt functions tests")
+runtests("tests/exslt/functions")
+
+print("## Running exslt math tests")
+runtests("tests/exslt/math")
+
+print("## Running exslt sets tests")
+runtests("tests/exslt/sets")
+
+print("## Running exslt strings tests")
+runtests("tests/exslt/strings")
+
+print("## Running exslt dynamic tests")
+runtests("tests/exslt/dynamic")
+
+print("## Running exslt date tests")
+runtests("tests/exslt/date")
+"}<_**next**_>{"sha": "45c3e28f2f12f86861102f3b0f3f2367f5b1a3cc", "filename": "third_party/libxslt/xslt-config.in", "status": "removed", "additions": 0, "deletions": 137, "changes": 137, "blob_url": "https://github.com/chromium/chromium/blob/5d32c4d7ac9cd3e4a45a5cc1fc547103b66816c7/third_party/libxslt/xslt-config.in", "raw_url": "https://github.com/chromium/chromium/raw/5d32c4d7ac9cd3e4a45a5cc1fc547103b66816c7/third_party/libxslt/xslt-config.in", "contents_url": "https://api.github.com/repos/chromium/chromium/contents/third_party/libxslt/xslt-config.in?ref=5d32c4d7ac9cd3e4a45a5cc1fc547103b66816c7", "patch": "@@ -1,137 +0,0 @@

1. Functional Analysis  
   - A static local variable `have_init` is declared and initialized to 0 the first time `call_snmp_init_once` is invoked.  
   - The `if (have_init == 0)` check ensures that `init_snmp(PACKAGE_NAME)` is called only on the very first invocation.  
   - After that conditional call, `have_init` is set to 1, preventing any subsequent calls to `init_snmp` in future invocations.

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - There is no direct handling of untrusted input, no buffer manipulations, and no string operations here—so common flaws like buffer overflows, injection, or format-string vulnerabilities do not apply.  
   - The only concern is thread safety: if two threads call this function at the same time, both might see `have_init == 0` before either writes back `have_init = 1`, causing `init_snmp` to run twice. That race could lead to double initialization or inconsistent internal state within the SNMP library.  
   - Aside from that potential race condition in a multithreaded context, the code itself does not introduce other security vulnerabilities.

3. Decision  
   No, the code is not inherently vulnerable. It correctly guards against multiple initializations in a single-threaded context; the only caveat is a possible race condition under concurrent calls.

- DCHECK(io_runner->BelongsToCurrentThread());  
  Verifies that TearDownTest is running on the expected thread (the IO runner) in debug builds.

- scoped_refptr<base::SequencedTaskRunner> db_runner = storage()->db_task_runner_;  
  Captures a reference to the database task runner so that it can be used to drain pending tasks later.

- storage()->CancelDelegateCallbacks(delegate());  
  Tells the storage layer to stop scheduling any further calls to the test’s delegate, preventing new callbacks from being enqueued.

- group_ = nullptr; cache_ = nullptr; cache2_ = nullptr; mock_quota_manager_proxy_ = nullptr;  
  Clears raw or scoped pointers that reference test fixtures or mocks, ensuring they won’t be used again.

- delegate_.reset(); service_.reset();  
  Releases ownership of and destroys the delegate and service objects (typically wrapped in smart pointers).

- FlushTasks(db_runner.get());  
  Runs all pending tasks on the database thread until its queue is empty.

- FlushTasks(background_thread->task_runner().get());  
  Runs all pending tasks on the background thread until its queue is empty.

- FlushTasks(db_runner.get());  
  Runs another drain of the database-thread queue to catch any tasks that might have been posted by the background thread in the interim.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Memory safety: The code uses smart pointers (scoped_refptr, reset() on delegate_ and service_) and nulls out raw pointers before tearing down threads. This prevents use-after-free of test fixtures and mocks.
- Race conditions:  
  • By cancelling delegate callbacks before resetting the delegate, it ensures no new tasks will re-enqueue callbacks after the delegate has been destroyed.  
  • Flushing the db runner both before and after draining the background thread further eliminates the chance that tasks posted during teardown will outlive their targets.
- Thread-safety: The initial DCHECK enforces correct thread context. Task runners are drained in a well-defined sequence.
- No external inputs or dynamic code generation are present, so common injection or deserialization flaws do not apply.

Overall, the teardown sequence diligently cancels callbacks, releases resources, and drains task queues. There is no evidence of buffer overflows, use-after-free, data races, or other exploitable flaws.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any exploitable vulnerabilities.

Separate repaint and layout requirements of StyleDifference (Step 1)

Previously StyleDifference was an enum that proximately bigger values
imply smaller values (e.g. StyleDifferenceLayout implies
StyleDifferenceRepaint). This causes unnecessary repaints in some cases
on layout change.

Convert StyleDifference to a structure containing relatively independent
flags.

This change doesn't directly improve the result, but can make further
repaint optimizations possible.

Step 1 doesn't change any functionality. RenderStyle still generate the
legacy StyleDifference enum when comparing styles and convert the result
to the new StyleDifference. Implicit requirements are not handled during
the conversion.

Converted call sites to use the new StyleDifference according to the
following conversion rules:
- diff == StyleDifferenceEqual (&& !context) => diff.hasNoChange()
- diff == StyleDifferenceRepaint => diff.needsRepaintObjectOnly()
- diff == StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsRepaintLayer()
- diff == StyleDifferenceRepaint || diff == StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsRepaintLayer()
- diff >= StyleDifferenceRepaint => diff.needsRepaint() || diff.needsLayout()
- diff >= StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsRepaintLayer() || diff.needsLayout()
- diff > StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsLayout()
- diff == StyleDifferencePositionedMovementLayoutOnly => diff.needsPositionedMovementLayoutOnly()
- diff == StyleDifferenceLayout => diff.needsFullLayout()

original_information.commit_message:
mnt: Correct permission checks in do_remount

While invesgiating the issue where in "mount --bind -oremount,ro ..."
would result in later "mount --bind -oremount,rw" succeeding even if
the mount started off locked I realized that there are several
additional mount flags that should be locked and are not.

In particular MNT_NOSUID, MNT_NODEV, MNT_NOEXEC, and the atime
flags in addition to MNT_READONLY should all be locked.  These
flags are all per superblock, can all be changed with MS_BIND,
and should not be changable if set by a more privileged user.

The following additions to the current logic are added in this patch.
- nosuid may not be clearable by a less privileged user.
- nodev  may not be clearable by a less privielged user.
- noexec may not be clearable by a less privileged user.
- atime flags may not be changeable by a less privileged user.

The logic with atime is that always setting atime on access is a
global policy and backup software and auditing software could break if
atime bits are not updated (when they are configured to be updated),
and serious performance degradation could result (DOS attack) if atime
updates happen when they have been explicitly disabled.  Therefore an
unprivileged user should not be able to mess with the atime bits set
by a more privileged user.

The additional restrictions are implemented with the addition of
MNT_LOCK_NOSUID, MNT_LOCK_NODEV, MNT_LOCK_NOEXEC, and MNT_LOCK_ATIME
mnt flags.

Taken together these changes and the fixes for MNT_LOCK_READONLY
should make it safe for an unprivileged user to create a user
namespace and to call "mount --bind -o remount,... ..." without
the danger of mount flags being changed maliciously.

original_information.commit_message:
powerpc/tm: Flush TM only if CPU has TM feature

Commit cd63f3c ("powerpc/tm: Fix saving of TM SPRs in core dump")
added code to access TM SPRs in flush_tmregs_to_thread(). However
flush_tmregs_to_thread() does not check if TM feature is available on
CPU before trying to access TM SPRs in order to copy live state to
thread structures. flush_tmregs_to_thread() is indeed guarded by
CONFIG_PPC_TRANSACTIONAL_MEM but it might be the case that kernel
was compiled with CONFIG_PPC_TRANSACTIONAL_MEM enabled and ran on
a CPU without TM feature available, thus rendering the execution
of TM instructions that are treated by the CPU as illegal instructions.

The fix is just to add proper checking in flush_tmregs_to_thread()
if CPU has the TM feature before accessing any TM-specific resource,
returning immediately if TM is no available on the CPU. Adding
that checking in flush_tmregs_to_thread() instead of in places
where it is called, like in vsr_get() and vsr_set(), is better because
avoids the same problem cropping up elsewhere.

original_information.commit_message:
mime-actions: use file metadata for trusting desktop files

Currently we only trust desktop files that have the executable bit
set, and don't replace the displayed icon or the displayed name until
it's trusted, which prevents for running random programs by a malicious
desktop file.

However, the executable permission is preserved if the desktop file
comes from a compressed file.

To prevent this, add a metadata::trusted metadata to the file once the
user acknowledges the file as trusted. This adds metadata to the file,
which cannot be added unless it has access to the computer.

Also remove the SHEBANG "trusted" content we were putting inside the
desktop file, since that doesn't add more security since it can come
with the file itself.

original_information.commit_message:
list-objects: pass full pathname to callbacks

When we find a blob at "a/b/c", we currently pass this to
our show_object_fn callbacks as two components: "a/b/" and
"c". Callbacks which want the full value then call
path_name(), which concatenates the two. But this is an
inefficient interface; the path is a strbuf, and we could
simply append "c" to it temporarily, then roll back the
length, without creating a new copy.

So we could improve this by teaching the callsites of
path_name() this trick (and there are only 3). But we can
also notice that no callback actually cares about the
broken-down representation, and simply pass each callback
the full path "a/b/c" as a string. The callback code becomes
even simpler, then, as we do not have to worry about freeing
an allocated buffer, nor rolling back our modification to
the strbuf.

This is theoretically less efficient, as some callbacks
would not bother to format the final path component. But in
practice this is not measurable. Since we use the same
strbuf over and over, our work to grow it is amortized, and
we really only pay to memcpy a few bytes.

The posix timer overrun handling is broken because the forwarding functions
can return a huge number of overruns which does not fit in an int. As a
consequence timer_getoverrun(2) and siginfo::si_overrun can turn into
random number generators.

accounting is correct. 3Remove the temporary (int) casts.

via timer_getoverrun(2) or siginfo::si_overrun limited to a positive value
between 0 and INT_MAX. INT_MAX is an indicator for user space that the

original_information.commit_message:
perf: Remove the nmi parameter from the swevent and overflow interface

The nmi parameter indicated if we could do wakeups from the current
context, if not, we would set some state and self-IPI and let the
resulting interrupt do the wakeup.

For the various event classes:

  - hardware: nmi=0; PMI is in fact an NMI or we run irq_work_run from
    the PMI-tail (ARM etc.)
  - tracepoint: nmi=0; since tracepoint could be from NMI context.
  - software: nmi=[0,1]; some, like the schedule thing cannot
    perform wakeups, and hence need 0.

As one can see, there is very little nmi=1 usage, and the down-side of
not using it is that on some platforms some software events can have a
jiffy delay in wakeup (when arch_irq_work_raise isn't implemented).

The up-side however is that we can remove the nmi parameter and save a
bunch of conditionals in fast paths.

- Based on the number of I²C messages (`num`), it handles two cases:

  • Case num == 2:  
    – Interprets the first message’s single byte as the STV0299 register index.  
    – Loops over the requested read length (`msg[1].len`), issuing a two‐byte read (`DW210X_READ_MSG`) for each successive register address and storing the low byte into the caller’s buffer.  

  • Case num == 1:  
    – Inspects the target I²C address (`msg[0].addr`) and, depending on the address:  
      • 0x68: Prepares a three‐byte write to the STV0299 register.  
      • 0x60: If flags == 0, writes four tuner‐PLL bytes; otherwise reads a single tuner status byte.  
      • DW2102_RC_QUERY: Reads two bytes of remote‐control data.  
      • DW2102_VOLTAGE_CTRL: Writes a two‐byte voltage‐control command.  

- After performing the bus operation via `dw210x_op_rw`, the routine releases the mutex and returns the number of messages processed.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- No dynamic allocations or pointer arithmetic on internal buffers (`buf6` is always accessed within its 7‑byte size).  
- The code correctly takes and releases a mutex, avoiding data races on the device context.  
- There is no integer overflow, format‐string, or unbounded‐loop vulnerability.  
- One potential weakness is that the code assumes the caller’s `i2c_msg` buffers are at least as long as the fields it reads or writes:  
  • For address 0x68 it reads `msg[0].buf[1]`.  
  • For address 0x60 it reads up to `msg[0].buf[3]`.  
  • In the two‐message case it writes up to `msg[1].buf[msg[1].len-1]` without checking upper bounds beyond `msg[1].len`.  
  However, in typical kernel usage, the I²C core and upper‐layer drivers allocate and pass correctly sized `i2c_msg` structures, so these assumptions hold.  

3. Decision

1. Functional Analysis

- The function cluster_pages_for_defrag() tries to collect up to num_pages sequential pages in a file (inode) starting at start_index, to prepare them for a defragmentation pass.
- It reads the file size (i_size_read), computes the last valid page index (file_end), and clamps the requested count to the actual number of pages in the file.
- It reserves delayed‐allocation space for those pages (btrfs_delalloc_reserve_space).
- For each page in the range:
  - It uses find_or_create_page() to pin the page in the page cache.
  - It checks for any pending ordered extents on that page, waits for them to finish (btrfs_start_ordered_extent), and then re‑acquires the page lock if the mapping has not changed.
  - If the page is not up‑to‑date, it issues a read (btrfs_readpage) and waits for completion; on I/O error it bails out.
  - It stores the locked, up‑to‑date page in the pages[] array.
- Once it has locked i_done pages (maybe fewer than requested if eof or error), it waits for any in-flight writeback to finish.
- It clears any delalloc/dirty accounting bits on the entire extent range covering those pages, then marks the extent for defragmentation (set_extent_defrag).
- It unlocks the extent locks and then, for each page, clears the page’s dirty flags for I/O, sets it back dirty (so it re‑writes), unmaps the “checked” marker, sets it extent_mapped, and finally unlocks and releases the page.
- It returns the number of pages it prepared (i_done), or an error code.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Race conditions on page mapping: The code explicitly re‑checks page->mapping after unlocking and rebinding a page around ordered‐extent waits and retries (goto again). That prevents use‑after‑free or operating on a stale page belonging to a removed mapping.
- Memory leaks / accounting imbalance: Delalloc reservations are paired with releases in both the successful and error paths. For the partial‑success path it releases only the unused portion, and in the total‐failure path it releases the entire reservation.
- Locks:  
  • Page locks are always held before touching page fields or states, then released and page_cache_release() is called in all paths for pages that were pinned.  
  • Extent bit locks (lock_extent / lock_extent_bits / unlock_extent… ) bracket clear_extent_bit, set_extent_defrag, unlock_extent_cached correctly.
- I/O error handling: If a read fails, the code aborts and cleans up any pinned pages and reserved space, returning –EIO.
- Deadlocks: The code acquires a sequence of page locks in index order, then a single extent lock covering the whole span. This ordering (pages first, then the larger‐range extent lock) is consistent within this function and with sub‑operations that first lock extent bits, so no obvious lock inversion occurs.
- Infinite loop risks: The “again:” retry mechanism can only spin if a page mapping constantly changes underfoot, but each cycle requires re‑creating the page; that is bounded by the system’s page‐cache reclamation. In steady state, the mapping change is rare, so this is not an exploitable hang.
- No unbounded resource usage: page_cnt is limited by the file length and num_pages, and memory allocations use GFP_NOFS or the write mask. There is no loop that can grow arbitrarily.
- Permissions, user input: start_index and num_pages come from higher‐level callers that already enforce filesystem invariants. Out‑of‑bounds start_index or zero i_size simply lead to an early return 0.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any obvious security vulnerabilities. It properly handles races on page mappings, balances resource reservations/releases, and serializes access with correct locking.

original_information.commit_message:
Btrfs: fix hash overflow handling

The handling for directory crc hash overflows was fairly obscure,
split_leaf returns EOVERFLOW when we try to extend the item and that is
supposed to bubble up to userland.  For a while it did so, but along the
way we added better handling of errors and forced the FS readonly if we
hit IO errors during the directory insertion.

Along the way, we started testing only for EEXIST and the EOVERFLOW case
was dropped.  The end result is that we may force the FS readonly if we
catch a directory hash bucket overflow.

This fixes a few problem spots.  First I add tests for EOVERFLOW in the
places where we can safely just return the error up the chain.

btrfs_rename is harder though, because it tries to insert the new
directory item only after it has already unlinked anything the rename
was going to overwrite.  Rather than adding very complex logic, I added
a helper to test for the hash overflow case early while it is still safe
to bail out.

Snapshot and subvolume creation had a similar problem, so they are using
the new helper now too.

original_information.commit_message:
sched/fair: Fix infinite loop in update_blocked_averages() by reverting a9e7f6544b9c

Zhipeng Xie, Xie XiuQi and Sargun Dhillon reported lockups in the
scheduler under high loads, starting at around the v4.18 time frame,
and Zhipeng Xie tracked it down to bugs in the rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list
manipulation.

Do a (manual) revert of:

  a9e7f6544b9c ("sched/fair: Fix O(nr_cgroups) in load balance path")

It turns out that the list_del_leaf_cfs_rq() introduced by this commit
is a surprising property that was not considered in followup commits
such as:

  9c2791f936ef ("sched/fair: Fix hierarchical order in rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list")

As Vincent Guittot explains:

 "I think that there is a bigger problem with commit a9e7f6544b9c and
  cfs_rq throttling:

  Let take the example of the following topology TG2 --> TG1 --> root:

   1) The 1st time a task is enqueued, we will add TG2 cfs_rq then TG1
      cfs_rq to leaf_cfs_rq_list and we are sure to do the whole branch in
      one path because it has never been used and can't be throttled so
      tmp_alone_branch will point to leaf_cfs_rq_list at the end.

   2) Then TG1 is throttled

   3) and we add TG3 as a new child of TG1.

   4) The 1st enqueue of a task on TG3 will add TG3 cfs_rq just before TG1
      cfs_rq and tmp_alone_branch will stay  on rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list.

  With commit a9e7f6544b9c, we can del a cfs_rq from rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list.
  So if the load of TG1 cfs_rq becomes NULL before step 2) above, TG1
  cfs_rq is removed from the list.
  Then at step 4), TG3 cfs_rq is added at the beginning of rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list
  but tmp_alone_branch still points to TG3 cfs_rq because its throttled
  parent can't be enqueued when the lock is released.
  tmp_alone_branch doesn't point to rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list whereas it should.

  So if TG3 cfs_rq is removed or destroyed before tmp_alone_branch
  points on another TG cfs_rq, the next TG cfs_rq that will be added,
  will be linked outside rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list - which is bad.

  In addition, we can break the ordering of the cfs_rq in
  rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list but this ordering is used to update and
  propagate the update from leaf down to root."

Instead of trying to work through all these cases and trying to reproduce
the very high loads that produced the lockup to begin with, simplify
the code temporarily by reverting a9e7f6544b9c - which change was clearly
not thought through completely.

This (hopefully) gives us a kernel that doesn't lock up so people
can continue to enjoy their holidays without worrying about regressions. ;-)

The long input was rejected needlessly; the long output caused
interval_out() to overrun its buffer.  ECPG's pgtypes library has a copy
of the vulnerable functions, which bore the same vulnerabilities along
with some of its own.  In contrast to the server, certain long inputs
caused stack overflow rather than failing cleanly.  Back-patch to 8.4
(all supported versions).

Reported by Daniel Schüssler, reviewed by Tom Lane.

Security: CVE-2014-0063

original_information.Summary: Integer signedness error in the CIFSFindNext function in fs/cifs/cifssmb.c in the Linux kernel before 3.1 allows remote CIFS servers to cause a denial of service (memory corruption) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a large length value in a response to a read request for a directory.
original_information.commit_message:
cifs: fix possible memory corruption in CIFSFindNext

The name_len variable in CIFSFindNext is a signed int that gets set to
the resume_name_len in the cifs_search_info. The resume_name_len however
is unsigned and for some infolevels is populated directly from a 32 bit
value sent by the server.

If the server sends a very large value for this, then that value could
look negative when converted to a signed int. That would make that
value pass the PATH_MAX check later in CIFSFindNext. The name_len would
then be used as a length value for a memcpy. It would then be treated
as unsigned again, and the memcpy scribbles over a ton of memory.

Fix this by making the name_len an unsigned value in CIFSFindNext.

original_information.commit_message:
Fix handling of parameter-entity references

There were two bugs where parameter-entity references could lead to an
unexpected change of the input buffer in xmlParseNameComplex and
xmlDictLookup being called with an invalid pointer.

Percent sign in DTD Names
=========================

The NEXTL macro used to call xmlParserHandlePEReference. When parsing
"complex" names inside the DTD, this could result in entity expansion
which created a new input buffer. The fix is to simply remove the call
to xmlParserHandlePEReference from the NEXTL macro. This is safe because
no users of the macro require expansion of parameter entities.

- xmlParseNameComplex
- xmlParseNCNameComplex
- xmlParseNmtoken

The percent sign is not allowed in names, which are grammatical tokens.

- xmlParseEntityValue

Parameter-entity references in entity values are expanded but this
happens in a separate step in this function.

- xmlParseSystemLiteral

Parameter-entity references are ignored in the system literal.

- xmlParseAttValueComplex
- xmlParseCharDataComplex
- xmlParseCommentComplex
- xmlParsePI
- xmlParseCDSect

Parameter-entity references are ignored outside the DTD.

- xmlLoadEntityContent

This function is only called from xmlStringLenDecodeEntities and
entities are replaced in a separate step immediately after the function
call.

This bug could also be triggered with an internal subset and double
entity expansion.

This fixes bug 766956 initially reported by Wei Lei and independently by
Chromium's ClusterFuzz, Hanno Böck, and Marco Grassi. Thanks to everyone
involved.

xmlParseNameComplex with XML_PARSE_OLD10
========================================

When parsing Names inside an expanded parameter entity with the
XML_PARSE_OLD10 option, xmlParseNameComplex would call xmlGROW via the
GROW macro if the input buffer was exhausted. At the end of the
parameter entity's replacement text, this function would then call
xmlPopInput which invalidated the input buffer.

There should be no need to invoke GROW in this situation because the
buffer is grown periodically every XML_PARSER_CHUNK_SIZE characters and,
at least for UTF-8, in xmlCurrentChar. This also matches the code path
executed when XML_PARSE_OLD10 is not set.

This fixes bugs 781205 (CVE-2017-9049) and 781361 (CVE-2017-9050).
Thanks to Marcel Böhme and Thuan Pham for the report.

Additional hardening
====================

A separate check was added in xmlParseNameComplex to validate the
buffer size.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function `_dbus_atomic_get` reads and returns the current value of `atomic->value` in a thread‑safe manner.
- If `DBUS_USE_SYNC` is defined:
  - It issues a full memory barrier (`__sync_synchronize()`) to ensure all prior memory operations are visible before the read.
  - It then returns `atomic->value` directly.
- If `DBUS_USE_SYNC` is not defined:
  - It acquires a mutex or spinlock (`_DBUS_LOCK(atomic)`).
  - It reads `atomic->value` into a local variable `res`.
  - It releases the lock (`_DBUS_UNLOCK(atomic)`).
  - It returns the value in `res`.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Race conditions / data races:  
  - In the `DBUS_USE_SYNC` case, the full memory barrier prevents reordering of loads/stores around this read, making the read safe with respect to other atomic operations.  
  - In the non‑sync case, the explicit lock/unlock guarantees mutual exclusion, so concurrent readers/writers cannot corrupt `atomic->value` or observe torn writes.
- Memory safety:  
  - The code simply reads a 32‑bit integer; there is no pointer arithmetic or unbounded buffers that could lead to buffer overflows or use‑after‑free.
- Deadlocks:  
  - The function acquires exactly one lock and releases it before returning. There is no nested locking here, so it does not introduce deadlock on its own.
- Invariants and initialization:  
  - It assumes that `atomic` points to a valid, initialized `DBusAtomic` structure and that the lock is correctly initialized. Misuse (e.g., passing NULL or an uninitialized lock) would be a caller error, not a flaw in this function.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain vulnerabilities—it correctly enforces atomicity on reading `atomic->value`.

1. Functional Analysis  
   - The function zend_hash_get_current_key_zval_ex takes a read‐only HashTable pointer ht, an output zval *key, and the current position pointer pos.  
   - It reads the current bucket index idx = *pos.  
   - IS_CONSISTENT(ht) is a runtime check (debug‐only) that the table’s internal state is valid.  
   - If idx equals HT_INVALID_IDX, there is no current element, so it initializes *key to NULL.  
   - Otherwise it computes the bucket address p = ht->arData + idx.  
     - If p->key is non‐NULL (i.e. this is a string‐keyed entry), it does ZVAL_STR_COPY(key, p->key) to return a new zval containing a reference‐counted copy of the string key.  
     - If p->key is NULL (i.e. this is an integer‐keyed entry), it does ZVAL_LONG(key, p->h) to return the numeric key stored in p->h.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Memory safety: the function only reads from ht->arData at a checked index; HT_INVALID_IDX prevents out‐of‐bounds.  
   - Reference counts: ZVAL_STR_COPY correctly bumps the string’s refcount; there is no leak or double‐free in this routine.  
   - Null pointers: pos and ht are assumed valid by the PHP engine; IS_CONSISTENT(ht) would catch a corrupt table in debug builds. The body never dereferences key when key itself is NULL (it writes into it).  
   - Integer overflow / signedness: idx is uint32_t and compared to a constant; no arithmetic on idx other than pointer arithmetic within the array.  
   - No user‐supplied data is written unchecked, so no buffer overflows or format‐string issues arise here.  

3. Decision  
   No, this code does not contain any vulnerabilities—it safely retrieves either a string or integer key from the hash table and handles the “no current element” case correctly.

- The function `handle_invlpg` is entered when the guest executes the INVLPG instruction under KVM.
- It reads the VM exit qualification field via `vmcs_readl(EXIT_QUALIFICATION)`, which encodes the operand (the linear address) of the INVLPG.
- It calls `kvm_mmu_invlpg(vcpu, exit_qualification)` to perform the actual TLB invalidation for that linear address in the KVM MMU.
- It advances the guest’s instruction pointer by calling `skip_emulated_instruction(vcpu)` so that execution can resume past the INVLPG.
- Finally, it returns 1 to indicate the exit was handled.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- All inputs to this routine come from controlled VMCS state on an INVLPG exit.  
- `exit_qualification` is a hardware‐validated field; it cannot be arbitrarily crafted to trigger out‐of‐bounds memory writes within this function.
- The subsequent call to `kvm_mmu_invlpg` is responsible for sanitizing and bounding the linear address before touching any internal data structures, so there is no direct pointer arithmetic or unchecked indexing here.
- No unbounded loops, no integer overflows, no use-after-free or buffer-copy operations occur in this snippet.
- The code properly sequences read of qualification, performs the invalidation via a dedicated kernel helper, and advances the instruction pointer.

3. Decision

No, this code does not contain any vulnerabilities. It safely handles the INVLPG exit and delegates bounds checking and TLB maintenance to the MMU layer.

original_information.Summary: arch/x86/kvm/vmx.c in the KVM subsystem in the Linux kernel before 3.17.2 on Intel processors does not ensure that the value in the CR4 control register remains the same after a VM entry, which allows host OS users to kill arbitrary processes or cause a denial of service (system disruption) by leveraging /dev/kvm access, as demonstrated by PR_SET_TSC prctl calls within a modified copy of QEMU.
original_information.commit_message:
x86,kvm,vmx: Preserve CR4 across VM entry

CR4 isn't constant; at least the TSD and PCE bits can vary.

TBH, treating CR0 and CR3 as constant scares me a bit, too, but it looks
like it's correct.

This adds a branch and a read from cr4 to each vm entry.  Because it is
extremely likely that consecutive entries into the same vcpu will have
the same host cr4 value, this fixes up the vmcs instead of restoring cr4
after the fact.  A subsequent patch will add a kernel-wide cr4 shadow,
reducing the overhead in the common case to just two memory reads and a
branch.

original_information.commit_message:
Implicitly bypass localhost when proxying requests.

This aligns Chrome's behavior with the Windows and macOS proxy resolvers (but not Firefox).

Concretely:
 * localhost names (as determined by net::IsLocalhost) now implicitly bypass the proxy
 * link-local IP addresses implicitly bypass the proxy

The implicit rules are handled by ProxyBypassRules, and it is possible to override them when manually configuring proxy settings (but not when using PAC or auto-detect).

This change also adds support for the "<-loopback>" proxy bypass rule, with similar semantics as it has on Windows (removes the implicit bypass rules for localhost and link-local).

The compatibility risk of this change should be low as proxying through localhost was not universally supported. It is however an idiom used in testing (a number of our own tests had such a dependency). Impacted users can use the "<-loopback>" bypass rule as a workaround.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function StreamTcpValidateChecksum takes a Packet pointer p and returns 1 if the packet’s TCP checksum validates (or is to be ignored), or 0 if it fails.
- It starts by assuming ret = 1 (valid).  
- If the packet’s flags include PKT_IGNORE_CHECKSUM, it returns 1 immediately.  
- If p->level4_comp_csum is –1 (meaning “not yet computed”), it:
  • Checks whether the packet is IPv4 or IPv6.  
  • Calls TCPChecksum (for IPv4) or TCPV6Checksum (for IPv6), passing in the source/destination addresses, a pointer to the TCP header cast to uint16_t*, the total length of TCP header+payload, and the stored checksum field.  
  • Stores the result (0 if valid, nonzero if invalid) in p->level4_comp_csum.  
- If the computed checksum is nonzero, the packet is marked invalid:  
  • ret is set to 0.  
  • An invalid‐checksum counter is incremented, either in p->livedev or in a global pcap counter.  
- Finally, ret (1 or 0) is returned.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- There is no user‐driven loop or unbounded memory allocation here—only a simple check and a call into established checksum routines.  
- The only arithmetic is adding payload_len + TCP header length; if those fields were grossly out of range, the underlying checksum routine might read past the packet buffer, but that would be a flaw in the packet‐parser or in TCPChecksum itself, not in this wrapper.  
- level4_comp_csum is used atomically only for caching the result; even if two threads raced to compute it, the worst outcome is two checksum calls instead of one, and the atomic counter update prevents a torn increment.  
- No pointers are written to, no integer division or modulus by zero, and no format‐string or other classic C‐level vulnerabilities appear here.

3. Decision

No, this function as written does not introduce any new vulnerabilities.

original_information.commit_message:
stream: support RST getting lost/ignored

In case of a valid RST on a SYN, the state is switched to 'TCP_CLOSED'.
However, the target of the RST may not have received it, or may not
have accepted it. Also, the RST may have been injected, so the supposed
sender may not actually be aware of the RST that was sent in it's name.

In this case the previous behavior was to switch the state to CLOSED and
accept no further TCP updates or stream reassembly.

This patch changes this. It still switches the state to CLOSED, as this
is by far the most likely to be correct. However, it will reconsider
the state if the receiver continues to talk.

To do this on each state change the previous state will be recorded in
TcpSession::pstate. If a non-RST packet is received after a RST, this
TcpSession::pstate is used to try to continue the conversation.

If the (supposed) sender of the RST is also continueing the conversation
as normal, it's highly likely it didn't send the RST. In this case
a stream event is generated.

This function, __copy_skb_header(new, old), initializes a freshly allocated socket buffer “new” by copying metadata from an existing buffer “old.”  In detail it:

• Copies basic metadata fields  
  – tstamp: packet timestamp  
  – dev: network device pointer  
  – pkt_type, protocol, mark, priority, skb_iif, pfmemalloc, local_df  

• Copies header offsets into the data area  
  – mac_header, network_header, transport_header  
  – inner_mac_header, inner_network_header, inner_transport_header (for encapsulated packets)  

• Copies routing and lookup state  
  – skb_dst_copy: destination cache  
  – skb_copy_hash: flow hash  
  – skb_copy_queue_mapping: CPU/queue mapping  

• Copies offload and checksum state  
  – csum, ip_summed, ooo_okay, no_fcs  

• Copies encapsulation markers and VLAN tags  
  – encapsulation, vlan_proto, vlan_tci  

• Copies security/XFRM state if enabled  
  – secpath: by calling secpath_get(old->sp) under CONFIG_XFRM  
  – skb_copy_secmark under CONFIG_INET or similar  

• Copies packet filter / netfilter state  
  – __nf_copy: netfilter related indexes and pointers  
  – ipvs_property under CONFIG_IP_VS  

• Copies traffic‑control state  
  – tc_index, tc_verd under CONFIG_NET_SCHED/CLS_ACT  

• Copies other scheduler/polling fields  
  – napi_id under CONFIG_NET_RX_BUSY_POLL

is active on the bridge interface itself as opposed to one of the
constituent interfaces in the bridge.

Unfortunately the operation that adds the mp->mglist node to the
list neglected to check whether it has already been added.  This
leads to list corruption in the form of nodes pointing to itself.

Normally this would be quite obvious as it would cause an infinite
loop when walking the list.  However, as this list is never actually
walked (which means that we don't really need it, I'll get rid of

a delete operation on the affected nodes.

delete operations can then cause modification of freed memory.

most commonly leading to crashes in jbd2.

- Construct the 128-bit counter block (IV) for RFC 3686 CTR mode by:  
  • Copying the fixed nonce (ctx->nonce) into the first bytes of iv.  
  • Copying the per-request “IV” field (req->info), supplied by the caller, immediately after the nonce.  
  • Initializing the last 32-bit word of iv to 1 (the starting counter value) in big-endian form.  
- Prepare a subrequest on the child cipher:  
  • Point it to the child tfm,  
  • Propagate callback flags and completion data,  
  • Set source buffer, destination buffer, data length, and the constructed iv.  
- Invoke encryption on the child cipher with crypto_ablkcipher_encrypt(), returning its status.

- CTR mode (RFC 3686) provides confidentiality only; it does not provide integrity or authenticity. As a result, an attacker who can tamper with ciphertext can flip bits in the decrypted plaintext at predictable locations. This is inherent to CTR mode and is not addressed by this code.  
- Reuse of the same IV (the concatenation of ctx->nonce and req->info) with the same key leads to keystream reuse, which can completely break confidentiality. The code does not enforce uniqueness of req->info across calls; it relies on the caller to supply a unique per-request IV. Misuse by higher layers could lead to keystream reuse vulnerabilities.  
- There is no side-channel or buffer-overflow issue visible in the snippet: iv is a fixed-size stack buffer, memcpy sizes are constants, and subrequest context is aligned.  
- Endianness conversion and memory alignment are handled correctly; there is no obvious memory misalignment or type-punning bug.

3. Decision

No, the code itself contains no direct implementation flaw. It correctly implements RFC 3686 counter-mode encryption. Its security depends on not reusing IVs (ctx->nonce ∥ req->info) and on pairing CTR with an authentication mechanism if integrity is required.

original_information.commit_message:
perf/core: Fix concurrent sys_perf_event_open() vs. 'move_group' race

Di Shen reported a race between two concurrent sys_perf_event_open()
calls where both try and move the same pre-existing software group
into a hardware context.

The problem is exactly that described in commit:

  f63a8daa5812 ("perf: Fix event->ctx locking")

... where, while we wait for a ctx->mutex acquisition, the event->ctx
relation can have changed under us.

That very same commit failed to recognise sys_perf_event_context() as an
external access vector to the events and thereby didn't apply the
established locking rules correctly.

So while one sys_perf_event_open() call is stuck waiting on
mutex_lock_double(), the other (which owns said locks) moves the group
about. So by the time the former sys_perf_event_open() acquires the
locks, the context we've acquired is stale (and possibly dead).

Apply the established locking rules as per perf_event_ctx_lock_nested()
to the mutex_lock_double() for the 'move_group' case. This obviously means
we need to validate state after we acquire the locks.

original_information.commit_message:
KVM: x86: fix missing checks in syscall emulation

On hosts without this patch, 32bit guests will crash (and 64bit guests
may behave in a wrong way) for example by simply executing following
nasm-demo-application:

    [bits 32]
    global _start
    SECTION .text
    _start: syscall

(I tested it with winxp and linux - both always crashed)

    Disassembly of section .text:

    00000000 <_start>:
       0:   0f 05                   syscall

The reason seems a missing "invalid opcode"-trap (int6) for the
syscall opcode "0f05", which is not available on Intel CPUs
within non-longmodes, as also on some AMD CPUs within legacy-mode.
(depending on CPU vendor, MSR_EFER and cpuid)

Because previous mentioned OSs may not engage corresponding
syscall target-registers (STAR, LSTAR, CSTAR), they remain
NULL and (non trapping) syscalls are leading to multiple
faults and finally crashs.

Depending on the architecture (AMD or Intel) pretended by
guests, various checks according to vendor's documentation
are implemented to overcome the current issue and behave
like the CPUs physical counterparts.

[mtosatti: cleanup/beautify code]

Signed-off-by: Stephan Baerwolf <stephan.baerwolf@tu-ilmenau.de>

  g. If the track uses an external data reference (dref), open it via mov_open_dref (this may point sc->pb at another file/stream).  Otherwise sc->pb = the top-level pb.  
  h. For video tracks:  
     – Compute a sample_aspect_ratio if none was explicitly stored and the stored width/height don’t match the track width/height.  
     – Compute avg_frame_rate and r_frame_rate from the number of frames, track duration, and STTS data.  
  i. For certain codecs (H.261, H.263, H.264, MPEG-4), reset width/height to zero so that the decoder will probe SPS/VOP headers to pick them up.  
  j. Free per-track arrays that are no longer needed after index building (chunk_offsets, stsc_data, sample_sizes, keyframes, stts_data, stps_data).  

  In the end it returns 0 on success (or a negative AVERROR on allocation/IO failures, or 0 after logging a broken-header error).
